en: The Sages composed [the teachings] and the Worthies expounded them, whereby the Great Way was propagated. The Tathāgata preached and the Bodhisattvas commented upon it, whereby the Buddha-dharma flourished.
Yet, as for those who compose, expound, preach, and comment—whether they be sūtras, biographies, or the Piṭakas—[they all serve this purpose].
These serve as the fundamental canons, yet they cause students to gaze upon them like the vast ocean.

Mātr̥ceṭa of the Buddha-dharma composed the *Mahāyāna-śraddhotpāda-śāstra*, which first provides the breadth of returning to the truth and subsequently offers the conciseness of giving rise to faith. Nāgārjuna recorded the *Avataṃsaka-sūtra*, which first presents the detailed version of the superior text.

This is a brief excerpt from the later version of the text. It not only equalizes the flow of the teaching for those of sharp and dull faculties, but can also comprehensively unify the ultimate truth (*tathatā*) such that the holy and the ordinary are one.

This is precisely the intent behind the *Sūtra in Forty-two Sections* by Kāśyapa Mātanga and Dharmaratna. Indeed, following the auspicious dream of the Han Emperor, Dharmaratna was preaching the Dharma in Yuezhi.

Given the vastness of the Tripiṭaka and the breadth of the Five Vehicles, he selected forty-two chapters from among the twelve divisions of the scriptures to serve as the guiding principles for all schools and as a vessel for crossing over to the East. For those who perceive their nature and study the Way, this is "nature" (xing);
for those who recognize the source of their own mind, this is "phenomena" (xiang); and for those who contemplate spiritual awakening, it is "bodhi."
The Esoteric [School] is that which is secret. Chan is that which, without passing through the various stages, naturally honors the supreme.
As for the four true paths of non-action and non-conditioning, these are the schools of existence in the Lesser Vehicle and the school of emptiness in the Greater Vehicle.

That which, like the one true ground, is such that there is nothing not seen or known, is the Dharma-realm of the *Avataṃsaka* and the knowledge-and-vision of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*. As for the Vinaya School...
To cease evil and practice good is the way of the general teachings; to penetrate the profound principles of the Buddha is the way of the Pure Land school.
To unify and encompass all schools—could there be anything superior to this? Yunqi lectured on it but did not complete it; Fengshan annotated it but did not elaborate upon it in detail.
Now, the Dharma Master Ciyun Boting, acting as an envoy for the Buddhas and Patriarchs, has once again composed a commentary and sub-commentary to clarify its meaning.

Thus, it is like a pearl manifesting its colors; when the sections are divided, it is like light distinguishing their forms. Piercing the eyes to reveal the marrow, it unties the knots of attachment in this very moment.
I contemplate with deep reverence the profound sincerity and filial piety of our Emperor.
By the august decree of the Empress Dowager, the Tripitaka was to be carved and printed;
Prince Yù oversaw the matter, and all the high ministers assisted him. I, Qú, am one who has humbly participated therein.
Now, Dharma Master Bóting has published this commentary on the preface, which embodies [the imperial intent].

The Sage’s intention was to broaden the transformation [of beings]. This work is both that which our Confucians are capable of transmitting and that which the followers of Śākyamuni are capable of expounding.
How could I dare not compose a preface for it? May those who wish to reach the Buddha-land find a path from the shifting sands to the Pamir Mountains;
may those who hold up a blade of grass, upon reading this commentary and sub-commentary once, manifest the sixteen-foot golden body. This is the preface.
Preface to the Sub-commentary on the Sutra in Forty-two Sections, respectfully inscribed by Shao Taigu, Court Gentleman for Rectitude and Vice Director of the Bureau of Astronomy:
That the six realms of existence are considered mundane is due solely to desire; that the three vehicles are considered sacred is likewise [due to the absence thereof].
It is simply the Way. Therefore, by pursuing the Way one ascends; by indulging in desire one falls. Yet both the Way and desire arise from within our own minds.

When the mind contemplates the Way, the principle of the Way grows long and the passions of desire are extinguished. When the mind contemplates desire, the passions of desire become strong and the principle of the Way becomes weak.
Thus, one knows that these are but movements of thought within one's own mind; how could they not be recognized? I—

The Buddha appeared in the world for a great and significant purpose: to lead one to recognize one’s own mind, to penetrate the principle of the Buddha, to sever craving and desire, and to cultivate the path of practice.

It is through these that perfect enlightenment is first achieved, and the teachings of the Three Vehicles are then proclaimed. From the initial chanting at the Kukkutārāma, the obstacles of the two attachments were immediately emptied;
the source of the mind was pointed directly, and the nature of reality was extensively elucidated. The primary aim lies in attaining the Middle Way and maintaining the truth; be careful not to—

Through faith and intention, one employs contemplation; thereafter, the craving for desire dries up, and one attains the ultimate Way. When the mind-ground becomes clear and serene, one returns to that which is originally possessed.
This is precisely what this sutra teaches. Is its merit not indeed great? Although the sutra is magnificent, how can it be otherwise?
Since it was brought from the White Horse [Temple] in the Western Heaven and the *utpala* flower bloomed within the fire, [it has been transmitted by] Zhu Fahu and Dharmaratna. It is supreme.
It was translated first and stored by Emperor Ming of the Han dynasty in the stone chambers of the Lan Tai (Palace of Orchids).

Although the teachings of the Image-Dharma flourished during the Jin and Wei dynasties, those who were venerated and followed adhered to other dharma-gates; thus, this single scripture could not be disseminated.

From the Tang and Song dynasties down to the present, a fine manuscript has never been seen, nor has anyone ever been heard to have commented upon this chapter. It remains hidden away like a treasure in the sea-store of the Dragon Palace—is this not so?
How lamentable! Alas! The Tripitaka and the twelve divisions of the scriptures are all the words of the Buddha. They are like honey: both the center and the edges are sweet.
How can one take up the latter while neglecting the former, abandon the root to pursue the branches, and set aside this wondrous Dharma without discussion?
Though I wish to follow it, there has been no way to do so until now. Having recently obtained a fine edition among the books of the marketplace, I have therefore submitted it to Yunqi.
I have annotated this legacy of instruction word by word, following the thematic gateways of Master Xianshou and manifesting the lineage of our tradition.

My desire is that not even a single mote of dust or a single land should fail to be these Forty-two Chapters; that they may be severed spontaneously without being severed; and that the worlds as numerous as the sands of the Ganges may all be comprised within these five hundred-odd words.
When the Way is realized, it is realized spontaneously; thus, even if the physical form does not reach them, the locus of hearing and perfuming shall be exhausted.
This constitutes the formation of the Dharma-body. Should those of shallow wisdom fail to understand, even their moments of doubt and faith shall lead them to the Buddha-wisdom.
The light of Dharmaratna’s teaching still radiates today; the spiritual transformations of Kāśyapa Mātanga likewise manifest clearly to this day. This is the sincere intent behind this composition.
I have briefly set forth its fundamental purpose to inform all future readers. At this time.

The Sutra of Forty-two Sections Spoken by the Buddha.
Translated by the śramaṇas Kāśyapa Mātanga and Dharmaratna during the Later Han Dynasty.
The Initial Preface:
At that time, after the World-Honored One had attained the Way, he reflected thus: "Detachment from desire and tranquility are the most supreme."
Abiding in great meditative concentration, he subdued all paths of Māra. He was to turn the wheel of Dharma to deliver sentient beings;
thus, in the Deer Park, he turned the wheel of the Four Noble Truths, delivering the five men including Kauṇḍinya and causing them to realize the fruit of the Path.
Furthermore, there were bhikṣus who presented various doubts and sought the Buddha’s guidance. The World-Honored One instructed and exhorted them, awakening each one to understanding.
They joined their palms in respectful assent and followed his venerable commands.
II. The Main Body of the Teaching:
At that time, the World-Honored One preached the True Sutra in forty-two chapters.
Chapter One: Leaving Home and Realizing the Fruit.
The Buddha said: "One who leaves home to renounce kin, recognizes the mind and penetrates the root, and understands the dharma of non-action (asaṃskṛta), is called a śramaṇa.
Such a person should practice the two hundred and fifty precepts with purity in both conduct and demeanor, cultivate the four true paths of practice, and become an arhat.
An arhat is one who can fly and manifest transformations, possess a lifespan spanning vast kalpas, and cause heaven and earth to tremble at will. Next is the stage of an anāgāmin."
The Anāgāmin (Non-returner), at the end of his life, ascends to the nineteenth heaven and realizes arhatship.
Next is the Sakṛdāgāmin (Once-returner). The Sakṛdāgāmin goes up once and returns once more, then immediately attains arhatship. Next is the Srotāpanna (Stream-enterer).
The Srotāpanna undergoes seven deaths and seven births, and then realizes arhatship. One whose craving and desire are severed is like one whose four limbs have been cut off.
No longer using them. Chapter Two:
Reaching the Principle and Honoring the Way.

The Buddha said: "Those who have left the home life as śramaṇas sever desire and eliminate attachment; they recognize the source of their own minds, reach the profound principle of the Buddhas, and attain awakening."
As for unconditioned dharmas (*asaṃskṛta-dharma*): there is nothing to be attained within and nothing to be sought without. The mind is neither bound to the Way nor does it form karma.
Without thought and without action, it is neither cultivated nor realized. Without passing through the various stages, it is spontaneously supreme; this is what is called the Way.
Chapter Three: Severing Attachment and Taking Only What Is Sufficient.
The Buddha said: "One who shaves off beard and hair to become a śramaṇa and receives the Dharma of the Way must renounce worldly wealth and possessions, begging for food until satisfied.
Eating but one meal at midday and staying overnight beneath a tree—be careful not to exceed these limits. It is attachment that causes people to be deluded and obscured."
[This concerns] the granting of consent.

Regarding the fourth chapter on transforming evil into good, the Buddha said: "Sentient beings take ten matters as good, and they also take ten matters as evil. What are these ten? [The first is] the body..."

The three [evils] of body, four of speech, and three of mind: the three of body are killing, stealing, and sexual misconduct; the four of speech are double-tongued speech, harsh speech, false speech, and frivolous speech;
the three of mind are envy, malice, and delusion. These ten matters, which do not accord with the Noble Path, are called evil conduct (*duścarita*).
If these evils cease, they are simply called the ten wholesome actions. In the "Chapter on Reforming Faults and Extinguishing Transgressions," the Buddha said:
"If a person has many transgressions yet does not repent, and fails to suddenly still their mind, then sin will come upon them like water flowing toward the body."
It returns to the sea and gradually becomes deep and vast. If a person commits a transgression, they naturally understand their error, reform their evil ways, and practice goodness;
thus their offenses are spontaneously extinguished, just as a disease gradually subsides once one has broken out in sweat.
Chapter Six: Enduring Evil Without Anger.
The Buddha said: "If wicked people hear of your goodness and come to disturb you, you must restrain yourself and remain free from anger or reproach.
It is they who come as evildoers that are themselves evil; the aura of merit and virtue always resides within you."
Chapter Seven: Rebuking the Buddha and Invoking Calamity. The Buddha said:

"There are those who, having heard that I uphold the Way and practice great benevolence and compassion, proceed to revile the Buddha. The Buddha remains silent and does not respond, and thus the reviling ceases.
[The interlocutor] asked: "If you follow someone with courtesy and they do not accept it, does that courtesy return to you? He replied: "It returns to me."
The Buddha said: "Now you revile me, yet I do not accept it. You alone shall bear the calamity; it will return to your own person.
It is like an echo responding to a sound or a shadow following a form; there is ultimately no way to escape it. Be careful not to do evil."
Chapter Eight: On the Destruction of the Worthy by the Malevolent.
The Buddha said: "When a wicked person harms a worthy one, it is like looking up at the sky and spitting. The spittle does not defile the sky; it falls back upon oneself."
When dust is blown by a headwind, it does not reach its destination but instead returns to soil one's own body. A worthy person cannot be defamed;
misfortune will surely destroy oneself. Chapter Nine:

Guarding One’s Resolve to Attain the Way. The Buddha said: "Though one hears much and loves the Way, the Way is difficult to realize. Guard one’s resolve and serve the Way; that Way is exceedingly great."
Chapter Ten: On the Great Merit of Rejoicing in the Gift of Others.
The Buddha said: "When one sees another giving on the Path, to rejoice in their assistance brings forth exceedingly great merit. A śramaṇa asked: "Does this merit ever come to an end?
The Buddha said: "It is like a single torch; if hundreds or thousands of people each come with their own torch to take a portion from it [the fire does not diminish]."
Fire removes rawness so that food may be cooked and dispels darkness; yet this torch remains as it was before, and merit is likewise so.
Chapter Eleven: Comparing the Fields of Merit.
The Buddha said: "Feeding a hundred ordinary people is not as good as feeding one virtuous person; feeding a thousand virtuous persons is not as good as feeding one..."

Regarding those who uphold the five precepts: feeding ten thousand such persons is not equal to feeding one *srotāpanna*. Feeding one million *srotāpannas* is not equal to feeding one *sakṛdāgāmin*. Feeding ten million *sakṛdāgāmins* is not equal to feeding one *anāgāmin*. Feeding one hundred million *anāgāmins* is not equal to feeding one *arhat*. Feeding one billion *arhats*... [is not equal to feeding one... *pratyekabuddha*. Feeding ten billion *pratyekabuddhas* is not equal to feeding one *tathāgata*, arhat, samyaksaṃbuddha. Feeding ten trillion *tathāgatas*, arhats, samyaksaṃbuddhas is not equal to building a *stūpa* for a *tathāgata*, arhat, samyaksaṃbuddha. Building ten trillion *stūpas* for *tathāgatas*, arhats, samyaksaṃbuddhas is not equal to maintaining a single lamp within a *stūpa* for a *tathāgata*, arhat, samyaksaṃbuddha. Maintaining ten trillion lamps within *stūpas* for *tathāgatas*, arhats, samyaksaṃbuddhas is not equal to reciting a single verse of the Dharma within a *stūpa* for a *tathāgata*, arhat, samyaksaṃbuddha. Reciting ten trillion verses of the Dharma within *stūpas* for *tathāgatas*, arhats, samyaksaṃbuddhas is not equal to reciting a single phrase of the Dharma within a *stūpa* for a *tathāgata*, arhat, samyaksaṃbuddha. Reciting ten trillion phrases of the Dharma within *stūpas* for *tathāgatas*, arhats, samyaksaṃbuddhas is not equal to reciting a single word of the Dharma within a *stūpa* for a *tathāgata*, arhat, samyaksaṃbuddha. Reciting ten trillion words of the Dharma within *stūpas* for *tathāgatas*, arhats, samyaksaṃbuddhas is not equal to reciting a single syllable of the Dharma within a *stūpa* for a *tathāgata*, arhat, samyaksaṃbuddha. Reciting ten trillion syllables of the Dharma within *stūpas* for *tathāgatas*, arhats, samyaksaṃbuddhas is not equal to reciting a single letter of the Dharma within a *stūpa* for a *tathāgata*, arhat, samyaksaṃbuddha. Reciting ten trillion letters of the Dharma within *stūpas* for *tathāgatas*, arhats, samyaksaṃbuddhas is not equal to making a single prostration before a *stūpa* for a *tathāgata*, arhat, samyaksaṃbuddha. Making ten trillion prostrations before *stūpas* for *tathāgatas*, arhats, samyaksaṃbuddhas is not equal to making a single circumambulation around a *stūpa* for a *tathāgata*, arhat, samyaksaṃbuddha. Making ten trillion circumambulations around *stūpas* for *tathāgatas*, arhats, samyaksaṃbuddhas is not equal to making a single offering of incense before a *stūpa* for a *tathāgata*, arhat, samyaksaṃbuddha. Making ten trillion offerings of incense before *stūpas* for *tathāgatas*, arhats, samyaksaṃbuddhas is not equal to making a single offering of flowers before a *stūpa* for a *tathāgata*, arhat, samyaksaṃbuddha. Making ten trillion offerings of flowers before *stūpas* for *tathāgatas*, arhats, samyaksaṃbuddhas is not equal to making a single offering of garlands before a *stūpa* for a *tathāgata*, arhat, samyaksaṃbuddha. Making ten trillion offerings of garlands before *stūpas* for *tathāgatas*, arhats, samyaksaṃbuddhas is not equal to making a single offering of perfumes before a *stūpa* for a *tathāgata*, arhat, samyaksaṃbuddha. Making ten trillion offerings of perfumes before *stūpas* for *tathāgatas*, arhats, samyaksaṃbuddhas is not equal to making a single offering of lamps before a *stūpa* for a *tathāgata*, arhat, samyaksaṃbuddha. Making ten trillion offerings of lamps before *stūpas* for *tathāgatas*, arhats, samyaksaṃbuddhas is not equal to making a single offering of music before a *stūpa* for a *tathāgata*, arhat, samyaksaṃbuddha. Making ten trillion offerings of music before *stūpas* for *tathāgatas*, arhats, samyaksaṃbuddhas is not equal to making a single offering of robes before a *stūpa* for a *tathāgata*, arhat, samyaksaṃbuddha. Making ten trillion offerings of robes before *stūpas* for *tathāgatas*, arhats, samyaksaṃbuddhas is not equal to making a single offering of food before a *stūpa* for a *tathāgata*, arhat, samyaksaṃbuddha. Making ten trillion offerings of food before *stūpas* for *tathāgatas*, arhats, samyaksaṃbuddhas is not equal to making a single offering of bedding before a *stūpa* for a *tathāgata*, arhat, samyaksaṃbuddha. Making ten trillion offerings of bedding before *stūpas* for *tathāgatas*, arhats, samyaksaṃbuddhas is not equal to making a single offering of medicine before a *stūpa* for a *tathāgata*, arhat, samyaksaṃbuddha. Making ten trillion offerings of medicine before *stūpas* for *tathāgatas*, arhats, samyaksaṃbuddhas is not equal to making a single offering of a canopy before a *stūpa* for a *tathāgata*, arhat, samyaksaṃbuddha. Making ten trillion offerings of canopies before *stūpas* for *tathāgatas*, arhats, samyaksaṃbuddhas is not equal to making a single offering of a parasol before a *stūpa* for a *tathāgata*, arhat, samyaksaṃbuddha. Making ten trillion offerings of parasols before *stūpas* for *tathāgatas*, arhats, samyaksaṃbuddhas is not equal to making a single offering of a banner before a *stūpa* for a *tathāgata*, arhat, samyaksaṃbuddha. Making ten trillion offerings of banners before *stūpas* for *tathāgatas*, arhats, samyaksaṃbuddhas is not equal to making a single offering of a flag before a *stūpa* for a *tathāgata*, arhat, samyaksaṃbuddha. An arhat is not equal to one who feeds a single pratyekabuddha; feeding ten billion pratyekabuddhas is not equal to feeding a single Buddha of the three periods of time;
feeding a thousand billion Buddhas of the three periods of time is not equal to feeding one who is without thought, without dwelling, without cultivation, and without realization.
The Buddha spoke in the "Twelfth Chapter on the Manifestation of Filial Piety":
"In all matters of humans serving Heaven, Earth, and the spirits, none is equal to being filial toward one's two parents; for one's two parents are the supreme deities."
Chapter Thirteen: Detailed Discussion on the Difficulty of Exerting Effort in Practice.

The Buddha said: "There are twenty difficulties for human beings. It is difficult to practice giving when one is poor; it is difficult to study the Way when one is wealthy and noble; it is difficult to renounce life when facing certain death;

it is difficult to encounter the Buddhist scriptures; it is difficult to be born during the era of a Buddha; it is difficult to endure the passions and remain free from desire; it is difficult to see what is beautiful..."

It is difficult to seek [the Way]. It is difficult not to confront calamities when one possesses power. It is difficult not to harbor anger when insulted. It is difficult to remain free from mental attachment amidst all affairs. It is difficult to study extensively and investigate deeply.

It is difficult not to look down upon those who have not yet studied. It is difficult to eliminate the pride of "I" (asmimāna). It is difficult for the mind’s actions to be impartial. It is difficult not to speak of right or wrong. It is difficult to encounter virtuous friends (kalyāṇamitra).
It is difficult to see one's nature and study the Path. It is difficult to follow along with and transform others. It is difficult not to [be disturbed] when facing external objects...
Difficult to move; difficult to skillfully understand the means.
Chapter Fourteen: On Guarding and Guiding the Pure Livelihood.
A śramaṇa asked the Buddha: "By what causes and conditions can one know past lives and realize the ultimate Way? The Buddha said: "It is through a pure mind."

One who guards their resolve may attain the Ultimate Way. It is like polishing a mirror: when the grime is removed, the brightness remains. By severing desire and seeking nothing, one shall obtain the knowledge of past lives.
Chapter Fifteen: Practicing Goodness with Great Resolve.
A śramaṇa asked the Buddha, "What is good? What is greatest? The Buddha said, "To practice the Way and maintain the truth is good;
for one's will to be in accord with the Way is greatest."

In the sixteenth chapter on the Heart-Mantra of the Power of Patience, a śramaṇa asked the Buddha: "What possesses great power? What is most luminous? The Buddha replied: "Patience possesses great power because it harbors no malice;

furthermore, it brings peace and health. One who practices patience is free from evil and will surely become honored among men. When the defilements of the mind are extinguished, there is no longer any stain."

Free from all blemish and impurity, this is the ultimate clarity. From the time before heaven and earth until this very day, throughout the ten directions, there is nothing that is not seen, nothing that is not known, and nothing that is not heard.
Having attained all-encompassing wisdom (*sarvajñatā*), it may truly be called clear.
Chapter Seventeen: Clarifying Turbidity and Seeing the Path. The Buddha said:
"If people harbor craving and desire, they do not see the Path. It is like clear water that one tries to grasp with the hand while many people stand together looking down into it;
none of them can see their own reflection. Because people’s minds are turbid due to the intermingling of craving and desire, they do not see it."
The Seeing of the Path. "You, śramaṇas, should abandon craving. When the defilement of craving is exhausted, the Path can be seen.

In the Eighteenth Chapter on the Extinction of Darkness and the Preservation of Light, the Buddha said: "Now, as for the seeing of the Path, it is like holding a torch and entering a dark room; the darkness is immediately extinguished and light appears."
It exists alone. When one studies the Way and perceives the Truth, ignorance is immediately extinguished and clarity remains forever.
Chapter Nineteen: The Meeting with Reality through Signlessness. The Buddha said:

"In my Dharma, there is mindfulness without the thought of mindfulness; practice without the act of practicing; speech without the utterance of speech; and cultivation without the act of cultivating."

Those who realize it are near; those who are deluded are far. The path of language is severed, and one is not constrained by material things. To err by even a hair’s breadth is to lose it in an instant.
Chapter Twenty: Awakening through Contemplation.
The Buddha said: "Contemplate heaven and earth and perceive their impermanence; contemplate the world and perceive its impermanence; contemplate the numinous awareness and realize it is bodhi."
One who understands this will attain the Way swiftly.
Chapter Twenty-one: On the Deduction that the Self is Empty.
The Buddha said: "You should contemplate that within the body, the four great elements each have their own names, yet none possess a self. Since the self is entirely non-existent,"
"It is merely like an illusion.
Chapter Twenty-Two: Seeking Fame at the Risk of One's Life.
The Buddha said: "When people follow their passions and seek fame and reputation, by the time that fame becomes prominent, the body has already perished. They are greedy for the world..."
To be known for one's constancy yet not study the Way is to squander one’s efforts and exhaust one’s body. It is like burning incense:
although people smell the fragrance, the incense itself has already been consumed; the fire that endangers the person remains behind.
Chapter Twenty-three: Greed for Wealth Brings Suffering.
The Buddha said: "Wealth and sensual beauty are such that people cannot abandon them. It is like a blade of grass smeared with honey;
it does not suffice for even a single meal’s pleasure, yet if a child licks it, he suffers the calamity of having his tongue cut."
In the twenty-fourth chapter, "Tying One's Wife and Drowning in Mud," the Buddha said:
"A person being bound by their wife, children, and home is worse than being in prison. While there is a time for release from prison,"
Wives and children harbor no thought of separation; they are emotionally attached to sensual forms. How could they weary of being driven about?

Even when faced with the peril of a tiger’s maw, their hearts remain contentedly submissive. They cast themselves into the mud and drown themselves; therefore, they are called "ordinary persons" (*pṛthagjana*). One who penetrates this gate is an Arhat who has transcended the mundane world.
Chapter Twenty-Five: Losing the Way through Attachment to Form. The Buddha said:
"There is no desire more extreme than that for form. As for this desire for form, it is so vast that there is nothing outside of it; yet, fortunately, it is but one."
If these two were identical, then no person throughout the world would be able to practice the Way.
Chapter Twenty-Six: On Diminishing the Way and Increasing [Worldly Gain].
The Buddha said: "A person driven by desire is like one holding a torch while walking against the wind; there will inevitably be the calamity of burning one's hand."
A celestial deity presented a jade maiden to the Buddha, intending to corrupt his resolve. The Buddha said, "A leather bag filled with manifold impurities—what have you come here for?

Depart; I have no need of you. The deity’s reverence increased all the more, and he consequently asked about the meaning of the Path. The Buddha explained it for him, and the deity immediately attained the fruit of *srotāpanna*.
Chapter Twenty-seven: Moving Against the Current and Following Nature. The Buddha said:
"Now, one who practices the Way is like a piece of wood floating in water, moving along with the current. It does not strike either bank; it is not taken by people;
it is not obstructed by ghosts or spirits; it is not held back by eddies; nor does it rot. Of this, I am certain."

This wood will certainly enter the sea. A person who studies the Way, who is not deluded by sensual desires and not disturbed by various evils, and who practices diligence with non-action—I guarantee that such a person will surely attain the Way.
Chapter Twenty-Eight: On the Distant Mind and Form. The Buddha said:
"Be careful not to trust your mind; your mind is not to be trusted. Be careful not to associate with form;
from association with form, calamity arises. Only after you have attained arhatship may you trust your mind."
Chapter Twenty-nine: Waiting for a Woman with Right Mindfulness.
The Buddha said: "Be careful not to look at the beauty of women, nor speak with them. If you must speak with one, do so with a mind fixed in right mindfulness."
I am a śramaṇa dwelling in this turbid world; I should be like a lotus flower, unsullied by the mud.

I should regard the elderly as my mother, the older women as my elder sisters, the younger women as my younger sisters, and the children as my own sons. One should contemplate with clarity: what is there in that body?
It is merely exposed filth and impurity, filled with all manner of unclean things. Thus, one should give rise to the mind of liberation and extinguish evil thoughts.
Chapter on the Thirty Paths for Avoiding Desire.

The Buddha said: "Now, one who practices the Way is like dry grass; when fire approaches, it must be avoided. When a practitioner of the Way encounters desire, he must certainly distance himself from it."
Chapter Thirty-one: On Severing the Mind Afflicted by Lust. The Buddha said:
"There is a person whose affliction with lust does not cease, and he wishes to remove his own genitals himself. The Buddha said to him: "If you were to cause the genitals to be severed..."
"It is better to sever the mind. The mind is like an official (gōngcáo); if the official stops, his followers all cease.
If the deviant mind does not stop, what benefit is there in severing the aggregates? The Buddha spoke this verse: "Desire arises within your mind; The mind arises through conceptualization.
When both minds are each stilled, It is neither form nor mental formations. The Buddha said, "This verse was spoken by Kāśyapa Buddha."
Chapter Thirty-Two: On Severing Attachment and Eliminating Sorrow.
The Buddha said: "From attachment and desire, sorrow arises; from sorrow, fear arises. If one is free from attachment, what sorrow and what fear can there be?"
Chapter Thirty-Three: Attaining the Fruit through Resolute Mind. The Buddha said:
"Now, one who practices the Way is like a single person going out to battle ten thousand men. Clad in armor, he may depart with a mind that is timid and weak;
or he may retreat halfway; or he may die in the fray. Yet, if his mind is free from fear, he may emerge victorious."
Return! A śramaṇa who studies the Way should firmly maintain his mind, be diligent and courageous, not fear the objects before him, and destroy all demons to attain the fruit of the Way.

Among the thirty-four places [of practice], in the Chapter on Realizing the Principle, a śramaṇa was reciting the *Kāśyapa-buddha-śāsana-sūtra* at night. His voice was mournful and strained; he was filled with remorse and wished to withdraw.
The Buddha asked him, "When you were formerly a householder, what profession did you follow? He replied, "I loved playing the lute. The Buddha said, "If the strings of a lute are too slack..."
"What? he asked. He replied, "It does not sound. "What if the strings are too tight? He replied, "The sound is cut off. "What if they are adjusted to the middle between tight and loose?
He replied, "All the notes will be harmoniously tuned. The Buddha said, "It is the same for a śramaṇa practicing the Way.
If the mind is well-adjusted, the Way can be attained. If one is violent toward the Way, one becomes exhausted; if the body is exhausted, the mind gives rise to affliction. The mind...
If one gives rise to vexation, one's practice will immediately regress. Once practice has regressed, retribution for transgressions will inevitably be added.
Only the path of pure and peaceful bliss shall not be lost.
Chapter Thirty-Five: Removing Defilements to Accomplish Practice.
The Buddha said: "It is like a person forging iron; by removing the dross, it is formed into a vessel, and the vessel becomes refined and excellent. So too for one who studies the Way:
by removing the defilements of the mind, their conduct becomes pure."
Chapter Thirty-Six: On Raising the Victory and Manifesting the Standard. The Buddha said:
"It is difficult for a person to escape the evil realms and obtain human birth. Having obtained human birth, it is difficult to be male rather than female.

Having obtained male status, it is difficult for the six sense faculties to be complete. Once the six faculties are complete, it is difficult to be born in a central land. Having been born in a central land,"
It is difficult to encounter the era of a Buddha. Having encountered the era of a Buddha, it is difficult to meet with the Way. Having met with the Way, it is difficult to give rise to faith.
Having given rise to faith, it is difficult to resolve upon the Bodhicitta. Having resolved upon the Bodhicitta, it is difficult to practice without cultivation and realize without attainment.
Chapter on the Fruit Attained by Recalling the Precepts Thirty-Seven:
The Buddha said, "O Son of the Buddha, even if you are thousands of li away from me, if you recollect my precepts, you will certainly attain the fruit of the Way.
Even if you are at my side and see me constantly, if you do not comply with my precepts, you will ultimately not attain the Way."
Chapter Thirty-Eight: Knowing Life and Realizing the Way.
The Buddha asked a śramaṇa, "In what interval does human life reside? He replied, "For a matter of days. The Buddha said, "My son, you do not yet know the Way."
He again asked another śramaṇa: "In what interval does a person's life reside? He replied: "In the interval of a meal. The Buddha said: "My son, you do not yet know the Way.
He again asked another śramaṇa: "In what interval does a person's life reside? He replied: "In the interval of a single breath. The Buddha said: "Excellent!"
"You understand this, my son. Chapter Thirty-nine:
On Learning the Buddha-Dharma and Believing the Sutras.
The Buddha said: "Those who study the path of the Buddha should believe and accord with everything the Buddha has spoken. It is like eating honey; [it is sweet] from the center to the edges."
All are sweet. My sutras are likewise; their meanings are all delightful, and the practitioner thereby attains the Way.
Chapter Forty: The Exhaustion of Evil.
In the "Perfect Enlightenment" chapter, the Buddha said: "When a śramaṇa practices the Way, he should gradually uproot the roots of craving and desire. It is like one who plucks hanging pearls."
If one plucks them one by one, there will come a time when they are exhausted; when evil is exhausted, one naturally attains the Way.
Chapter Forty-one: On Seeking Escape from Suffering. The Buddha said:
"Now, those who practice the Way are like an ox carrying a heavy load walking through deep mud; utterly exhausted, it does not dare move to the left or right."
Looking back and around, one may find relief only by emerging from the mire. A śramaṇa should contemplate that sensual desire is more treacherous than mud;
by maintaining a straightforward mind and focusing on the Way, one may escape suffering.
Chapter Forty-Two: Viewing Phenomena as Illusions.
The Buddha said: "I view the rank of kings and lords as a speck of dust passing before my eyes; I view treasures of gold and jade as mere shards and pebbles."
One views garments of fine silk as worn-out rags; one views the great trichiliocosm as a single *kośāmbi* fruit; one views the waters of Lake Anavatapta as oil for anointing the feet;
one views the gates of skillful means as a heap of conjured jewels; one views the Unsurpassed Vehicle as gold and silks in a dream;
one views the Buddha-way as flowers before one's eyes; one views meditative concentration as a pillar of Mount Sumeru; and one views *nirvāṇa* as...

Awakened day and night, he views the inverted as upright, like the dance of the six dragons; he views equality as the single true ground; he views the flourishing of transformation as the trees of the four seasons.
This concludes the third circulation.
The great bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha had spoken, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.

Regarding the first cause for the teaching: it means that the appearance of the Tathāgata does not occur through a single condition nor by a single matter.
For example, Sumeru, the King of Mountains, cannot be made to tremble without cause or by minor matters. The emergence of this present sutra is likewise so; it possesses many causes and conditions.
First, it is because he wishes to cause those living at home to reform their errors and turn toward goodness. Second...
1. To cause those who have left the household life to swiftly transcend birth and death; 2. To cause those of the provisional vehicles not to be deluded regarding the perfect reality;
3. To cause them to sever the root of desire, craving, and saṃsāra; 4. To contemplate that the realm of objects is impermanent, suffering, and empty; 5.
To cause them to awaken to the fact that the faculties and the body are non-self and impure; 6. To demonstrate the cultivation of all... [the text continues].

1. Because one practices non-empty tranquility; 2. Because one desires to know that illusions are empty so as not to cling to the marks of phenomena; 3. Because one desires to clarify the nature of the mind and realize the profound principle of the Buddha; 4. Because one desires to maintain true permanence and swiftly attain the fruit of the Way; 5. Because one desires to sever the bonds of afflictions and transcend the world of birth and death;

6. Because one desires to cultivate the path of the Bodhisattvas and benefit all sentient beings; 7. Because one desires to enter the stage of non-retrogression and never again fall back; 8. The passage beginning with "For example" from the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* uses a metaphor to corroborate the aforementioned teaching; "Now, below" provides the application to the present case. First, the sequence.
It is distinct. Before the Buddha appeared in the world, ordinary people committed various heinous acts, while non-Buddhists gave rise to various false views.
They were deluded regarding the six sense objects and sank into the four realms of existence; they were entangled by the five hindrances and submerged beneath the three miserable paths.

When the Buddha descended as a spirit and preached this wondrous scripture, he was able to cause ordinary people and non-Buddhists not to give rise to deviance or error, and their transgressions were extinguished.
“Merit-born” means being free from suffering and attaining happiness. It says below: “Sentient beings take ten matters as good and also take ten matters as evil.

it is difficult not to speak of right and wrong. Patience possesses great power because one harbors no malice. One who is patient has no evil and will surely become a person of virtue.”

those of the provisional vehicles refer to those of the Three Vehicles and Five Vehicles. Before hearing this sutra, the Bodhisattvas would regress from the Great Vehicle and turn toward...

From this, one knows that for those who seek enlightenment through the provisional teachings of the five vehicles, none surpass this sutra. "Four [types of birth] below": All sentient beings establish their very life and nature through lustful desire.
Therefore, desire is the root of saṃsāra. As the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* says: "The bonds of thought and craving are joined together."
Because love cannot be severed, the succession of parents and children throughout all worlds continues without end; these are rooted in desire and greed.
The *Daśabhūmika-vibhaṅga-sūtra* states: "At that time, there were four hundred million beings in the assembly."
One knows for oneself that birth here and death there continue in an unbroken succession; this is the source of desire.

Now, in expounding this sutra, it is clarified from beginning to end that severing craving, abandoning desire, removing lust, and distancing oneself from form are the foundations for attaining liberation.
If the heart of craving is not eliminated, one cannot escape the defilements. As it says below: "Be careful not to look upon female forms, nor even converse with them. Furthermore:

It says: "One should contemplate that sensual desire is even more [filthy] than mud" (there are nineteen such sections in total). Section five below states: "The objects of the six sense-fields are like illusions, bubbles, and shadows.
The triple world is a house on fire, where the eight sufferings burn together. Ordinary people and non-Buddhists do not realize this;

they cling to it as true, eternal, and blissful, thereby giving rise to various delusions and karmic actions, revolving without ceasing. Therefore, this sutra is taught to cause them to awaken to impermanence. As stated below:
He contemplates that heaven and earth are impermanent, and that the world is impermanent (20b). Furthermore, it is said:
he regards the royal throne as a speck of dust in a crevice, precious jewels as shards of tile, fine silk as tattered rags, and the flourishing of transformation as the four seasons (42b).
The *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra* states: "The forms he perceives are like those seen by the blind; the sounds he hears are like echoes; the fragrances he smells are like the wind."

One does not discriminate among the flavors of food one eats; one experiences all tactile sensations as if through the realization of wisdom; and one contemplates all phenomena as being like illusions and transformations.
The *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* says: "Seeing and hearing are like illusory cataracts; the three realms are like flowers in the sky. The *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* says:

"Those who abide in the samādhi of dreams realize that the world is entirely like a dream. Thus, since the realms of dust and suffering are empty, how could they be worth craving or clinging to? (End of Section Six, Part One)
Every part of the male and female body possesses immeasurable faults and afflictions. One is perpetually bound by the fetters of the prison of desire.
One is constantly devoured by various worms within a pit of stench and filth. Like a walking latrine, it is impure in five ways;
like a leaking sack, its nine orifices flow incessantly. The venomous snake of anger gives rise to a harmful mind that destroys wisdom.
Life is like a foolish rākṣasa that seizes the view of self to devour the body of wisdom;
it is as unsubstantial as a plantain tree or a bubble on water, as impermanent as a flame, a shadow, or a flash of lightning. Though one nourishes and swallows it, it instead becomes an enemy;
though one constantly nurtures it, it knows no gratitude. It is loathed by the whole world like a wicked thief, and regarded by the wise alike as a dead dog.

Abandon it! Alas, how is it that all deluded beings, since beginningless time, have clung to this body as "self"? Because they treasure this self, they greedily seek fame and profit to bring glory and benefit to it;
they harbor resentment when things oppose their wishes, fearing they will harm or diminish it. They engage in irrational calculations that continue in an endless succession.
If one can constantly contemplate that this body is fundamentally without self and impure, then the three poisons will naturally [subside].
"Extinction" means that the three realms are naturally detached from it. As stated below: "One should contemplate that the four great elements within the body are without self" (Chapter 21).
Furthermore, there are those who lust after women's beauty, yet they do not realize that silken robes merely cover a sack of pus, and brocade quilts merely conceal a bucket of excrement and urine.
They pin fragrant flowers upon a head reeking of stench, and fasten musk sachets to the side of a stinking skin-bag. Outwardly...

Coated with artificial powder, its interior is merely a swarm of worms. Like a fish-sauce stall or a latrine hole, filled with dung-balls and sores, it is like a painted vase containing much pus, blood, excrement, and filth.
It is also like a tree in the Śītavana cemetery of the Western Regions:
its fruit appears as bright white as a newborn infant, yet in an instant it falls to the ground, bloating, rotting, and becoming foul-smelling and filthy. Such is the female body.
It is the same. Foul-smelling, rank, and filthy—how can you deluded and ignorant Chinese still flaunt your "refined elegance"?
It is like a latrine worm delighting in excrement; it is like a dull-witted man giving rise to perverted views; it is like a blue fly chasing after stench.
You seek fleeting pleasure before your eyes, failing to realize that after death you will suffer retribution for many kalpas. Even if your wife and children...
Alas, there is no way to save you. Even if your own flesh and blood were to fill the space before you, who could take your place?
The Buddha preached this sutra to cause one to leave behind female form. No affliction is more urgent than having a body; no suffering is more severe than having desire.
Therefore, when seeing the bodies of women, one should regard them as bags of excrement, walking latrines, sacks of pus, and nests of worms—foul sores and impurities.
The contemplation on a vessel of fire, a flower with arrows, a bottomless dry well, shackles and fetters, the bloated corpse of one afflicted by consumption, abscesses, and poison;
the contemplation on a skull and skeleton-chain being burned by fire and reduced to dust, and so forth.
If one can practice in this manner, one will naturally transcend the five desires and realize the four fruits of the path. As it says below: "Do not abandon [the perception of] form as it is..."
Honey upon a blade; the affliction of having one’s tongue cut (23). It is also said: Being bound by wife and children is worse than prison;
attachment to sensual forms leads one to cast oneself into the mud and drown (24). One is unable to practice the Way (25). Holding a torch and burning one’s hand (26).
Calamities and misfortunes arising unexpectedly (28). Various anxieties and fears (32), and so forth. This is [the state of] non-existence.

Regarding those of the two vehicles who dwell in partial emptiness, they now uphold the sevenfold precepts and advance upon the Four Noble Truths:

(1) contentment, (2) practicing the three kinds of goodness, (3) repentance, (4) filial piety toward one’s parents, (5) [the precept of] not drinking intoxicants, (6) clear great power, (7–12) the extinction of various māras, (13) generating the bodhicitta, and (14–15) skillful means for transforming and delivering others. This is precisely what it means to enter the Mahāyāna.

The eight consciousnesses, the sense organs, the physical body, and the objective world—undergoing myriad transformations through arising and ceasing—are all like the reflection of the moon in water or the shimmering light of flowers in the sky.
The Sage, knowing these to be illusory and false, possesses no mind of grasping or rejecting; thus, he is at ease wherever he goes and attains great peace and happiness.
Ordinary people, however, cling to these as real; their passions of love, hatred, grasping, and rejecting blaze forth intensely. Because of this...
Delusion gives rise to karma; because of karma, one undergoes suffering. All of this stems solely from an inability to recognize and penetrate [the truth].
It is like two people looking at the moon reflected in water: the fool falsely claims it is the real moon and attempts to grasp it, exhausting himself with toil and distress;
the wise person understands it to be illusory and remains seated with hands in his sleeves, happy and at ease. As the *Yongjia ji* says:
When the mind corresponds with emptiness, what anxiety is there in revilement or praise, and what joy in commendation?

When the body corresponds with emptiness, what suffering is there in being cut by a blade or smeared with fragrance, and what pleasure? When the conditioned environment corresponds with emptiness, what gain is there in giving or what loss in plundering?
Now the teaching arises precisely to bring knowledge of illusion: to illuminate with *prajñā* that the five aggregates are all empty. This is the assembly.
Since the color of foam is already void, what existence can there be for the receptacle of a water bubble? The perception of a mirage is not real; the nature of the plantain tree is merely empty.
Illusory consciousness flickers away without support. When the great element of space is profound and motionless, one exhausts the root of the four great elements.

If even their essential nature and characteristics do not exist, how could the branches, twigs, shadows, or echoes of the six sense faculties possibly exist? Since the view of a self-body does not [exist]...

Established thus, false objects have no source. Reason reaches its limit here: both person and phenomena are empty. Seeing that within the five aggregates there is no sovereign master is the wisdom of the emptiness of the person (*pudgala-śūnyatā-prajñā*).
Seeing that the six sense faculties are all like illusions and transformations is the wisdom of the emptiness of phenomena (*dharma-śūnyatā-prajñā*).
The text below states: "Internally there is nothing to be attained; externally there is nothing to be sought" (Section 2). "In contact with affairs there is no mind;
facing objects there is no movement" (13). "Thought is without successive thoughts; action is without successive actions" (19). "There is no cultivation and no realization" (36).

"Like a transformation, like a dream," etc. (42). [Section] 9, Part B: This mind is the dwelling-place of ordinary beings and sages, the source of sense-faculties and objects. The ignorant and deluded cling to it...
When it functions as the *ālaya-vijñāna*, it becomes the cause of the suffering of birth and death;

when the sages realize it as the *tathāgatagarbha-citta*, they receive the fruit of the eternal bliss of *nirvāṇa*. Sentient beings, however, cling to their own habitual inclinations with such intensity that they do not believe in the existence of the *tathāgatagarbha*.
Moment by moment, they remain oblivious to the nature of the *tathāgata-dharmadhātu*; step by step, they create the causes for the karmic fruits of sentient beings.
Evil karma increases daily; the conditions for suffering are inexhaustible. Within a state of security, they give rise to a mind of decline and affliction;
within liberation, they produce the fruit of bondage. They receive bodies with flaming mouths and needle-like throats, where the fires of hunger burn them throughout kalpas.

They take on bodies with fur and horns; at every turn they are ensnared and bound by nets. Some fall into the Avīci Hell, where they embrace intense suffering and dwell eternally amidst wheels of fire.
Others are born in the palaces of the asuras, where they incite strife and combat, and swords and blades rain down constantly.
Some briefly inhabit the human realm, where in a single kṣaṇa they are tormented by the convergence of the eight sufferings. Or they happen to reside in celestial palaces.
In an instant, one falls into the five signs of decay and sinks forever into the three obstructions, never emerging from the four maras;

all this is because one fails to know the *tathāgatagarbha* mind, loses the wondrous nature of *vijñaptimātratā*, turns one’s back on the True Father, and hires oneself out in foreign lands, abandoning the Great Wisdom King to seek refuge in other kingdoms.
For this reason, the Buddhas are startled and enter the burning house to preach the teachings of the Three Vehicles.

To guide sentient beings toward transcendence from the triple world, the method for awakening lies solely in clarifying the mind. The mind has degrees of magnitude, and its underlying principle has levels of depth.
By clarifying the nature of the six consciousnesses and realizing the principle of True Suchness as the emptiness of self, one achieves the fruits of the Hīnayāna teachings.

By clarifying the nature of the eight consciousnesses and realizing the principle of True Suchness as the emptiness of phenomena, one achieves the fruits of the Mahāyāna *paryāya* (partial) teachings.
Clarifying the mind-nature of non-arising, one penetrates the principle of the True Suchness of the two-fold emptiness and achieves the fruit of the Initial Teaching of the Mahāyāna.

Clarifying the mind-nature of the Tathāgatagarbha, one penetrates the principle of the True Suchness that is not empty of what is expressed by words and achieves the fruit of the Final, Ultimate Teaching of the Mahāyāna.

By clarifying the mind-nature of the wisdom that realizes its own enlightened realm, one attains the fruit of the Sudden Teaching of the One Vehicle through penetrating the principle of ineffable *tathatā*.

By clarifying the perfectly interfused and inexhaustible mind, one attains the fruit of the Perfect Teaching of the One Vehicle through penetrating the principle of the *tathatā* of the single true *dharmadhātu*.
When this rational nature is thus unified, one can naturally proceed from the state of an ordinary person to perfect, wondrous enlightenment. As it says below:
The conscious mind reaches the source (Chapter 1). It penetrates the profound principle of the Buddha (Chapter 2). Observing that numinous awareness is itself bodhi (within Chapter 20).
It is further said: "The mind is like a minister" (within Chapter 31). When studying the Way, one should firmly maintain the mind (within Chapter 33).

If the mind is harmonized and balanced, the Way can be attained (within Chapter 34). [Ten strokes below: All sensory objects arise from the transformations of consciousness; they have no [independent existence].
All phenomena arise in accordance with conceptualization; apart from consciousness there are no objects, and apart from conceptualization there are no dharmas.
To understand this clearly and penetrate it suddenly is to realize one’s former errors: the stump seen as a ghost is empty, and the fly is the disappearance of the thought of a snake.

One will never again wait for the flowers in the sky to bear fruit, nor attempt to take hold of objects within a dream to store them securely. Thus, one enters into tranquil contemplation of the void.
The lapel [of this robe] is like the soaring wings of a bird gliding through the void; nurturing one's nature according to conditions is like a hollow boat drifting with the waves.
Exhausting the old without creating the new, one accords with reality and merges with the Way. Thus, the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* says:

"Because sentient beings, from time immemorial, have followed after forms and sounds, pursuing thoughts in their constant flux, they have never awakened to the pure, wondrous, and eternal nature of their own essence. They do not follow...
