The drifting boat and so forth: now suffering and its accumulation descend, while cessation and the path ascend; their natures are each determined—this is *dhṛti* (sustenance).
Suffering and accumulation constitute the ordinary person, while cessation and the path constitute the sage; karma itself differentiates them—this is *viniyoga* (function).

As for "truly pervading the three times," it is because the two sevens and the three sevens are not separately set forth. Regarding "six encompassing five": first, the Flower Garland Assembly (*Avataṃsaka-sūtra*) illuminates [the matter] beforehand.

At that time, having departed from the cravings for the ten unspeakable dharmas, and being preeminent in the unobstructed dharma of nirvana, he dwells in the meditative contemplation of the dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*).
He subdues the ten inexhaustible māras, turns the fundamental wheel, and delivers those sentient beings whose faculties are matured through the sudden and perfect [teachings].

Next, contemplate the time when the *Āgama* assembly first turned the light: it was free from the passions of outflow (*āsrava*), characterized by the wondrous Dharma of quiescent, exclusive emptiness and *nirvāṇa*;
it dwelt in the contemplation of the conditions of the Truths (*satya*) and meditative absorption (*dhyāna*); it subdued the four Māras within the realms;

and it turned the wheel of the Dharma of the Lesser Vehicle (*hīnayāna*) to deliver ordinary beings and non-Buddhists among gods and humans. Then, contemplate the time when the *Saṃdhinirmocana* assembly turned the light: it was free from the desire for even the outflow-free Dharma (*anāsrava*).
Dwelling in the supreme realm of quiescent non-abiding nirvana, one abides in the dhyāna-contemplation of *vijñapti-mātra*.
One subdues the four māras beyond the realms and turns the Dharma wheel of the three vehicles, delivering those of the two vehicles who cling to inferior teachings.

When the time comes for the wondrous wisdom to subsequently illuminate, one becomes detached from the marks of all out-flowing and non-out-flowing phenomena, abiding in the dhyāna of true emptiness within the supreme realm of signless, tranquil nirvana.

Contemplation: Subduing the demons who grasp at the characteristics of phenomena within and without the realms; turning the Dharma wheel of the One Vehicle to deliver those of the provisional teachings of the Three Vehicles;

and when the three reflections of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* and *Nirvāṇa* assemblies shine forth once more, one leaves behind the dispositions of all phenomena, whether with outflows or without outflows, and dwells in the dhyāna of the true mark of all dharmas—the supreme, tranquil state of the Tathāgata’s Great Parinirvāṇa.

Contemplation: Subduing the demons of non-dharmic appearances within and without the realms, one returns to the fundamental wheel to deliver those sentient beings whose roots for the One Vehicle have matured.

Since the subsequent text states that the Truths were turned at the Deer Park, it is self-evident that the meaning of the Lesser Teaching is manifest there, while it is implicitly contained in other assemblies.
Furthermore, whenever a Buddha appears in the world, he must necessarily possess the eight phases: descending from Tuṣita, entering the womb, and being born.
[The six events are: conception in the womb, renunciation, subduing Māra, attaining the Way, turning the Wheel of Dharma, and entering Nirvāṇa.

Herein, "attaining the Way" encompasses the first four phases, while "delivering sentient beings" encompasses the phase of Nirvāṇa. The remainder should be considered accordingly. △ Second, the sequence of turning the wheel and delivering people serves as proof that [the Buddha] presides over the assembly.
In the Deer Park (Mṛgadāva), he turned the Wheel of the Dharma of the Four Noble Truths, delivering the five men beginning with Kauṇḍinya so that they realized the fruits of the Path. [Commentary:
It is called the Deer Park because it is the dwelling place of herds of deer; it is also called the Park of the Sages (Ṛṣivana) because ancient sages resided there.
It is also called the Āmra Garden, named after its trees. The Four Noble Truths refer to the principles of the four true truths:

suffering, origin, cessation, and the path. "Suffering" (duḥkha) has the meaning of oppression and affliction; it refers to the three types of suffering, the eight types of suffering, and so forth. "Origin" (samudaya) has the meaning of summoning and inducing [rebirth].

The two delusions of view and thought (*dṛṣṭi- and bhāvanā-heya-kleśa*) and so forth are "extinction" (*nirodha*), which takes the exhaustion of burdens as its meaning; this refers to the two types of *nirvāṇa*: with remainder and without remainder.
The "path" (*mārga*) takes the removal of afflictions as its meaning; this refers to the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment (*saptatriṃśad-bodhipākṣika-dharma*).

The former two constitute worldly cause and effect, while the latter two constitute supramundane cause and effect. Suffering can be known; suffering is definitively suffering, and so forth. Therefore—
It is called the Truth (*satya*). There are three modes of turning: first, the turning that indicates characteristics, which means "this is suffering" up to "this is the path";
second, the turning that exhorts practice, which means "suffering should be known, the origin should be abandoned, cessation should be realized, and the path should be cultivated";
third, the turning that constitutes realization, which means "suffering has been known by me and need not be known again," up to "the path has been cultivated by me and need not be cultivated again."

Furthermore, this is the twelvefold wheel of the Dharma (*dvādaśāṅga-dharmacakra*). Moreover, when the Dharma of the Four Noble Truths is turned, one is able to give rise to the noble eye of wisdom (*āryaprajñācakṣus*), which has three distinct characteristics termed knowledge (*jñāna*), illumination (*vidyā*), and awakening (*buddhi*). These possess distinctions based on the past, future, and present.
Alternatively, when eye, knowledge, clarity, and awakening arise in succession and follow one another, this is precisely the Wheel of Dharma with its twelve aspects.

If there were only the practice (saṃskāra) without informative expression (vijñapti), it would not be called the Dharma; if there were informative expression without the practice, it likewise would not bear the name of a wheel.

Because there are three faculties that give rise to the three types of wisdom and accomplish the three paths, there are thus three turnings of the wheel. "Kauṇḍinya" is his family name; it is derived from the word for a fire-vessel.

He was of the Brahmin caste; his ancestors had served the sacrificial fire, and from this lineage he was named Ājñāta, which translates as "One Who Has Known" or "One Who Has Understood," or alternatively "One Who Has Realized the Ultimate Limit. As for the five others, they were Aśvajit and Bhadrika.

Kāśyapa, Kauṇḍinya, and Aśvajit—this means "Horse-Victorious"—Bhadrika—this means "Small Virtuous One"—along with Kauṣṭhila, were paternal relatives. Daśabala-Kāśyapa and Kauṇḍinya were maternal relatives.

Regarding those who realized the fruit of the Way: after the Prince entered the mountains, his father the King, filled with longing, commanded three members of his household and two maternal uncles to seek out his dwelling place and attend to his every movement. Two of them became attached to the five desires;
when the Prince first began his ascetic practices by eating hemp and wheat, they abandoned him and departed. Three remained attached to asceticism; later, the Prince...

Having accepted the milk-rice offering of food, ghee, and oil, he abandoned his ascetic practices and departed once more. Upon attaining the fruit of Buddhahood, he reflected upon whom he should deliver first.
Considering the hardships endured by the five men who had attended him, he went to Vārāṇasī (translated as "City Encircled by the River";
it is the site of the Āmra Garden). There, he preached the Four Noble Truths; Kātyāyana attained the purity of the Dharma-eye, while the other four had not yet attained it. The Buddha then...
He preached the Four Noble Truths once more. Four of the men attained the purity of the Dharma-eye. He then addressed them, saying: "One is attached to the five desires;
one is attached to asceticism. Both are not the Middle Way. To depart from these two extremes is called the Middle Way.

Next, he again preached the Four Noble Truths for them, and all five simultaneously attained the patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharmakṣānti*) and realized the fruit of Arhatship. When the Buddha asked them three times whether they understood the Dharma, they replied that they did.
No. He replied three times that he already knew. The earth deities proclaimed it, the space deities transmitted it, and so on until it reached the Brahma world.

Kātyāyana was the very first to behold the Buddha’s marks, hear the drum of the Dharma (the teaching), partake of the fragrance of the Way (practice), taste the nectar (principle), enter the stream of the sages (the first fruit), and achieve the state of outflowlessness (the fourth fruit). Because he stood at the forefront of all humans, devas, and arhats, he alone is singled out.
Cunda [is mentioned] because he subsumes the remaining four [disciples]. Turning the wheel of the Four Noble Truths is the Dharma; the five people who realized the fruit are the Saṃgha;

adding the World-Honored One from before constitutes the Buddha. Previously, the World-Honored One contemplated the excellence of the Dharma for transcending desire; now, he causes them to realize the Path. Regarding what wheel of Dharma he previously contemplated turning:

now he reveals the medicine of the Dharma of the Four Noble Truths. First, it was heard at Ṛṣipatana. Regarding which sentient beings he previously contemplated delivering: [he delivered the five bhikṣus].

Now, regarding the five disciples headed by Aññā-Koṇḍañña, one should understand from the preceding chapter that it primarily concerns the accomplishment [of the first], whereas this chapter subsumes the remaining five accomplishments.
Regarding the timing of their inclusion within the Deer Park, the *Xian-shou jiao-zhang* (Chapter on the Teachings of the Worthy Head) states: "Or it was preached after three weeks."
As in the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* and others, it is said that he taught after six or seven weeks, as in the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya* and the *Sarvāstivāda-vinaya-śāstra*.

Or it is said that he taught after seven times seven days (forty-nine days), as in the *Caryā-prasthāna-sūtra*. Or it is said that he taught after eight times seven days (fifty-six days), as in the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya*.
Or it is said that he taught after fifty-seven days, as in the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*. Or it is said that he first ordained five people in his second year, as in the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya*.
The *Dvayāvatāra-sūtra* (in prose): "Turning the wheel" refers to the accomplishment of hearing; "realizing the Way" refers to the accomplishment of faith.

The following forty-two chapters all explain the characteristics of the Four Noble Truths. Regarding the term "assembly" instead of "five people," the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* quotes the *Pañcaviṃśati-sāhasrikā-prajñāpāramitā-sūtra*, stating:
"When the Wheel of Dharma was first turned, Cunda attained the first fruit [of the path], and eighty thousand devas attained the [fruit of] non-arising."

Regarding the patience toward sentient beings and so forth: (Text) Since these six [perfections] have already been accomplished, how could they not serve as sufficient proof? Thus, those in distant lands and other ages will naturally believe them with certainty, leaving no room for further dispute.

[Commentary] Regarding "the eight sufferings" and so forth: this refers to the ten sufferings and the one hundred and ten sufferings. All birth and death within the six realms of the three worlds are characterized by suffering.
Regarding "the two delusions" and so forth: delusion and karma coexist, as they are capable of producing the suffering of birth and death.
“Accumulation” (*āsrava*) refers to birth and death. When delusion and karma are exhausted, there is no longer the accumulation of birth and death;

therefore, it is said that the exhaustion of accumulation constitutes cessation (*nirodha*). The essence of the Truth of Cessation consists of these two types of *nirvāṇa*: when the fetters of the person (*pudgala-bandhana*) are exhausted, it is called *sopadhiśeṣa* (with remainder); when the body is incinerated and wisdom is extinguished, it is called *nirupadhiśeṣa* (without remainder).
Although these are not the Ultimate Truth (*paramārtha-satya*), they are able to harmonize with the principle. “Affliction” (*kleśa*) refers to the defilements. Although [the text] is extensive...

Thirty-seven. Briefly stated, these consist only of morality (*śīla*), concentration (*samādhi*), and wisdom (*prajñā*). These constitute the primary and auxiliary paths that can eliminate afflictions (*kleśa*) and lead universally to *nirvāṇa*.
Regarding cause and effect: accumulation (*saṃudaya*) is the cause and suffering (*duḥkha*) is the effect; the path (*mārga*) is the cause and cessation (*nirodha*) is the effect.

As for placing the effect first and the cause later: this is because those of the Hīnayāna have dull faculties; they know suffering, sever accumulation, aspire to cessation, and cultivate the path. "And so forth" means...

That is to say: there is origination that can be abandoned; origination is definitively origination. There is cessation that can be realized; cessation is definitively cessation. There is a path that can be cultivated;
the path is necessarily the path. The *Sāsanānuśāsana Sūtra* states: "The Truth of Suffering is truly suffering; it cannot be made into pleasure.
And so on, until: "The Path is the true path; there is no other path. World-Honored One, the moon might be made hot, and the sun might be made cold.

The Buddha taught the Four Noble Truths; they cannot be made otherwise. (Text) "Truth" (*satya*) means that which is real and not false. Furthermore, the following explanation has two meanings. First, it reconciles the profound by applying it to the truths:
beneath each truth, the arising of wisdom (*jñāna*) and so forth occurs. Although there are three turnings for each of the [first] three truths, the wisdom and other factors are no different;
thus, there are twelve [aspects]. Regarding "past, future, and present": wisdom is past, clarity is future, and awakening is present.

Alternatively, according to another textual interpretation, the twelve [factors] are established based on the turning [of the wheel]. During the first turning of the Four Noble Truths, the four mental states of eye (*cakṣus*), knowledge (*jñāna*), clarity (*vidyā*), and awakening (*buddhi*) arise;
the same applies to the second and third turnings. Thus, there are twelve. Specifically, the *duḥkha-dharma-kṣānti* (receptivity to the dharma of suffering) is the "eye";

the *duḥkha-dharma-jñāna* (knowledge of the dharma of suffering) is "knowledge"; the *duḥkha-anvaya-kṣānti* (subsequent receptivity to suffering) is "clarity"; and the *duḥkha-anvaya-jñāna* (subsequent knowledge of suffering) is "awakening. This pattern holds for the remaining three truths as well. Together—
There are forty-eight [categories]. "Only" refers to the lower [category]. Teaching is used to explain the Dharma; practice is used to explain the wheel.

The Dharma takes "opening up understanding" as its meaning; if one does not understand the principle, it is not the Dharma. Practice without teaching—how could that possibly lead to understanding the principle?
The wheel takes "crushing and grinding" as its meaning; if it does not crush delusions, it is not a wheel. Teaching without practice—how could that possibly crush delusions?
Therefore, the twelve [aspects] of the teaching are the "turner," while the twelve [aspects] of the practice are the "turned.
To this, an objection is raised: Why must there be three turnings? The response states: It is because sentient beings possess the three types of faculties—superior, middling, and inferior;

because they give rise to the three distinct wisdoms of hearing, reflection, and cultivation; and because the three paths of seeing, cultivation, and realization have a sequential order. Thus it is said.
"Knowledge of realization" (*kṣayajñāna*) refers to the knowledge that realizes the Four Noble Truths. Some say it is "non-knowledge," which is simply the knowledge of cessation (*nirodha*).

It may also be designated by the name "knowledge of non-arising" (*anutpādajñāna*). Regarding its interpretation, the *Śūraṅgama-samādhi Sūtra* states: "When I first called myself 'one who understands,' it meant one who has realized the ultimate limit (*bhūtakoṭi*";
this refers simply to knowing the limit of the True Truth). Both the *Vibhāṣā-śāstra* and the *Abhidharma-piṭaka* employ this term; there are translations for it found in various sūtras.
It is for the sake of attaining the Way, meaning that one first attains the fruit of the Way. This is why it is said "equal" (*sama*).
Regarding Aṅgīrasa (Ānanda), some say Śakramana, others say Bhadramana, others say Managula, and others simply call him Mahānāman.
Because these various names for the Śākyas are confused and indistinguishable, the present definitive interpretation states: Mahānāman means... [the text continues].
"Hā" is translated as "grown up," referring to a male; it is a general term for an eldest son. As for Śāriputra’s son, Mānava, this refers to Ājñāta-kauṇḍinya.

Among those from the four castes who left the household life, they were all named Śākya. Because he was the very first to attain liberation when the Buddha had recently attained enlightenment, the *Pinfu gongde lun* (Treatise on the Analysis of Merit) states: "The Buddha’s eldest son is Cunda; his youngest son is..."
Subhadra, Bhadrika, and Mahānāma Koliya: Bhadrika was the eldest son of King Śuklodana, and Mahānāma Koliya was the eldest son of King Droṇodana; therefore, they are both called Mahānāma.
When he is referred to simply as Mahānāma, one knows which of them it is by observing the other four names, such as when it says "Kauṇḍinya, Aśvajit, and Mahānāma."
Kulika Kāśyapa is the same as Maṇibhadra; some say he is Aṅgīrasa-Bhadra-Maṇi-Kulika Kāśyapa.
Kulika is the same as Kulina, which is Kauṇḍinya; there are those who confuse it with "Kuli," but that is incorrect.
As for "reaching the Brahma-world": when a Wheel-Turning King appears in the world, his voice reaches the Heaven of Controlling Others' Emanations through the ten wholesome deeds.

Because he was born in the heavens of the desire realm, when Cunda attained the Way, his voice reached the Brahma Heaven; because he was free from desire and tranquil, it penetrated directly to the Brahma realm.
When the Buddha attained the Way, his voice reached the Nirmāṇarati Heaven; because the Buddha’s Way is ultimate, it ascended to the very peak of existence (*bhavāgra*).
The *Saṃyukta Āgama* states that King Vaiśravaṇa held a parasol and lamp to follow Kapphiṇa, while Śakra followed [the Buddha].
Brahmā, holding a parasol and lamp, followed Kāśyapa; Śakra, holding a parasol and lamp, followed Aññā-Koṇḍañña; and Ānanda, holding a parasol and lamp, followed behind the Tathāgata.
(The text) also conveys this same meaning. Question: Why were these five people delivered first? Answer: They were pursued by karmic conditions from former lives.
First, in the past, when the Tathāgata was the Rishi Kṣāntivādin, he preached the Dharma for a group of women who sang...

When King Li (Rāja) became enraged and cut off the Buddha’s arms and other limbs, his blood miraculously turned into milk; the Buddha vowed that he would be the first to hear the Dharma and attain the taste of the nectar of immortality.
The king was Ajñāta Kauṇḍinya, and the seer was the Tathāgata himself. Second, in a past age of famine, the Buddha transformed into a large fish with red eyes;
five carpenters were the first to cut the flesh from the fish, and the Buddha vowed that they would be the first to be liberated in a future life.

Regarding these [practices] and the patience toward the non-arising of phenomena (anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti), there are three points: Long ago, World-Honored One, when you were a prince named Sujāti, you fled with your parents to a neighboring country to avoid danger.
Before they had arrived, their provisions were exhausted; thus, every day the prince cut three jin of his own flesh [to provide for them].
He divided [the meat] into two parts to offer to his parents and kept one part for himself.

Indra tested him, and because his vow was found to be true, his bodily wounds immediately healed as they were before. Śakra praised him, saying, "May you, when you attain Bodhi in a future age, deliver us first.
The Prince was the Buddha; the Heavenly King was Chen Ruli (Nandika). Fourth, during the time of Kāśyapa Buddha:

Nine persons were practicing the Way; five of them had not yet attained the fruits [of their practice]. They vowed that among the teachings of Śākyamuni Buddha, they would be the very first to attain awakening and achieve the fruit of Arhatship.
This is explained in detail in the *Inguobaoen jing* (Sutra on the Retribution of Kindness). The first two Buddhas had previously vowed to deliver them first.

The latter two self-vows were heard first; therefore, they are established first. Regarding the turning of the Four Truths, the former was explained individually, while this explains them collectively.
First, the Three Jewels are presented because the Three Jewels were the initial names proclaimed at the Deer Park; thus, the *Lotus Sūtra* says:
"And also the Arhats, with the distinct names of Dharma and Saṅgha" (text). Following the previous reflection, next [the text] corresponds to the three reflections in the *Lotus Sūtra*.
It is also said: Having reflected upon this matter, he immediately proceeded to Vārāṇasī. "The mark of the cessation of all dharmas cannot be proclaimed in words;
yet, by the power of skillful means, I have preached it for the sake of the five bhikṣus. This is called 'turning the wheel of Dharma,' and from it there arises the sound of nirvāṇa.
(Text) Because he preaches through skillful means, there is the sound of nirvāṇa; thus one contemplates that the Dharma is subtle and without falsehood.
[It is] so. When [the Buddha] acted for the sake of the five bhikṣus, he considered that their spiritual capacities (*indriya*) were not in vain.

When he proceeded to Vārāṇasī and turned the wheel of the Four Noble Truths, he considered that there was indeed merit in hearing [the Dharma]. Question: Why are they called "five bhikṣus" in the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, yet referred to as "persons" (*pudgala*) in the present sutra? Answer:
First, the former refers to them in terms of the ordained monastic community (*pravrajita-saṃgha*), while this refers to them in terms of laypeople (*gṛhastha*). [End of] Explanation.

The *Karuṇāpuṇḍarīka* states: The Buddha explained the various sufferings of the three realms of existence (*tribhava*), and Ājñātakauṇḍinya was the first to realize and understand them, attaining the purity of the Dharma-eye (the vision of the Truths of the First Fruit).
Subsequently, for the sake of the four others, he again preached the Four Noble Truths, and they too were freed from the dust and defilements.
At that time, those five men, having seen the path, desired to leave the household life. The World-Honored One called out to them, "Come, Bhikṣus," and their hair and beards—

His hair fell off of its own accord, and he immediately became a śramaṇa. [The Buddha] again preached that the five aggregates are suffering, empty, and without self; [the disciple] realized arhatship.
Second, this refers to the very beginning of the gradual teaching, intended to transform the ordinary person into a sage; therefore, it says "person.
That [other instance] refers to the final, profound discourse on the secret and wondrous, intended to transform the provisional into the real; therefore, it says "bhikṣu. Furthermore,
The Buddha was born into the human world; humans serve as witnesses for him. Among the six realms of existence, only humans possess the capacity for such realization.

Devas obtain wholesome benefits from among humans. Only within the human path are the fourfold assembly complete. Furthermore, the monastic community demonstrates that the Buddha’s activities are identical to those of ordinary people.

For these reasons, this sutra specifically mentions "human beings. Based on this, one should understand the following: the three [sections] conclude the six, and the six are subsumed into the six types.
This can be verified; so why should there be any doubt? Thus, the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states: "The time, place, and persons are described in order to inspire faith" (text).
△ Second, the Prologue of the Arousing [of the Inquiry], in three parts. First, the assembly presents their doubts.
Furthermore, there are bhikṣus who, regarding various doubts they have raised, seek the Buddha’s guidance on how to proceed.
[Commentary] "Initiation" refers to the revelation and emergence of the teachings that constitute the main body of the scripture.

This is exemplified by Vimalakīrti manifesting illness, the *Laṅkāvatāra* Sūtra expressing joyous laughter, the *Vajracchedikā* begging for food, the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* emitting light, the *Ullambana Sūtra* saving one's mother, and Amitābha gladdening the faculties.
Now, this sutra takes the presentation of doubts and their subsequent resolution as its introduction. Why is this? When doubt departs, faith arises spontaneously;

when understanding comes, the principle manifests naturally. Through this, one cuts off delusions, realizes the truth, transcends the mundane, and enters the state of sainthood. Were it not for the removal of doubt, there would be no awakening.

From where does the fruit of the Way arise? It was for this reason that my faithful appearance gave way to doubt. As soon as I heard the discourse on the span of the Buddha’s life, Wei Ti’s delusions were dispelled;
when the teaching of the Pure Land was first clarified, the benefit gained in that single moment of inquiry and resolution—how could it be called small?

Furthermore, "there were also" refers to those preceding [the five]. This means that when the Buddha preached the Four Noble Truths, not only were the five people present in the assembly, but there were also immeasurable śrāvakas who likewise heard it together. *Bhikṣu* is a Sanskrit term; here it is translated as "mendicant."

One begs for food to sustain the body and begs for the Dharma to sustain the mind; thus it is also called "Terrifying Māra," because when one leaves the household life and abandons desire, Māra is greatly terrified.
It is also called "Destroying Evil," because one is able to destroy all afflictions and evil latent tendencies. For those who harbor doubts:

This means that within the various phenomena—such as the three realms of existence, the five aggregates, the ten wholesome paths of action, and the four noble truths—one gives rise to manifold delusions.

"Seeking" (*qiú*) means earnest entreaty; "advancing and ceasing" (*jìnzhǐ*) means taking and abandoning. That is to say, one advances to take up the gateway to awakening and abandons the net of doubt.
[Commentary]: Regarding the phrase "furthermore, there were immeasurable śrāvakas," first, this refers to those gathered in the same assembly.
As the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states: "The Dharma wheels of all Buddhas are of two kinds: first, the manifest; second, the secret.

At the time of the first turning, the śrāvakas saw eighty thousand devas, while only one person, Ājñātakauṇḍinya, attained the purity of the Dharma-eye—this is the manifest. The bodhisattvas, however, saw immeasurable [beings]."
Asaṃkhyeya people attained the two vehicles (*dvayāyāna*). Immeasurable asaṃkhyeya people attained the patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*).
Immeasurable asaṃkhyeya people resolved their minds upon the unsurpassed path (*anuttara-mārga-citta*) and practiced the six *pāramitās*.

Asaṃkhyeya people attained the first stage (*bhūmi*) up to the tenth stage. This is the esoteric [meaning]. (Text) By this, it should be understood that within this very assembly there were naturally immeasurable followers of the two vehicles.
...it was a person. Second, regarding the different times: the *Śākyaputra-pūrvapraśna-saṃgraha* and the *Xuánjì* both state that the *Dvādaśavyākaraṇa-sūtra* says:
"In the second year after the Buddha attained enlightenment, he converted the five bhikṣus; in the third year, he converted the three Kāśyapa brothers;
in the fifth year, he converted Śāriputra, Maudgalyāyana, and others. (Text) Thus, as for those converted at various locations, it is also...

Furthermore, there are immeasurable [meanings]. From the passage "The bhikṣu... downwards, there are also translations as "pure precepts" (śīla) or "right livelihood" (samyag-ājīva), which together constitute five meanings.
Now, since begging for food subsumes pure livelihood and breaking evil subsumes upholding the precepts, there are thus three meanings.
Various doubts refer to such questions as: Within the three realms of existence, is there suffering or is there no suffering? Is there permanence or is there impermanence?

Within the five aggregates, is there a self or is there no self? Is this pure or is it impure? Among the ten wholesome actions, do they accord with the Noble Path or do they not accord with the Noble Path?
Within the Four Noble Truths, can they be cultivated and realized or cannot they be cultivated and realized?
Regarding the term "etcetera" (*ādi*): when severing the views of existence and non-existence (*satkāya-dṛṣṭi* and *vicikitsā*), does one attain the four fruits [of the śramaṇa], or not?

When realizing nirvāṇa, does one transcend the three realms (*traidhātuka*), or not? As for "proceeding" (*jin*) and "stopping" (*zhi*): furthermore, when the characteristics of phenomena (*dharmalakṣaṇa*) are obscure and hidden, to provide a comprehensive explanation is called "proceeding.

When something can be understood through general principles and is thus left unelaborated, it is called "stopping. When the essential points of the teachings are critical, to examine them in detail is called "proceeding."
When the matter is not urgent, one abridges it and says "cease" (*zhi*). When the principles are profound and difficult, one elucidates them and says "advance" (*jin*).

When they are shallow and easy, one classifies and connects them and says "cease. When the understanding is authentic and correct, one encourages excellence and says "advance. When there is error and delusion, one sets it aside and says "cease.
When the faculties are dull and inferior, one causes them to engage in debate and says "advance. When the faculties are superior and sharp, one causes them to withdraw and reflect and says "cease."

Such wondrous responses all reside in the Buddha. The *Shu* (Commentary) follows the meaning of "seeking" (*qiú*) by focusing on the capacities of sentient beings (*jī*), while the *Chāo* (Sub-commentary) follows the meaning of "responding" (*yìng*) by focusing on the teachings (*jiào*).
Both interpretations are valid. △ The World-Honored One’s Wondrous Responses.
The World-Honored One instructed and enlightened him one by one.

[Commentary: "Instruction" (*jiao*) refers to the teacher’s admonition; "edict" (*zhao*) refers to the sovereign’s command. Now, as the Buddha is the Dharma-King and the model for humans and devas, the words and phrases he bestows are like the commands of a ruler;
hence they are called "instruction and edict. To suddenly shatter ignorance is called "opening" (*kai*); to clear away [obstructions] is called "expanding" (*huo*).
However, "penetrating through" is called awakening. Furthermore, it means to open up and remove the obstacles of delusion, thereby causing one to awaken to the emptiness of the essence.
Regarding each and every doubt, it is said: "Great doubt leads to great awakening; small doubt leads to small awakening."

[Commentary] Regarding "sudden" (*dùn*) below: the former [section] applies generally to both the subject (*neng*) and the object (*suō*), whereas the latter is restricted to the transformer (*huàzhě*). The former applies generally to those being transformed (*suǒhuà*).

Therefore, Jiaoguang said: "To open what was closed is called 'opening' (*kāi*); to awaken from oneself is called 'awakening' (*wù*). (Text). Furthermore, regarding "below": the latter is restricted to the transformer; this meaning is fundamentally from Qingliang.
Consider this: when the Buddha was at the Deer Park, he first spoke to Kauṇḍinya, saying: "In the world there are eight sufferings: namely, the suffering of the proliferation of the five aggregates;
the suffering of birth; the suffering of illness; the suffering of old age; the suffering of death; the suffering of separation from what is loved; the suffering of encountering what is hated;
and the suffering of not obtaining what one seeks. All such sufferings have 'self' as their root. One should know suffering and abandon its origin."
The realization of cessation and the cultivation of the path: if a person does not know the Four Noble Truths, they shall not attain liberation.
Next, he spoke to the four men, saying: "You should know that form, sensation, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are in reality impermanent, suffering, empty, and non-self."
Furthermore, he went to the royal city and stayed at the Śāla Grove. For King Bimbisāra, he said:
"Great King, you should know that this body of the five aggregates has consciousness as its root. Because of consciousness (which is mental consciousness), the faculty of mind arises;
because of the faculty of mind, form arises. This phenomenon of form arises and ceases without abiding. One who contemplates in this way..."

One who is able to thoroughly understand the impermanence of the body, thus contemplating the body without grasping at its characteristics, is immediately able to abandon the notions of "I" and "mine.

If one can contemplate form (*rūpa*) and remain detached from "I" and "mine," then one knows that the arising of form is itself the arising of suffering, and the cessation of form is itself the cessation of suffering.
One who contemplates in this manner is said to be liberated; they do not [construct further conceptualizations].
"This contemplation is what is called bondage. Having heard this Dharma, the King’s mind was opened and his understanding clarified;
together with eighty thousand ministers and nayutas of devas, each was freed from defilement and attained the purity of the Dharma-eye.
According to the answers provided above, one knows that there is no doubt that remains unawakened. △ Third, the entire assembly receives benefit.
[The text reads: "With palms joined in reverence, he assented and followed the Honored One’s command.
[Commentary: "Palms joined" means that the body and hands are not dispersed. "Reverence" means the mind and heart are held in awe and admiration.

"Assent" means the speech is one of faithful veneration. "Follow" means to comply. This encompasses all three karmas [of body, speech, and mind]. Furthermore, there are three kinds of compliance: first, the ear-faculty gives rise to consciousness and believes...

To hear the words and phrases without understanding their meaning is to follow the words. Second, to direct the consciousness toward the words, grasping their meaning but failing to attain the underlying intent, is to follow the meaning.
Third, to investigate the meaning and grasp the intent, such that when the essential purpose is attained, one forgets both the words and the literal meaning, is to follow the intent.
If one fails to accord with even one of these three, one is far removed from the Way.

What is meant by "conformity" (*anuloma*)? A decree issued by a Heavenly Son is called an "edict" (*śāsana*). The Buddha’s precepts and edicts are likewise so named. [Commentary] As for the phrase "in combination":

because the Tathāgata’s inconceivable transformations of the three wheels [of body, speech, and mind] are at work, there is no one among the assembled multitude whose three karmas fails to receive benefit.

If we consider them in opposition: "instruction" refers to the teaching of the Dharma through the karma of speech; it is called the Wheel of Right Teaching (*samyag-deśanā-cakra*). Now, by means of this—

To "yield" (*nuò*) and "comply" (*shùn*) with it means to open; this refers to the manifestation of bodily action (*kāyakarman*), and is called the Wheel of Supernatural Powers (*ṛddhivikurvaṇā-cakra*). Now, by joining the palms to comply with it, one awakens;

this refers to the discernment of the faculties through mental action (*manaskarman*), and is called the Wheel of Mind-Reading (*cetopariya-cakra*). Now, by reverently complying with it—furthermore, below.
This refers to having faith in the teaching that the five aggregates (*pañcaskandha*) are suffering, empty, impermanent, and non-self;

this is the literal meaning. Upon investigating this body, its characteristic is the combination of form (*rūpa*) and mind (*citta*). Form consists of the four great elements (*mahābhūta*): earth, water, fire, and wind. Mind consists of the four aggregates:

feeling (*vedanā*), perception (*saṃjñā*), formations (*saṃskāra*), and consciousness (*vijñāna*). If these were identical to the self, there would consequently be eight selves. By further successive investigation, one arrives at thirty-six constituents.
If each of the eighty thousand pores were the self, then there would be hundreds of thousands of selves;

thus one awakens to the fact that this body is merely a collection of conditions, appearing as a composite phenomenon, fundamentally devoid of a self or a person. This is the meaning of "conformity. When one turns over and examines the self from every perspective, the self cannot be found.
Consequently, the mind no longer clings to the three realms, but cultivates only the wisdom of the contemplation of non-self to sever greed and all other afflictions.
[He] realized the *tathatā* (true suchness) of the emptiness of self (*pudgala-śūnyatā*), attained the fruit of an Arhat, and his wishes were fulfilled.

Thus, the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* says: "The listeners gaze intently as if drinking from a thirst; with single-minded focus they enter into the meaning of the words; leaping for joy, their hearts rejoice upon hearing the Dharma. (Text).
In the world, that which has not passed through the Phoenix Pavilion and the Imperial Secretariat cannot be called an imperial edict (*śāsana*). The golden mouth of the Buddha [is likewise].
This is consistent with the teachings on bodhisattvas, celestial immortals, and transformed persons; therefore, it is called an "imperial decree.
△ Second, the Main Body of the Teaching (Zhengzongfen) has two parts. First, the section briefly indicating the general characteristics.
At that time, the World-Honored One preached for them the True Sutra in Forty-two Sections.
[Commentary] Regarding the "Principal Section" (zhengzong): this refers to the correct meaning that constitutes the primary tenet of this sutra.
It distinguishes itself from the preceding section, which is the introduction to this sutra, and the subsequent section, which consists of the words for its dissemination. As for "at that time":
When he spoke thus, resolving doubts and inspiring reverent compliance, the True Sutra was such that, in terms of its phenomena, it could not be destroyed by water or fire;
in terms of its principle, it was not constrained by material things. Its essence is non-action (*wuwei*), and its nature and characteristics are fully endowed with all meritorious virtues.
Its function gives rise to two types of cause and effect: its principle takes the *dharmatā* of *tathatā* as its essence; its teaching manifests upon the consciousness of the Tathāgata;
its practice flows forth from the heart of great compassion; and its fruit is accomplished through the realization of cessation (*nirodha*) via the cultivation of the path.
Therefore, it is called "True. [Commentary:

Regarding the section below "True," first the meaning of "True" is explained by way of two dharmas. As for "water and fire not destroying [it]," the *Han Ming Fǎběn nèi zhuàn* (Inner Biography of the Dharma Origin of Emperor Ming of the Han) states:
In the fourteenth year of Yongping, the Daoist masters of the Five Peaks, Chǔ Shànxìn and Fèi Shúcái...
On the morning of the first day of the first month, during the imperial audience, [the Daoists] submitted a memorial requesting a contest with the Buddhist teachings.

Kāśyapa Mātanga and Dharmaratna addressed the Emperor, saying: "The Dharma of our Buddha is a world-transcending teaching; neither water nor fire can destroy it. We pray that you will put this to the test.

The Emperor ordered an altar to be constructed and issued a decree that on the fifteenth day of the first month, the texts should be burned in fire. Thereupon, the *Lingbao* scriptures of the Daoist school...
The various scriptures were reduced to ashes; yet the Buddhist scriptures and images remained solemnly unmoved.
The radiance and color of the śarīra rose straight up into the air, circling like a parasol and covering the entire assembly, eclipsing the sun’s orb.
At that time, the Grand Tutor Zhang Yan said to Chu Shanxin and the others, "If what you have tested yields no result, it is surely false. You should go to the Western Regions."
The True Dharma of the Buddha Family. (Text) An inscription by Emperor Taizong of the Tang Dynasty on the Platform for Burning Scriptures reads:

The path is desolate, overgrown with long green moss; Each time I ascend this place, I linger and turn back. The Blue Ox needlessly spoke of departing at the Pass of Passes; The White Horse personally came from the Land of Seals.
To determine the truth or falsehood of reality, rely upon the blazing flames; To distinguish the authentic from the spurious, this high platform was built. Spring.
Even the wind would resent such disorder; it shall blow away the ashes of the Way from those years. (Text) For one who is not constrained by things, the path of language is severed.

Thus, the body [of the teaching] follows. Next, the true meaning is explained by means of the three great elements (*mahābhūta*). Regarding "the nature of the unconditioned" (*asaṃskṛta-svabhāva*), it says below:
To realize the source of one's own mind and awaken to unconditioned dharmas (*asaṃskṛta-dharma*) is what is called the Way (*mārga*). The *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* says:
"Observe the conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta-dharma*) in the world: which among them is indestructible? Yet, one never hears of empty space (*ākāśa*) decaying or perishing. Why is this?"
Emptiness is not something produced, for it is without destruction or cessation. (Text) Since emptiness regarding phenomena is thus, so too is the principle of the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*).
The *Abhidharmakośa-bhāṣya* states that unconditioned space (*ākāśa-asaṃskṛta*) is precisely this meaning; therefore, it is called "True. Second, regarding cause and effect:

this refers to the causes of goodness and the results of happiness for worldly humans and devas, as well as the causes of goodness and the results of happiness for the two vehicles (*yāna*) and others who transcend the world. If...
Now, as for the *xiánjīng* (immortal scriptures), because they are interspersed with worldly and heterodox elements, they lack the merit of worldly cause and effect.
As for the scriptures spoken by the various devas, they lack the merit of supramundane cause and effect; how, then, could they be called "true"?

These are now the Buddha’s scriptures, like the imperial edicts of a Son of Heaven, differing from the speech of various kings and officials; therefore, they are called "true. Question: In the scriptures of the Lesser Vehicle (*hīnayāna*), why...

There are three great points. Answer: With respect to the capacity of those being taught, it applies to both the Small and the Great Vehicles; however, within the teaching that enables transformation, there is no distinction between small and great.

Furthermore, within the true nature of *ātma-śūnyatā* (self-emptiness) and *tathatā* (suchness), how could there not be essence, characteristic, and function? Since it applies to a portion of both, there is no hindrance to this correlation.
Regarding the principle below, the true meaning is subsequently explained through four gates. As for "that which manifests upon consciousness," this refers to the Buddha.
Whatever has been proclaimed, whether in terms of words or meaning, all is manifested by the pure consciousness associated with the Tathāgata’s wondrous discerning wisdom (*pratyavekṣaṇājñāna*).
Regarding the phrase "flowing from the heart of great compassion," the *Liang* commentary explains: True Suchness (*tathatā*) is the most supreme among all phenomena;
because one gives rise to non-conceptual wisdom (*nirvikalpajñāna*) by taking True Suchness as its object, that non-conceptual wisdom is...
It flows from suchness. This wisdom is the most supreme among all forms of wisdom. From this wisdom, subsequently attained wisdom (prṣṭhalabdha-jñāna) flows forth;
within subsequently attained wisdom, great compassion arises. This mind of great compassion is the most supreme among all meditative concentrations.
Because of this great compassion, the Tathāgata, desiring to establish the True Dharma and to rescue sentient beings, taught the twelve [links of dependent origination].
This scripture is the outflow of great compassion; this Dharma is the most supreme among all dharmas.
(Text) Therefore, it is called "True.
△ Second, the extensive explanation of the specific characteristics, divided into three parts. First, the twelve chapters on the section for manifesting the virtues of the fruit to engender faith.

Three. First, clarifying the supramundane fruit, in two parts. First, presenting the fruit to inspire faith and aspiration. Third, first providing a general indication of the person capable of cultivation.
The Buddha said: "One who leaves home to renounce kin, recognizes the mind and penetrates the source, and understands the unconditioned dharma (*asaṃskṛta-dharma*), is called a śramaṇa."

[Commentary] First, the virtues and deeds are set forth; there are five, namely: taking leave of one's parents, expounding the Dharma, and so forth. "Taking leave of one's parents" means departing from those who are dear and affectionate.
There are two types of renunciation: first, renunciation of the body, which refers to taking leave of one's parents; second, renunciation of the mind.
This refers to the understanding of consciousness (*vijñāna*). Furthermore, there are four meanings: first, leaving the household of worldly convention, which is also to take leave of one's kin;

second, leaving the household of the five aggregates (*pañcaskandha*), which is the awakening of the mind of consciousness; third, leaving the household of afflictions (*kleśa*), which is the realization of the fundamental source; and fourth, leaving the household of birth and death (*saṃsāra*).

"Unconditioned" (*asaṃskṛta*). "Mind" (*citta*) refers to the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*). This single mental consciousness, when applied through the six sense faculties (*ṣaḍ-indriya*), is termed the "six consciousnesses.
"Root" (*mūla*) refers to craving (*tṛṣṇā*). Craving is the root of all suffering; as the *Āgama* says: "Greed, hatred, and delusion are the roots of the world.
(Text) "One who understands consciousness" means that these three poisons (*triviṣa*) act as the perfumers (*vāsaka*).
Presently, the form and mind serve as the perfumed (bhāvyamāna), whereby one creates karma, undergoes retribution, and transmigrates through the three realms;

this constitutes the root of defilement. If, however, the three wholesome roots—non-attachment and so forth—serve as the perfuming agent (bhāvaka), with the present form and mind serving as the perfumed, one cultivates the path, severs delusions, and transcends the three realms; this constitutes the root of purity. Thus, regarding defilement and purity...

The three realms of existence are non-existent. Apart from this poisonous consciousness (*vijñāna*), there is nothing else upon which to rely. Therefore, the *Qingliang* commentary on the Hīnayāna states:

"One merely relies upon the six consciousnesses and the three poisons to establish the roots of defilement and purity. (Text) If one does not understand this, it cannot be called a thorough comprehension of consciousness.

As for the "unconditioned" (*asaṃskṛta*), it is so called because it is devoid of volitional construction (*abhisamskāra*). Furthermore, it is named "unconditioned" by way of distinguishing it from the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*). To realize [this]...
Xuánzàng states: Briefly, there are four meanings. First, neither arising nor ceasing, because it excludes the four marks [of conditioned phenomena].

Second, neither going nor coming, because it does not belong to the three periods of time. Third, neither that nor this, because it is free from self and other. Fourth, transcending both gain and loss.
Because it neither increases nor decreases, it reveals the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*), which is free from these four [characteristics] such as arising.
(Text) Now, there are three types of the unconditioned: first, the unconditioned of space (*ākāśa-asaṃskṛta*); second, the unconditioned of analytical cessation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha-asaṃskṛta*);

and third, the unconditioned of non-analytical cessation (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha-asaṃskṛta*). The Treatise says: Space has non-obstruction as its intrinsic nature; because there is no hindrance, matter moves within it. Analytical cessation...

It has the nature of disjunction (*visamyoga*). It is the attainment of liberation through the removal of fetters. Cessation obtained by the power of discernment (*pratisaṃkhyā*) is called "cessation through discernment" (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*).
"Cessation not through discernment" (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*) is the permanent obstruction of future arising; its attainment differs from the former in that it does not depend upon discernment.

However, it is simply due to the absence of conditions that it is termed "cessation not through deliberation" (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*). (Text) Having realized these three dharmas, they are silent, profound, and empty;

they abide in a state of serene permanence, without any activity. This is called "understanding the unconditioned" (*asaṃskṛta*). "Mind" refers to the fundamental [nature]; "ability to cultivate and abandon" refers to the means;
and "unconditioned" refers to the cessation realized. The term "below" concludes the names of the persons. *Śramaṇa* is a Sanskrit word; here it is translated as "merit" (*gōngláo*).

This refers to the fact that the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*) involves meritorious labor. It is also called "diligent practice" (*yoga*), meaning diligent practice for the sake of attaining *nirvāṇa*.

Alternatively, it is translated as "diligent cessation," which means diligently practicing various virtues and ceasing all evils. The "Treatise on Sacrifices to the Gods" (*Jiaoshi zhi*) in the *Hanshu* states:

"Śramaṇa, in the language of Han, means 'one who has ceased the mind. They shave their hair and leave the household; they sever worldly attachments and wash away desires, returning to non-action (*wuwei*). (Text)
The person is established by means of the Dharma, and the Dharma is manifested by means of the person; thus, the title of "Śramaṇa" is not easily assumed. [Commentary] etc.

This points to the renunciant who recognizes the mind and realizes the three virtues of the fundamental source. Regarding the phrase "exiting from below," when body and mind are contrasted, there should be four permutations:
first, neither body nor mind has exited—this is the ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*). Second, the body has exited but the mind has not—this is the non-Buddhist (*tīrthika*).

Furthermore, there are four types of those who leave the household life: first, those who leave the body but not the mind, such as those with the aspiration for the Way (bodhicitta), like Vimalakīrti;
second, those who leave both body and mind, the assembly of bhikṣus. Below that, in contrast to those who advance the Buddha-dharma, there are also four:

first, advancing the house of True Reality (paramārtha-satya); second, advancing the house of the Dharma-body (dharmakāya); third, advancing the house of contemplative wisdom (vipaśyanā-jñāna); fourth, advancing the house of non-arising (anutpāda). Thus, Nanshan...

It is said: A true renunciant fears the manifold sufferings of the four enemies, loathes the impermanence of the triple world, takes leave of the deepest affection for one's kin, and abandons profound attachment to the five desires. One who can act thus is called a true renunciant;
such a person may then cause the Three Jewels to flourish and deliver beings of the four modes of birth. Their merit is immeasurable and their benefit is profoundly deep, manifesting in the present.
"Matter and mind" refers to the three factors of the present: the sense organs (*indriya*), their objects (*viṣaya*), and consciousness (*vijñāna*).

"Arising and so forth" points to birth and extinction, coming and going, this and that, gain and loss. Regarding "empty space," Qingliang says: "The Hinayana explanation of empty space refers only to external emptiness (text).
That is to say, within the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*), it is free from all obstructions, just like empty space—vast, penetrating, and unimpeded; this is spoken by way of analogy."
This is the name. Regarding "practicing within form": this refers, for example, to dharmas such as form and mind practicing within the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*).
Regarding "discernment" (*viveka*): discernment means selection; it is the wisdom of differentiation (*pravicaya-prajñā*), because it individually and specifically discerns the four noble truths.

Cessation has two meanings. First, the manifestation of principle through the extinction of afflictions is called cessation; this name is derived from that which manifests it. Second, the quiescent nature of reality itself is called cessation;
this name is derived from that which is manifested. What is now termed "cessation through deliberation" (pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha) refers to the cessation obtained by the power of discernment.
It is like a cart drawn by oxen being called an "ox-cart. This is the meaning. [It serves to] permanently obstruct...
That which is "destined to arise" refers to those dharmas that are capable of arising in the future. Qingliang says: "Dharmas destined to arise in the future will arise when conditions assemble;
when conditions are deficient, the dharma does not arise and thus attains non-analytical cessation (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*).

This obstructs the dharma destined to arise, causing it never to occur again; this is called 'ultimate obstruction. Therefore, the verse says: 'Ultimately obstructing that which is destined to arise'—this is a distinct attainment."

Regarding the term "attainment by way of distinction" (*prāpti-viśeṣa*) in reference to non-analytical cessation (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*): it means that non-analytical cessation possesses a substantial nature (*dravyasat*), because a distinct attainment arises within the absence of conditions.
It is called "non-analytical cessation" because it does not depend on analytical cessation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*), but rather depends solely on the deficiency of conditions.
(The commentary ends here. In the Mahāyāna, [phenomena] exist solely as transformations of consciousness; in the Hīnayāna, they exist externally apart from the mind. Therefore...
Qingliang says: "The Hīnayāna explains that the three unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta*) are all substantially existent dharmas.
(Text) This distinguishes that the interpretations of the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna each differ. Regarding "the mind" below: the preceding was an individual explanation; this is a summary.

The mind fundamentally pervades both the defiled and the pure. Why? Because the mind is the head of transgressions and the chief of merits, as stated in the *Nyāyānusāra-śāstra*. Based on the present...
In the context of consciousness, mind, and so forth, these serve as the causes for both defilement and purity. (Text) Greed and the like are the root of experiencing suffering;
non-greed and the like are the root of liberation. The mind can sever greed, anger, and so forth; the mind can cultivate non-greed and so forth.
Furthermore, the mental consciousness is capable of cultivation, and suffering is fundamentally what can be severed. In the *Han shu*, the *Ruìyìng* (Sūtra of Auspicious Responses) states:
"One who quiets the mind and reaches the fundamental source is therefore called a śramaṇa. (Text) Alternatively, the full name is *śramaṇa*, which means "one who exhausts the path" (*fàndào*).
Because he serves as a fertile field of merit (*puṇyakṣetra*), he is able to sever the famine and deprivation of sentient beings; and because he cultivates the Eightfold Noble Path, [he is so named].
It is able to sever all wrong paths. Thus, the *Kāśyapa-parivarta* states: "The śramaṇa is the Eightfold Noble Path;
the fruit of the śramaṇa is the permanent and ultimate severance of all greed, hatred, and delusion through that path.
In worldly parlance, "śramaṇa" means "one who is destitute," while "na" means "path. Such a path severs all hunger and destitution, and severs all [afflictions].
The wrong path. For this reason, the Eightfold Noble Path is called *śramaṇya* (the state of a recluse).

Because one attains the fruits [of practice] from within this path, they are called *śrāmaṇaphala* (the fruits of the recluse). Furthermore, "recluse" (*śramaṇa*) is a general term for those who have left the household life;
since all who have gone forth, whether in the Buddha-dharma or among non-Buddhist paths, are called recluses, there are four permutations when distinguishing them. First: [text continues].
The first are those who are sons of the Śākyas but not śramaṇas; these are the royal lineage of the Śākya kings. The second are those who are śramaṇas but not of the [Śākya] lineage;

these are the Brahmins and others. The third are those who are neither śramaṇas nor sons of the Śākyas; these are the other two low-caste lineages. The fourth are those who are both śramaṇas and sons of the Śākyas;
these are the community of bhikṣus. Thus, the Ekottarika Āgama states: The Buddha addressed the bhikṣus...
The Master said: "Among the four castes, there are those who leave the household life; they no longer retain their original surnames, but are simply called śramaṇas, sons of the Śākyas.
This is like the waters of the four great rivers, all of which flow from the Anavatapta spring. Regarding people relying on the Dharma:

the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa* says, 'Now, one who leaves the household life does so for the sake of the unconditioned Dharma (*asaṃskṛta-dharma*). (Text) Regarding the Dharma relying on people: it is people who can propagate the Way; it is not the Way that propagates people."

Therefore, the final two lines serve as an admonition and exhortation. When a person possesses such responsibilities and bears such designations, how can one who has become a śramaṇa afford to neglect them?
△ Next, the detailed explanation of the fruits realized consists of four parts; first, the realization of the four stages of fruition.
He constantly observed the two hundred and fifty precepts; his conduct was pure in every movement. He practiced the four true paths of cultivation and became an Arhat.
An Arhat is one who can fly through the air and manifest transformations, possess a lifespan extending across vast kalpas, and cause the heavens and earth to tremble at will.
[Commentary] "Constantly" and below: first, the causes and effects are presented in general. The first three phrases refer to the cause.

Regarding the "two hundred and fifty precepts," these are the five categories of precepts observed by a bhikṣu. "Advancing" refers to the practice of "performing all wholesome deeds," which constitutes the aspect of active observance (*kriyā-dhāraṇa*).
"Ceasing" means not committing any evil; this is "observance through cessation. The Vinaya takes the cessation of evil and the practice of good as its primary principle.
"Purity" (śīla) is the Sanskrit term; here it is translated as "coolness," because by departing from the causes of feverish affliction, one attains the fruit of coolness.
Precepts are the foundation of samādhi and the basis for the four fruits [of the śramaṇa]. Therefore, they are presented first.
For those who practice the Four Noble Truths, this refers to the cultivation and realization of the meditative contemplation of the Four Truths. As the *Śāriputra-śīla-sūtra* states:

"By relying on these precepts, one attains various dhyānas and concentrations, as well as the wisdom that extinguishes suffering. (Text) Therefore, concentration and wisdom are explained next. Taken together, these constitute the Three [Trainings].
Training. Its opening comprises thirty-seven factors: right speech, action, and livelihood are *śīla* (precepts); the four foundations of mindfulness and so forth are *samādhi* (concentration);
joy, discernment, volition, and so forth are *prajñā* (wisdom). The term "Arhat" refers to the fruit. It has three meanings when translated: first, "slayer of thieves."
1. Because the ninety-eight latent proclivities (*anuśaya*) have been exhausted; 2. Because there is no further arising, as one will not undergo the retribution of birth and death in future lives;
3. Because one is worthy of offerings, being a sublime field of merit for humans and devas. Regarding the term "attainment" (*siddha*): from cause to fruit, there are five stages of practice.

First is the stage of equipment (*sambhāra-avasthā*), wherein one cultivates the five stabilizing practices (*pañca-vastu-sthiti*) and the specific and general mindfulness of characteristics (*smṛtyupasthāna*), taking the Truth of Suffering (*duḥkha-satya*) as the object of focus.
The objects of focus. Second, the stage of application (*prayoga-avasthā*): at the stage of *uṣmagata*, one cultivates right effort while contemplating the objects of the Four Noble Truths.

At the stage of *mūrdhan*, one cultivates the functions of the bases of psychic power (*ṛddhipāda*), with the contemplation being the same as before, yet becoming even more luminous. At the stage of *kṣānti*, one cultivates the five faculties (*pañcendriya*); regarding the Four Noble Truths, one possesses the endurance and aspiration never to fall back.

At the stage of *laukikāgradharma*, one cultivates the five powers (*pañcabala*); regarding the Four Noble Truths, one will inevitably and continuously give rise to true outflow-free wisdom (*anāsrava*).
Because there is nothing superior to this within the worldly dharmas, the stage of penetration (prativedha-avasthā) establishes the factors of enlightenment (bodhyaṅga).

This is because one realizes the Four Noble Truths as they truly are, thereby giving rise to the eight patiences (kṣānti) and eight knowledges (jñāna) that are untainted (anāsrava), suddenly severing the conceptual afflictions of views (dṛṣṭi-kleśa) pertaining to the three realms, and realizing the truth revealed by the emptiness of the person (pudgala-śūnyatā).
This is also called the stage of the path of seeing (darśana-mārga-avasthā). Fourth, the stage of cultivation (bhāvanā-avasthā)...
Stage: One cultivates the Eightfold Noble Path. Why is this? Having already seen the Path, one proceeds with ease within the Eightfold Noble Path;

through repeated contemplation focused on the Truth, one advances to sever the afflictions of thought (*bhāvanā-heya-kleśa*), ultimately reaching the city of the two kinds of *nirvāṇa*. Fifth, the Stage of No-More-Learning (*aśaikṣa-bhūmi*):
having completely severed the afflictions of views and thought within the three realms, one realizes the eighty-nine grades of unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) dharmas.
They accomplish the fivefold Dharma-body and perfect the ten dharmas of one beyond training (*aśaikṣa*). [They realize: "Birth has been exhausted; the holy life (*brahmacarya*) has been established;
what was to be done has been accomplished; there is no further state of existence. For this reason, they are called "beyond training. Now, there are three types of *śrāvakas*:

first, those of superior faculties and sudden capacity, who achieve a great transcendence and severance; second, those of middling faculties and capacity, who achieve a small transcendence and severance; third, [those of gradual capacity...]

Those of inferior capacity and gradual disposition sever [the afflictions] in stages. Now, to achieve the four fruits within a single lifetime constitutes a great transcendence over those of superior faculties.
Therefore, this is not a partial accomplishment, but a complete and perfect realization. [The character] "Ā" (阿) follows; next, the characteristics of the fruits are specifically shown.

"Flying and transforming" refers to the three knowledges (*traividya*), the six supernormal powers (*ṣaḍabhijñā*), and the eighteen miraculous transformations. It also refers to a lifespan extending through vast eons.

This refers to one who has attained arhatship and will no longer be reborn within the three realms. There are pure buddha-fields that transcend the three realms; in those untainted realms (anāsrava-dhātu), there is no designation for afflictions.
One receives a body of transformation (nirmāṇakāya) and enjoys the bliss of samādhi. This applies even to one at the stage of the first fruit (srotāpanna).
For humans, it takes seven births for [the afflictions] to begin their cessation; only after eighty thousand kalpas does one attain the arising of the mind [of awakening].
If one attains the second fruit in a single lifetime, one enters nirvana after two births; having passed sixty thousand kalpas, one is then able to give rise to the mind [of awakening].
If one attains the third fruit in a single lifetime and does not return to the desire realm, one enters nirvana; after forty thousand kalpas, one attains the arising of the mind [of awakening].
If one attains Arhatship within a single lifetime, one can immediately manifest the meditative absorption of cessation (*nirodha-samāpatti*) and remain therein for twenty thousand *kalpas*.

Upon emerging, one is then able to generate the resolve for enlightenment (*bodhicitta*). His current lifespan shall last for the final twenty thousand *kalpas* of this period. Regarding "abiding while shaking heaven and earth":

it means that during every movement—whether walking, standing, sitting, or reclining—he is able to stir and shake heaven and earth, moving the spirits and deities, causing non-Buddhists to take refuge, and causing the Lord of Māras to pay homage.
[This refers to] the hand. [The *Chao* states: Regarding the five categories: first, the four *pārājika* (translated as "abandonment," or alternatively "extreme evil") rules;

second, the thirteen *saṃghāvaśeṣa* (Sanskrit for "monastic remainder") rules; third, the two *aniyata* (undetermined) rules; and fourth, the one hundred and two *pāyattika* (translated as "falling") rules.

Ten *śaikṣa* rules; four *prāyaścittika* rules (in Chinese, "confessing to another"); five *duṣkṛta* rules (translated here as "misdeeds"), which comprise the rules of training (*śaikṣadharma*) numbering one hundred;
and seven rules for the settlement of disputes (*adhikaraṇa-śamatha*). This is called the full ordination (*upasampadā*) for those who have left the household life.
Furthermore, this single phrase is the wording of the compilers. As stated in the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya*: "Guard well the words of speech;
purify your own intentions; let the body commit no evil. When these three paths of action are pure, one can attain such practice;
this is the path of the Great Sages. This is the precept scripture (*śīla-sūtra*) spoken by the Tathāgata Śākyamuni during the twelve years [following his enlightenment].
From this point onward, it will be explained in detail. (Text) Regarding "constant practice": because one is never for even a moment separated from speech, silence, movement, or stillness.
Regarding "taking cessation as the primary practice," the verse from the *Śīla-sūtra* of the Tathāgata Kāśyapa says:
"Commit no evil whatsoever; practice all that is good; purify your own mind—this is the teaching of all Buddhas. (Text) Three.
"Those who obscure the foundation" refers to those whose ethical discipline (*śīla*) is not pure and whose meditative concentration (*samādhi*) does not manifest before them.

Regarding "the basis for the four fruits," the *Śūraṅgama-samādhi Sūtra* states that Upāli said: "Both natural transgressions and prohibited transgressions are entirely purified; body and mind are stilled and extinguished, and one becomes an Arhat. (Text). From "Right Speech" onwards:
although the factors of the path (*mārga-aṅga*) are numerous, they are fully subsumed within the three trainings (*tri-śikṣā*). Discipline (*śīla*) subsumes three [of these], namely:

Right speech, right action, and right livelihood. Those subsumed under concentration (*samādhi*) are ten: namely, the four bases of power (*ṛddhipāda*), the faculty of concentration (*samādhīndriya*), the power of concentration (*samādhibala*), the factor of enlightenment of investigation (*dharmapravicaya-saṃbodhyaṅga*), the factor of enlightenment of concentration (*samādhi-saṃbodhyaṅga*), the factor of enlightenment of equanimity (*upekṣā-saṃbodhyaṅga*), and right concentration (*samyak-samādhi*). Those subsumed under wisdom (*prajñā*) are eighteen:

namely, the four foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*), the four right efforts (*samyakprahāṇa*), the faculty of energy (*vīryendriya*), the faculty of wisdom (*prajñendriya*), the power of energy (*vīryabala*), the power of wisdom (*prajñābala*), the factor of enlightenment of investigation (*dharmapravicaya-saṃbodhyaṅga*), the factor of enlightenment of energy (*vīrya-saṃbodhyaṅga*), the factor of enlightenment of joy (*prīti-saṃbodhyaṅga*), right view (*samyagdṛṣṭi*), and right intention (*samyaksaṃkalpa*).

It is solely right effort (*samyag-vīrya*). It encompasses four factors through the simultaneous penetration of concentration (*samādhi*) and wisdom (*prajñā*), namely: the faculty of mindfulness (*smṛtīndriya*), the power of mindfulness (*smṛtibala*), the factor of enlightenment of mindfulness (*smṛtisambodhyaṅga*), and right mindfulness (*samyak-smṛti*).

It encompasses two factors through the simultaneous penetration of all three trainings (*triśikṣā*), namely: the faculty of faith (*śraddhendriya*) and the power of faith (*śraddhābala*). As for the ninety-eight latent tendencies (*anuśaya*):

Regarding the "eighty-eight afflictions" (*āśrava*): this adds the ten afflictions of the realm of thought (*bhavāgra*) to [the eighty-eight]. Regarding "the third, those worthy of offerings" (*arhat*):
Question—The Tathāgata is also called "Worthy of Offerings. How does he differ from the *śrāvakas*? Answer—The *arhat* is limited to being an object of offering for humans and devas;

the Buddha, however, is the one to whom Māras, outsiders, humans, devas, those of the two vehicles, and Bodhisattvas should offer. Regarding the "five stages of settling the mind" (*pañca-viṣkambhana-citta*): this refers to one who has much greed... [and so forth].
The contemplation of purity for those with much anger; the contemplation of compassion for those with much delusion; the contemplation of causes and conditions for those with many hindrances;
and the contemplation of mindfulness of the Buddha for those with much distraction. As for the mindfulness of specific and general characteristics:

specifically, one contemplates the body as impure, feelings as suffering, the mind as impermanent, and phenomena as selfless. Generally, one contemplates the body as impure, and that feelings, the mind, and phenomena are all impure.

This continues up to the contemplation of the selflessness of phenomena (*dharmanairātmya*). Regarding the body, sensations, and mind, they too are without self. As for the right efforts (*samyakpradhāna*):
this refers to preventing unarisen evil from arising, eliminating evil that has already arisen, causing unarisen good to arise, and increasing good that has already arisen;
these are the four right efforts. As for the bases of power (*ṛddhipāda*): this refers to desire, intention, energy, and wisdom; these are the four bases of power.

The five faculties (*pañcendriya*) refer to faith, diligence, mindfulness, concentration, and wisdom. The five powers (*pañcabala*) are the same as the aforementioned five faculties when they have been cultivated, increased, and developed into powers capable of destroying evil obstacles.
The factors of enlightenment (*saptabodhyaṅga*) refer to mindfulness, investigation of phenomena, diligence, joy, tranquility, concentration, and equanimity.
Regarding the eight patiences and eight knowledges: [they consist of] observing the truth of suffering within the desire realm...

Regarding untainted concentration and wisdom: if they occur within the path of uninterrupted transition (*ānantarya-mārga*), they are termed "patience regarding the dharma of suffering" (*duḥkha-dharma-kṣānti*); if they occur within the path of liberation (*vimukti-mārga*), they are termed "knowledge regarding the dharma of suffering" (*duḥkha-dharma-jñāna*).

When contemplating the truth of suffering in the realms of form and formlessness, if it occurs within the path of uninterrupted transition, it is termed "subsequent patience regarding suffering" (*duḥkha-anvaya-kṣānti*).
Within the path of liberation, this is termed the "subsequent knowledge of suffering" (*duḥkha-anvaya-jñāna*). The remaining three truths may be understood by analogy with this.
By means of these sixteen moments of mind, one suddenly severs the seeds of afflictions arising from discrimination within the three realms.

One perceives all phenomena as definitively devoid of self and devoid of what belongs to a self, thereby manifesting the principle of the tranquil cessation of ultimate truth and attaining the state of being untainted (*anāsrava*).

The seven factors of enlightenment (*saptabodhyaṅga*). As for the eightfold noble path (*āryāṣṭāṅgamārga*), it refers to right view, right thought, right speech, right action, right effort, right concentration, right mindfulness, and right livelihood.
Regarding the two kinds of *nirvāṇa*, they are *sopadhiśeṣa* (with remainder) and *nirupadhiśeṣa* (without remainder). As for the eighty-nine categories [of defilements]:

there are eight categories realized through the eight knowledges of the path of vision (*darśanamārga*)—namely, the four truths of the desire realm and the four truths of the two upper realms combined as one—and eighty-one categories of the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*).
One merely severs the afflictions during the path of uninterrupted realization (*ānantarya-mārga*) and realizes the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) during the path of liberation (*vimukti-mārga*).

As for the fivefold body of the Dharma (*pañca-dharmakāya*), it refers to precept (*śīla*), concentration (*samādhi*), wisdom (*prajñā*), liberation (*vimukti*), and the knowledge and vision of liberation (*vimukti-jñāna-darśana*).

The first three manifest virtue through their causes, while the latter two demonstrate capability by way of their fruition. This is because one cultivates the three trainings as the cause and attains the bodies of precept, concentration, and wisdom as the fruit. Thus, [the afflictions] are exhausted.

Knowledge (*jñāna*) refers to the simultaneous abandonment of both defilements and their latent tendencies, which is called the "body of liberation" (*vimukti-kāya*). Non-arising knowledge (*anutpāda-jñāna*) refers to clear and thorough awakening and illumination, which is called the "body of knowledge and vision" (*vidyā-darśana-kāya*).
As for the ten qualities of one beyond training (*daśa-aśaikṣa-dharmāḥ*): right speech, right action, and right livelihood comprise the "body of morality" (*śīla-kāya*);

right mindfulness and right concentration comprise the "body of meditative concentration" (*samādhi-kāya*); and right view, right intention, and right effort comprise the "body of wisdom" (*prajñā-kāya*); while right liberation comprises the body of liberation.

Liberation from the self is the body of right knowledge (which comprises the body of knowledge and vision). The holy life (*brahmacarya*) is the cause, cultivated through the training in ethical discipline; its fruit is called "slaying the thief. This is what is to be accomplished.

Because he cultivated the training in concentration (*samādhi-śikṣā*), his fruit is named "Worthy of Offerings" (*Arhat*). Because he cultivated the training in wisdom (*prajñā-śikṣā*), he attained the knowledge that birth has been exhausted (*kṣaya-jñāna*) and the knowledge of non-arising (*anutpāda-jñāna*);
thus his fruit is named "Non-arising. With these four knowledges perfected and having transcended the three realms, there is no further dharma to be learned;

he has become an Arhat. The remainder is as found in the *Abhidharmakośa*, the *Mahāvibhāṣā*, and the *Da-chao*. However, regarding the passage "The Śrāvakas... below, [it is from] the *Laṅkāvatāra-sūtra*.

It is said: "The fruit of *srotāpanna* has three distinctions, namely: inferior, middling, and superior. The inferior [type] undergoes rebirth at most seven times within the various realms of existence;
the middling [type] undergoes three or five births; the superior [type] enters *nirvāṇa* in this very life. (Text) The *Jiaozhang* states:
"There are two types of persons who have attained the first fruit: first, those who gradually depart [from saṃsāra], having severed the six grades of desire..."

1. Attaining the fruit of Once-returner (*sakṛdāgāmin*): having abandoned the nine grades [of afflictions], one attains the fruit of Non-returner (*anāgāmin*). Having abandoned the upper two realms, one attains Arhatship. 2. Sudden transcendence:
within a single lifetime, one suddenly abandons the nine grades of cultivated afflictions (*bhāvanā-heya*) of the three realms and immediately attains Arhatship;

there is no further fruit beyond this. 3. Neither gradual nor sudden: this is further divided into two. First, if a person who has already partially transcended desire enters the Path of True Vision (*darśana-mārga*).
One who has doubly abandoned the first six grades of afflictions of the desire realm attains the stage of Once-returner (*sakṛdāgāmin*).
