(Text) Regarding the existence or non-existence of vehicles: all Buddhas have only the Single Buddha Vehicle (*ekabuddhayāna*). There is no realization, nor is there even one [other vehicle].
It is the Buddha-vehicle (*buddhayāna*). The *Laṅkāvatāra* says: "The three vehicles and the one vehicle—these 'non-vehicles' are what I have taught.

This is the dharma-gate of the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*), which abides in non-existence. Why establish three vehicles? [They include] the various meditations (*dhyāna*), the immeasurables (*apramāṇa*), and so forth. It further says:

The vehicle of the devas and Brahmā, the vehicle of the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas, and the vehicle of the Buddhas, the Tathāgatas—I have taught these various vehicles as long as the mind continues to function.
These vehicles are not ultimate; when that mind is extinguished, there is neither vehicle nor one who rides it, and no establishment of vehicles.
I teach this as the One Vehicle (Ekayāna) for the purpose of guiding sentient beings; thus do I distinguish them.
Regarding the explanation of the various vehicles (yāna): each subsequent one is superior to the preceding.

This is because among people there are distinctions of superior and inferior, merit has degrees of greatness and smallness, stages have levels of high and low, and severance [of afflictions] has depths and shallows; therefore, the karmic rewards for those who provide offerings likewise differ.

Regarding "small retribution for much giving" and "much retribution for small giving," the *Bodhisattva-pūrva-caryā-sūtra* (Pusa benxing jing) states: What is meant by "giving much but receiving little retribution"?

Although one gives much, it is done without a heart of joy and respect; one is arrogant and conceited; and the recipient of the gift holds false and inverted views and is not a noble person (*satpuruṣa*).
This is like plowing a field: although the seeds sown are many, the harvest of fruit is very meager. What is meant by "giving little"?
The merit is great. Although what is given may be small, it is bestowed with a pure mind and without expectation of reward.
Furthermore, the recipient is a noble person—whether a Buddha or a Pratyekabuddha—who is like a fertile field. Though the seeds sown are few, the harvest of fruit is exceedingly abundant.

The *Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* states: "If one constantly gives away immeasurable wealth but does not dedicate it toward awakening, nor aspire for all sentient beings to together realize the wisdom of all modes (*sarvajñajñāna*), then although such a person practices much generosity, they will acquire little merit.

Conversely, if one gives even a small amount of wealth and is able to dedicate it toward awakening and sentient beings, then through practicing such a small act of giving, one will acquire great merit."
One receives great merit. (Text) First, it is said: "Below. The Sūtra says: "If a person does not eat, their life will end within seven days;

their complexion will become haggard, their body emaciated and their strength weakened, their mind will be distressed and their frame precarious, and they will be so exhausted that they cannot speak. If one is able to give [to them], [merit is gained]."

In every lifetime one shall receive retribution: wealth, long life, physical excellence, being beloved by others, great strength without depletion, peace and security free from affliction, and people gathering his words of Dharma.
Regarding inexhaustible merit, the *Cūḍapanthaka-sūtra* states that there are seven kinds of inexhaustible merit:
first, gardens, groves, and ponds; second, the construction of monasteries (*vihāra*); third, beds, clothing, and bedding; fourth...

1. Wealth, grain, and other such items; 2. Property belonging to the Saṃgha for traveling monks; 3. Property belonging to the Saṃgha for those suffering from illness; 4. Food and drink; 5. Medicinal decoctions.

Regarding the *nyagrodha* tree, the *Piyū-jing* (Analogies Sutra) states: When the Buddha went outside the city of Śrāvastī to beg for alms, there was a woman who paid him homage and placed rice into his bowl.
The Buddha offered a blessing for her: "Plant one and it shall produce a hundred; plant a hundred and it shall produce a billion. She attained [this merit].
He saw the Truth of the Path. His husband did not believe the Buddha’s words. "You have seen the *nyagrodha* tree;

it was planted when the seed was as small as a mustard grain, yet it grew to a height of forty *li*. Each year it yields tens of thousands of *hu* of fruit. The merit produced by sowing a bowl of alms-food is likewise so.
Upon hearing this, the husband and wife’s minds were opened, and they attained the first fruit of the Path. (Text) A noble princess raised a king’s maidservant. One day, while sweeping...
In her previous life, she obtained a single copper coin and immediately offered it to the Sangha. After her death, she became the daughter of King Aśoka;
from her right hand emerged gold coins that were inexhaustible. She went to question the Arhat Yaśas, and only then did she learn the cause of her former deeds.

It is difficult. Yet, both difficulty and ease arise from the mind. If doubt arises in the mind, what is not difficult becomes difficult; if the mind is free of doubt, then even what is difficult is not difficult.

He practiced great generosity. Śakra, Lord of Devas, tested him by commanding a border king to become a pigeon while he himself transformed into a hawk.

The pigeon flew to the feet of King Prasenajit, and the hawk followed closely behind. The king cut the flesh from his thigh, continuing until his entire body was exhausted and he weighed his very marrow, [offering it to save the pigeon].

[The man] gave [his flesh] to the pigeons, and the hawk returned to its original form. He was asked, "What was your resolve? He replied, "I vowed to attain Buddhahood in order to rescue and deliver those multitudes.
Śakra, the Lord of Devas, marveled at this and applied celestial medicine to him; his wounds were instantly healed.
Even cases such as Bi Gan having his heart torn out, or Yi and Qi dying of hunger, were all instances of those who sacrificed their lives to perfect their virtue.
[Commentary] "To attain... and below follows the third section: the difficulty of supramundane practice. First is the difficulty of initiating practice based on the teachings.
The scriptural canons are accumulated like mountain peaks, all of them being ambrosial *amṛta* and *sarpis*. Yet, while the eight sufferings burn us with intensity, how can we hope to behold them?

When the Buddha was in the world, I was submerged in saṃsāra; when I emerged from it, the Buddha had entered parinirvāṇa. Therefore, being before the Buddha or after the Buddha is what is meant by [the difficulty].

Difficult indeed! Beautiful forms are what people desire; rare and exquisite things are what the multitude greedily seeks. To neither desire nor seek them may be called difficult. Wealth and honor press upon one from all sides;
to repay resentment with uprightness and to feel apprehension when facing affairs are but common sentiments.
Now, you wish to be without mind and not give way to anger—how could this not be difficult? If one can sacrifice one's entire body to seek even half [of the truth], it is possible.
Verse: Receiving the prophecy upon crafting an image of the Buddha; husband and wife sharing one bed yet sleeping separately;

seeing the five exquisite sensual pleasures without deriving joy from them; feigning deafness when faced with insults; and feeling compassionate mercy without resentment even when being shot with arrows.
If one acts without desire, like a wooden man watching flowers and birds, and does not unexpectedly commit slaughter—
just as a performer watches or a judge hears lawsuits— then these various hardships will no longer be difficult.

[Commentary] Regarding the "inferior teachings," first the difficulties are clarified. As for the Buddha’s successive explanations of these difficulties, the Sūtra states that there are eight difficulties:
first, the hells; second, the hungry ghosts; third, the animals; fourth, the borderlands; fifth, long-lived heavens;
sixth, although one obtains a human body, it is crippled or afflicted by various diseases; seventh, being born into a family with false views; eighth, being born into... [the text continues].
Whether preceding the Buddha or arising after him, these [principles] are derived from the *Analects* (*Lunyu*) via two direct phrases. They state: "Repay enmity with straightforwardness;
repay virtue with virtue. Be cautious when facing affairs; prefer planning before achieving them. These, however, pertain to those who possess anger and mental afflictions.
One must instead be like Bo Yi and Shu Qi, who did not harbor old grudges, or like Laozi and Zhuangzi, who were tranquil and non-active; only then can one be called [truly virtuous].
It is without anger and without mind. If one can humble oneself, it will not be difficult next. Regarding the "half-verse," the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* states:

In the past, the Buddha was a Brahmin who sat in meditation in the Snowy Mountains, seeking the Dharma and practicing the Way. Śakra, the Lord of Devas, went to test him, transforming himself into a rākṣasa and reciting half a verse, which said:
"All conditioned phenomena are impermanent; they are the nature of arising and ceasing. The Bodhisattva then sought out the remainder of the verse.

[The Bodhisattva] replied, "Half [of my body remains]. He asked, "Your belly is hungry; it is difficult to describe [your hunger]. What do you wish to eat? He replied, "Human blood. [The Bodhisattva] requested, "I pray that you will explain [the Dharma];
I shall offer my own body as a gift. He then spoke this verse: "When birth and death have ceased, nirvana is bliss.
The Bodhisattva inscribed this verse everywhere upon trees and stones, then climbed a tree to relinquish his body. The rākṣasa caught him with his hands, and he returned to his original form.
Having paid homage, they departed. Regarding those who receive the prediction [of enlightenment], the *Sūtra on the Merit of Image-Making* states:

When Śakra invited the Buddha to ascend to the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven to spend the three-month summer retreat and preach the Dharma for his mother, King Udayana, longing to see him, wished to create a wooden image.
The celestial being Viśvakarman manifested as a craftsman; as he wielded his axe to hew fragrant wood, the sound [resounded] above.
Pervading all the heavens, he arrived at the site of the Buddha’s assembly. The Tathāgata praised him from afar and bestowed upon him the prediction of Bodhi.
Thus one knows that particular and universal characteristics do not depart from the Three Jewels of Sustenance; the Reward Body and Dharma Body do not depart from the manifested images.

Therefore, upon seeing the Honored One’s countenance once, or hearing the sound of the Sūtra once, it is as if one has beheld the Buddha and heard the Dharma; one should naturally give rise to great [faith].
How fortunate! Yet the old woman to the east of the city was born at the same time as the Buddha and dwelt in the same place, passing through this world together;
yet she never saw the Buddha nor received his Dharma voice. For this reason, her mind harbored the doubt that such a misfortune might not be unique to her own time.
Regarding those who sleep separately, the *Buddha-bhadrakalpika-sūtra* (The Sutra of the Buddha’s Past Deeds) states: "The youth Piṇḍola..."
The daughter Bhadrā became his wife. They practiced together with a shared aspiration, never touching one another with impure intent.
Whenever the son slept, the woman would rise to practice walking meditation (*caṃkrama*); whenever the woman slept, the son would likewise practice walking meditation.

Thus they spent twelve years together in the same room without sharing a bed. Later, while the woman was sleeping, her hand dangled down toward the ground. Suddenly, a snake approached—her husband [woke].
Fearing that it might sting her daughter, he held it on his wife’s arm and placed it upon the bed. At that time, the wife rebuked him, saying, "Why have you now given rise to such a thought?
The husband told her the truth of the matter. Afterwards, they both went forth to join the Buddha and renounced the household life, and both attained the Way.
The husband was none other than Mahākāśyapa, and the wife was the Bhikṣuṇī Jāmbunada-prabhāsā; it was they.

Regarding those who find no joy, the *Xingyuan chao* states: One hundred years after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, there was a king of Pāṭaliputra named Aśoka (also known as A-yù, which translates as "Sorrowless").

Because his younger brother, Vitāśoka (which translates as "Remover of Sorrow"), revered and believed in non-Buddhist paths, he came to doubt that the monks were capable of transcending worldly concerns.
Desiring to employ a skillful means to lead him into the Buddha-dharma, he said to the minister: "I am now going to bathe;
you should take the clothes and the celestial crown I have removed and give them to my younger brother, commanding him to ascend the royal throne.
Say to him: 'The King has no heir; you shall succeed to the throne. Now let us test him—what could be wrong with this? When the king emerged and saw his anger, he issued a command.

He was to be executed. The ministers remonstrated and urged him [to spare him], but the King said, "Postpone it for seven days. He then provided him with various kinds of music, dancing girls, and attendants.
All the ministers and citizens went to inquire after his well-being. Furthermore, there were maidservants with disheveled hair carrying bells who walked before the executioner;
the executioner stood at the gate with a sword in hand. When the seven days had elapsed, he was led to the King's presence. The King—
He asked his younger brother, "During the seven days you served as king, you had music and entertainment at your disposal and were attended by court ladies; did you feel any craving for these things?
The royal brother replied, "During those seven days, I felt no craving for the sounds of the women’s singing and dancing, nor for the palace, nor for the bedding."
Regarding famous garments and various precious jewels, because he contemplated the fear of death, he was unaware of such matters.
Seeing an executioner standing outside the gate holding a sword, and hearing the sound of a ringing bell, the stake of death pierced his heart;
he knew nothing of the five exquisite sensual pleasures and could not sleep in peace. The King said to his younger brother: "For seven days, contemplate life..."
Fearing death and finding no joy, they do not give rise to craving or attachment. The disciples of the Buddha observe birth and death day after day;
how could they find joy or give rise to a mind of affliction? They view the body as an enemy and the three realms of existence as a house on fire.
Deeply delighting in the Dharma of liberation, they do not crave the five desires; their minds are like lotus flowers.

He remained in the water without being soiled. His younger brother, because of this, turned his mind back toward the faith and took refuge in the Triple Gem; he subsequently left the household life and attained the fruit of an Arhat.
As for "not hearing": when Fu Bi was young, there were those who constantly reviled him, yet Fu remained as if he did not hear them.
Someone reported this to him. Fu said, "I fear he was merely reviling someone else. He added, "He called out my name clearly.
Fu replied, "There are many people in the world with the same name; he was not reviling me. Later, Lü Mengzheng served as a State Councilor.
As he was entering the court, a court official pointed at him and said, "Is this youth also participating in the administration? Li Mengzheng feigned not having heard it.
His colleagues wished to inquire after his name, but Mengzheng firmly stopped them, saying, "Once I know a person's name, I shall never forget it for the rest of my life."

"It is better not to have heard [the Dharma] at all. As for "The Compassionate One": King Udayana’s principal queen took refuge in the Buddha and received the precepts, attaining the stage of *srotāpanna*.

When the king listened to slanderous words and drew his bow to shoot the queen, she saw him and felt neither fear nor anger; with a single-minded focus on the Buddha, she felt compassion for the king.
The arrow circled three times and returned to rest before the king. This occurred with every one of the hundred arrows. The king was greatly...

Filled with dread, he went to the Buddha to confess his transgression. Regarding the phrase "without a mind," it refers to the *Jingzhuye zhang jing* (Sūtra on Purifying Karmic Obstructions), which states:
The bhikṣu Vimalaprabha was out begging for alms when he encountered a courtesan skilled in sorcery. Consequently, they engaged in sexual desire together.
Upon returning, he reproached himself and went to the Buddha to repent for his sin. The Buddha asked, "Did you have a mind [of intent]? He replied, "I did not."
"It is the mind. The Buddha said, "Since you have no mind, how can you say that you have committed an offense? In the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra*, it is said of the Heaven of Delighting in Transformations:
"I have no lustful mind; I merely respond to your actions. When we lie together, the flavor is like chewing wax. I had no intention to kill."
When Emperor Wu of the Liang dynasty was informed of a grave crime, he would remain displeased for the entire day; even when a plot of rebellion was discovered, he would weep as he granted clemency.
Emperor Taizong of the Tang dynasty said to his attendants: "Because I consider the death penalty to be most solemn, I have the case reviewed three times before execution is carried out.
This is killing only as a last resort, not out of intentional malice. (From the *Śāriputra-abhidharma-śāstra* / *Shan jian lü*).
It is said: Prince Diśu of King Aśoka renounced the world and caused the Buddha-dharma to flourish. At that time, there was a minister who, having perverted the king’s intent, killed various bhikṣus.
Diśu shielded and protected them; the minister immediately set aside his sword and went to inform the king, saying, "Let the Saṃgha recite the precepts.
When the monks did not comply with the command, the minister executed them according to their offenses. Diśu prohibited this, and upon hearing it, the king fainted from distress.
After the *sūtra* recitation had concluded, [the King] was rebuked, saying: "I commanded that the precepts be recited; why have you killed? The King went before the Saṃgha and said:
"I do not understand this matter. Who has incurred the offense? A monk asked the King: "Did you have the intention to kill? The King replied:
"I originally sent him forth with the intent of merit; I had no intention to kill. The monks said: "If it is as the King says, the King himself is without fault."

Regarding the offense: the one who kills incurs the sin. The preceding proof [concerning] suicide was intended to show there is no volition; this proof [concerning] instigating another to kill is intended to show there is no volition.
Therefore, it is likened to a wooden man watching flowers or an actor being executed—both are devoid of the afflictions of greed and hatred.

[Commentary] "Broadly speaking" refers to the second point: the difficulty of studying the Path and realizing its fruits. A single phrase is difficult to comprehend; how much more so when one seeks to master the entirety of the Tripiṭaka?

Even the Elder [Śāriputra] was subject to derision, so how could one expect to show deference to beginners? Those who are empty-minded yet haughty, relying on their own pretenses, can well be understood.

The spirit of competition is thick; it is difficult to discourse on the "Equalization of Things. Sentiments regarding right and wrong are intense, and those who conceal evil while extolling good are few.

Much is heard with the ears and spoken from the mouth, yet those who merely repeat what they have overheard on the road are many. As soon as one has a slight awakening, they claim to have "seen their nature and enlightened their mind.
Before the principles are fully exhausted, how can one thoroughly penetrate cause and effect? One must surely be like Ānanda in his vast learning.

Through the respectful salutation of one who is not held in low esteem, Nanda prostrated to Upāli; through the inquiry of Śakra regarding the jackal, he endured suffering and humiliation without contention;
by following his teacher’s instructions, he traveled everywhere to study. A young woman attained profound contemplation, seeing the Truth and realizing the fruit;
an elderly monk focused his mindfulness, severing delusions and realizing the Real. Thus, if every encounter becomes easy, what else could be difficult to accomplish?
[Commentary] Following the first phrase, the initial difficulty is clarified. Regarding the Tripiṭaka, which encompasses both the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna:
as for the one who reviled the Sthavira, after the parinirvāṇa of Vipaśyin Buddha, there was a young bhikṣu who had mastered the Tripiṭaka and received offerings from many people.
There was also an elderly bhikṣu, a mahallaka, whose voice and appearance were ugly and loathsome. The youth reviled him with such words. The sound [is as follows].
"The sound was not like the barking of a dog. The elder bhikṣu asked, "Why do you revile me? I have attained the fruit of Arhatship.
He then raised his right hand, emitting a great radiance that illuminated the ten directions. "How could you fail to recognize this and commit such evil karma?
The Tripiṭaka master was struck with terror; he prostrated at the elder's feet and repented. Because he had reviled the Elder, for five hundred lifetimes he would always [be born as...]
In the form of a dog, those who possess something to rely upon may use their extensive learning and intellectual mastery to look down on others;

or they may pride themselves on their literary compositions and technical skills; or they may rely on their eloquence and sharp rhetoric; or their illustrious lineage and noble clan; or their age and longevity; or their merit and virtue.

Thus they give rise to various forms of arrogance and develop great conceit. Although there are many manifestations of pride, the "I-conceit" (*asmimāna*) is its root. As for the one who equalizes all things, it was Zhuangzi.
The Master has the "Discourse on Equalizing All Things. It states that birth and death are simultaneous; there is neither completion nor destruction.

In the world, nothing is greater than the tip of a fine autumn hair, while Mount Tai is considered small. Nothing is more long-lived than an infant who dies prematurely, while Pengzu is considered short-lived.
Heaven and earth are born together with me; the myriad things are one with me. The *Prajñāpāramitā* says:
"This Dharma is equal; there is no high or low. The *Awakening of Faith* says: "Do not revere those who uphold the precepts, nor loathe those who violate them; do not value long-standing practice."

Do not look down upon beginners. Since you currently still harbor views of self and others, and maintain a distinction between self and other, how could you possibly level out long and short or unify prosperity and decline?
To enter the phrase: when one meets a true spiritual friend (*kalyāṇamitra*), one penetrates the very source of the Dharma; whereas what is heard by chance along the road is mere hearsay.
This is the abandonment of virtue. Nowadays, people do not associate with virtuous friends; they merely cultivate their speech and ears. Consequently, they have no affinity for true knowledge.
To briefly explain the phrase "seeing one's nature": the Way encompasses both teaching-practice and principle-fruition. The path of the superior and noble belongs to teaching and practice;
this path of seeing one's nature belongs to principle and fruition. It is certainly not difficult. Ānanda did not...
This can be easily understood. Regarding Nanda, the *Puyao jing* (Sutra of the Universal Radiance) states:

When the Buddha’s younger brother Nanda first shaved his hair, he performed prostrations in succession until he reached Upāli, at which point he stopped and did not prostrate, saying, "He is my domestic servant. The World-Honored One then said:
"Regarding the sequence of the precepts, one does not abide in [distinctions of] noble or base; one should contemplate the Noble Dharma and not give rise to arrogance.
At that time, Nanda abandoned his own conceit and paid homage to Upāli, whereupon the great earth shook. As for the questioner, the *Adbhutadharma-paryāya* (Sutra of Unprecedented Events) states:
Śakra asked the jackal, "What merit is there in giving to the greedy and giving the Dharma? He replied: "To bestow..."
Giving food and drink relieves the needs of a single day; giving wealth and treasures relieves the deficiencies of a lifetime.

To increase [the roots of merit] while still bound [to saṃsāra], yet teaching and transforming others through the Dharma, is called the "gift of Dharma" (*dharmadāna*); it can cause sentient beings to transcend the world. The commentary explains:
When the Lord of Devas humbled himself before a jackal, he was free from any perception of self and other, or of high and low. It is as follows:
"Śāriputra, when you offered a bowl of rice to the Buddha, the Buddha immediately gave it as a gift to a dog.
You asked: 'You gave me the rice, while he gave the rice to a dog; who obtains the greater merit? He replied: 'The Buddha obtained greater merit by giving to the dog.
Why? Because merit arises from the mind; it does not emerge from the field [of the recipient]. The mind is the internal master, whereas the field is an external matter.'"
Śāriputra’s merit does not equal even a thousand-millionth part of the Buddha’s mind. Because the Buddha acts with a mind of equanimity, his merit is superior;
because Śāriputra acts with a mind of acceptance and rejection, his merit is slight. It is clearly understood that superiority and inferiority arise from the mind, not from the field [of merit].
Regarding "the one free from contention": once, a bhikṣu went to the door of a jeweler while begging for alms. The jeweler was working for the king to pierce pearls.
There was a great maṇi-jewel. He went inside to fetch some food. A goose saw the jewel; it reflected upon the bhikṣu’s robe, making it appear red.
Its appearance resembled meat, so the goose immediately swallowed it. When the jeweler brought the food out, he searched for the jewel but did not know where it was.
He said to the bhikṣu, "Have you taken my jewel? The bhikṣu feared that the goose’s life would be harmed, and...
"I venture to inform you. The pearl-maker immediately beat him with a staff and bound him, until his eyes, ears, nose, and mouth all bled.
A goose came to drink the blood, and the goose was also beaten to death. The bhikṣu then explained the cause; the pearl-maker cut open the goose and obtained the pearl.
He immediately wailed and wept in sorrowful repentance, speaking these verses: "Namo to you who firmly uphold the precepts! For the sake of a goose’s body, you endured suffering;

You never committed an act of violation or deficiency— Such a reality is truly rare to find. If even as an animal you endured suffering without making distinctions, How could you possibly engage in double-tongued speech among humans?
"Universal Seeker" (Pien-chan) refers to Sudhana’s universal pilgrimage to fifty-three spiritual friends.
A virtuous friend (*kalyāṇamitra*). Regarding the "woman," the *Ratnakaraṇḍa-sūtra* states: Long ago, there was a woman who had deep faith in the Triple Gem.
She invited monks for a vegetarian feast and sought the Dharma with a sincere heart. The bhikṣus, not understanding her intent, hid themselves and returned to the monastery.

However, this woman contemplated that conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta-dharma*) are impermanent, suffering, empty, and lack self-mastery. Through profound contemplation, she attained the [fruit of] Stream-enterer (*srotāpanna*).
The fruit of stream-entry (*srotāpanna*). (Text) This realization of the nature of reality is not difficult. Regarding "the old monk," that sutra further states:

In the past, there was a bhikṣu who was elderly and mentally obscured. Seeing various young bhikṣus expounding the Dharma of the four fruits, he felt envy in his heart and said, "I pray that you will grant me the four fruits. The youths mocked him, saying, "One must obtain a fine..."
When it was time to eat, the old man was greatly delighted and immediately prepared a feast. The youths teased him, saying, "Sit here in the corner of this house;
we shall give you the fruit [of the path]. The old man rejoiced and followed their instructions.
The youths then struck him on the head with a leather ball and said, "This is the fruit of a *srotāpanna*. Upon hearing this, the old man focused his mind upon it.

Without scattering [the sand], he immediately attained the first fruit (srotāpatti). The youths again teased him, saying, "Although you have now attained the first fruit, you still have seven more births and seven more deaths.
He then moved another corner [of the sand]. The youths again struck him with a ball and said, "We grant you the fruit of a sakṛdāgāmin.
The elder became even more focused in his mindfulness and immediately realized the second fruit. The youths spoke again, saying, "Although..."
They attained the second fruit [of the path], yet they still faced the hardship of coming and going through birth and death. You should move your seat again.
The younger ones struck them once more with the ball and said, "We grant you the fruit of an Anāgāmin. The elders applied themselves with even greater sincerity and further realized the third fruit.
The younger ones again teased them, saying, "Although you have attained the third fruit, you will still undergo existence within the realms of form and formlessness."
"The body is subject to outflows; it is impermanent and subject to change, and moment by moment it is suffering. You should move your seat again.

He struck the younger ones with a ball once more and said, "I shall grant you the fruit of Arhatship. The elder ones applied themselves with redoubled sincerity and further realized the four fruits of the path.

He was immediately filled with great joy and prepared a vegetarian feast to express his gratitude. He engaged in a discussion on the *dharmapadas* with the younger monks; they were all somewhat obstructed in their understanding.
An elder spoke to them, saying, "I have indeed already attained the fruit of Arhatship. Thereupon, the younger monks all sought repentance for their playful transgressions.
Therefore, if one seeks with a sincere heart, there is nothing that cannot be obtained. (This passage serves as proof that studying the Path is not difficult. This is [the meaning].
[The text] concludes with "Below. [Commentary]:
Following "Below," there are three points regarding the difficulty of extensively transforming sentient beings. Sentient beings are boundless, and their mental activities are inexhaustible;

how can they all be delivered so as to cause them to transcend birth and death? It is difficult because, for example, a *śrāmaṇera* may retreat from his resolve, and a student may lack aspiration. [This is illustrated by the case of] the Eye.
The eye craves forms; the ear discriminates sounds; the nose smells various fragrances; and the tongue relishes flavors.

To flow against the current of these sense-faculties and reach the state of non-arising and non-extinction—how could this be easy to attain? Since the root of the afflictions of sentient beings is vast, the Dharma-medicine of the Tathāgata is likewise manifold.

There are responsive capacities, whether rigid or supple, deviant or correct; accordingly, there are teaching-gates of compassion and majesty, or of opposition and compliance. [It is not that one] cannot...
Each of these was skillfully understood. How could one cause every person to enter the Way?

Is it not like Kātyāyana’s excellent teaching on returning to the precepts, or Śāriputra’s clever transformation of the "washing gold," or Pilindavatsa who did not perceive the sound of the carriage, or Subhūti who did not hear the sound of the drum, or Mālikā who used wine to save the kitchen official, or the Great Compassionate One who used killing to bring merchants back to life? Examine this carefully.
That being so, even what is difficult is not truly difficult. Thus we know that the difficulty inherent in speech lies with the person.

For one who possesses the resolve of the mind, entering the conflagration at the end of the kalpa, ascending to the Brahma Heaven, grasping empty space, or casting away the great trichiliocosm would not be considered difficult.
Yet for one who lacks such resolve, even to behold a Buddhist scripture is still difficult; how much more so to propagate the teaching above and transform those below? Now...

The Buddha raised these difficult words precisely because he wished for us to give rise to a mind of fierce courage and establish firm vows, thereby being able to practice what is difficult to practice;
such a person is rare among ordinary people.

[Commentary] Below the section on the "multitude," first the difficulties are clarified. Regarding those who retreat from the resolve: the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states that in the past there was an arhat who led a śrāmaṇera.
Carrying his robes and bowl, the śrāmaṇera suddenly gave rise to the mind of great bodhi.
The arhat, knowing this, took back the robes and bowl and ordered him to go on ahead. As they traveled further, they encountered a pool of water teeming with many tiny insects.
Reflecting that sentient beings are numerous and difficult to transform and deliver, he then withdrew from his great resolve. It was the original rule for an Arhat to carry the robe and walk behind;
the śrāmaṇera asked why, and he replied: "You have generated the great resolve and should precede me, an Arhat.

Since you have now withdrawn from the aspiration for the Path, you are but an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*) and ought not to stand before me, a holy one (*ārya*). Regarding those who do not wish to comply, the *Dharmaparyāya of the Lotus Sūtra*, in the "Chapter on Entrustment," states:
Furthermore, there were eight thousand persons, both those in training and those beyond training, who made this vow:
"We, too, shall extensively proclaim this sutra in other lands. Why is this? Because in this Sahā world, people are for the most part wicked and evil;
they harbor overweening pride, their merit is meager, and they are turbid with anger, deceitful, and crooked, for their minds are not sincere. [The six] faculties of the stream-enterers: six.
The faculties flow toward the six sense objects. To "go against" this flow means to turn back the current and revolve it into the One, so that the six functions no longer operate.

"Neither arising nor ceasing" means being as such, unmoving. Question: What is the difference in meaning between this "immovability in the face of objects" and the aforementioned "absence of mind when encountering things"?
Answer: The former refers to not giving rise to thoughts of good or evil while performing actions through the three karmas; the latter refers to...
The six sense organs encounter their objects without being moved by thoughts of defilement or purity. Regarding the two phrases concerning sentient beings, the *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra* states:

"Just as a physician treats various ailments, because illnesses differ, the prescriptions and medicines are diverse; so too do I, for the sake of all sentient beings, eliminate the disease of afflictions.
Knowing the superiority or inferiority of their faculties, I expound the various Dharma-gates. Regarding the two phrases on "response," [it refers to those who are] stubborn and fierce.
One subdues sentient beings through majestic power; one gathers gentle and soft sentient beings through compassion; one accords with those of wrong views by engaging in their activities;
and one advances those of right understanding toward the Path through compliance. If one wishes to fully liberate them, [one should act thus].

This is indeed difficult. For this reason, the two vehicles (śrāvaka and pratyekabuddha) cannot destroy the cognitive obstacles (*jñeyāvaraṇa*). Even in the Mahāyāna, there are afflictions as numerous as the sands of the Ganges;
how could it be as easy as the lower [vehicles]? Next, it is not difficult. First, saving people is not difficult. Regarding those who are skilled in teaching, the Vinaya states:
Kātyāyana was well able to teach and transform others so that they returned to the precepts, causing even a butcher to receive the one-night fast (*upavāsa*) and a lecher to receive...
Regarding the precept for the day: when one later receives retribution, one perceives the signs of prior pleasure during both day and night.
The *Dīrgha Āgama* states that there was a non-Buddhist who adhered to the view of annihilationism (*ucchedadṛṣṭi*), claiming that there is no other world. To refute him, it was said:
"If there were no other world, then there would be today but no tomorrow. Furthermore, he asked: "I see people die and never return; how can you say they undergo suffering?"
"There is no other world. [The Teacher] replied: "Suppose a criminal is being detained; could he ever return? (2) Question: "If one is born in heaven, why does one not return? Answer:
"It is like a person who has fallen into a latrine and escaped; would they ever be willing to enter that latrine again? Furthermore, one day in heaven corresponds to a hundred years here.
Having been born there for only three or five days, one has not yet had the leisure to develop a mind of returning. Even if there were those who did return,"
“You have already transformed [your consciousness]. How can you possibly know this? (3) Question: “I boil sinners in cauldrons and cover them with a tight lid;
I watch for them, but their spirits do not emerge. Therefore, there is no other world. Answer: “When you sleep during the day, people standing beside you see your spirit emerge. (4) Question:
“I flay the skin from dead men, cut their flesh into pieces, and crush their bones, yet I cannot find their spirits.”
[Question: One knows that there is no other world. [Answer: It is like a child splitting firewood; if one seeks fire by splitting it inch by inch, how could fire ever be obtained?
(5) [Question: When I weigh a dead person, they are heavier. If the spirit had departed, they should be lighter. Since they are not lighter, there is no departing spirit.
"Therefore, there is no other world. [The respondent] answers: "It is like iron combined with fire; the iron is light. When the iron loses the fire, it becomes heavy.
When a person is alive, they possess a spirit (*śiva*), and thus are light. When a person dies and loses the spirit, they become heavy" (6). [The opponent] asks:

"I have seen those at the point of death who, when turned over to search for their spirits, could not find them. Therefore, I know there is no other world. [The respondent] answers: "It is like a person turning over a shell to seek the sound of it."
"Can one even obtain a reputation? (7) The non-Buddhists praised his subduing [of opponents].

Furthermore, when the Brahmins learned in worldly treatises asked five hundred Śākyas, "Is there anyone among you who can debate with me?", the five hundred Śākyas replied, "The lowest of our renunciants is Cūḍapanthaka;
if you defeat him in debate, we shall give you our name. Thereupon, the experts in worldly treatises were defeated. Later, on the road, they encountered Panthaka and questioned him.
"What is meant by 'name'? He replied, "One should ask about the meaning. "What is meant by 'questioning'? He asked, "Are you able to debate the meaning with me?

He replied, "I am able to debate with the Brahma King; how much more so with you, who are blind and sightless? He asked, "Blindness is the absence of eyes, and the absence of eyes is blindness; is this not redundant?
Cūḷapanthaka performed eighteen miraculous transformations, whereupon [the other] said, "This monk can only perform flight-transformations."
He still did not understand the meaning. Kātyāyana heard this from afar with his divine ear; he immediately concealed Pāṇḍava and manifested himself to him, appearing exactly like him.
Descending from the air, he asked, "What is your name? He replied, "My name is 'Man-puruṣa' (Male Man). He asked, "'Man' is the same as 'puruṣa'."
"‘Man’ is simply ‘male. Is this not redundant? The scholar of worldly scriptures replied: ‘Stop, stop! Set aside these miscellaneous discussions;
we may now discuss the profound meaning. He then asked: ‘Is it possible to attain nirvāṇa without relying on the dharmas? He answered: ‘Without relying on the dharmas of the five aggregates.’"

One can attain *nirvāṇa*. (1) Question: Upon what do the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*) depend for their arising? Answer: They arise dependent upon craving (*tṛṣṇā*). (2) Question: How is craving severed? Answer:
By relying on the Eightfold Noble Path (*āryāṣṭāṅgamārga*), one is able to sever craving. (3) When the worldly scriptures heard this, they were freed from dust and defilement.
Regarding the skillful transformation [of beings], the *Vyākhyāyukti* states: Maudgalyāyana was instructing two disciples, yet for a long time they had attained no realization. He asked:
"Śāriputra," [the Buddha said]. Śāriputra replied, "By what teaching? The Buddha answered, "The son of a goldsmith was taught the meditation on impurity;
the son of a washerman was taught the meditation on counting the breath. Śāriputra said, "That is incorrect. It was the son of a smith..."

One should teach counting the breaths. To the son who washes clothes, one should teach the meditation on impurity. Maudgalyāyana followed these instructions and immediately attained arhatship. He praised Śāriputra, saying:
"I was always by the riverbank, practicing the washing of clothes for my own purification; I settled my mind upon white bones.
Because our dispositions were similar, it was easy for me to attain realization, requiring no great effort, and it entered my mind with great speed. The goldsmith... [always...]
The bellows: inhalation and exhalation are wind; because they share similar characteristics, it is easy to take pleasure in entering *ānāpāna* (mindfulness of breathing).
Among sentient beings, there are respective degrees of superiority and inferiority in their habitual practices. When practicing within one's own domain, one attains what is to be attained.
To practice within the domain of another is like a fish fallen onto dry land. This is the second turning of the Wheel of Dharma, the great general of the Buddha-dharma.
Among all the śrāvakas, he has attained the most supreme wisdom. Below the *Balarāma* [section], next is "Not Difficult Regarding Objects.
The *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* says: The minister Puṣkara, filled with joy, came forward to pay homage. The Buddha asked, "What dharma have you attained that brings you such joy? He replied:
The bhikṣu Balaṃ was sitting beneath a tree when five hundred chariots passed by one after another. A person approached and asked, "Did you see the chariots passing?
He replied, "I did not see them. Again he asked, "Did you at least hear the sound of the chariots? He replied, "I did not hear it either."
He asked, "Were you sleeping? He replied, "I was not sleeping; I was simply in meditative contemplation. He then praised him, saying, "The sound of the cart was *khakkha*.

You were awake yet did not hear it. How single-minded is your application! It is truly rare to reach such a state. Thereupon, he attained the joy of the Dharma (*dharmaprīti*). The Buddha said, "I am also like this.
Long ago, while traveling through Aśmaka, a violent thunderbolt struck, killing four oxen and two farmers at once."
At that time, [the man] was terrified of death and said, "I too have not heard it. He remained fixed in awareness while walking up and down.
Another person paid homage and followed me as I walked. I asked, "Why are you so hurried? He replied, "Just now, four oxen and two men were struck dead by lightning.
Did the World-Honored One alone not hear it? I said, "I did not hear it. He asked, "Were you sleeping? I said, "I was not sleeping; I was simply in samādhi. Thus he spoke.
Others also sighed in admiration and attained the joy of the Dharma. Regarding "one born into emptiness," the *Māyopama-samādhi-sūtra* states:
"Even if the great earth were made into a drum and Mount Sumeru into a drumstick, and they were struck against the ear of Subhūti, they could not cause even the slightest movement of his mind.
Why is this? Because he has entered the samādhi of emptiness. Below the section on Mālikā, the subsequent skillful means are not difficult.
The *Adbhuta-dharma Sūtra* states: King Prasenajit was out hunting and became extremely hungry.
He ordered the execution of his kitchen official, Sukāra (this being his name), as he was the only one who met with the king's approval. At that time, Queen Mallikā heard of this;
she immediately prepared wine and food, took several courtesans, and went to the king’s location. They drank together and enjoyed themselves, whereupon the king’s anger subsided. The Queen—
He then falsely conveyed the king’s command: "Do not kill the kitchen official. When the king arrived the following morning, his countenance was haggard.
The queen asked, "What ailment do you have? The king said, "Last night, driven by the fires of hunger, I killed the kitchen official in a fit of rage;
I am now filled with regret and sorrow. The queen laughed and said, "That man is still here. The king was greatly delighted and immediately went with the queen to visit the Buddha.
Regarding the confession of offenses: this refers to upholding the five precepts while having transgressed these two—those against drinking alcohol and speaking falsehoods.
What are the circumstances of such cases? The World-Honored One replied: "In cases of such violations of the precepts, one attains great merit and incurs no fault.
Why is this? Because it is for the sake of benefiting others. As the *Ratnakūṭa Sūtra* states regarding the time of Dīpaṃkara Buddha: there were five hundred merchants.
They entered the sea to gather treasures. Among them was a thief who intended to kill the others in order to seize their jewels.

At that time, there was a leader named Mahākāruṇika (Great Compassion). During the night, he received a divine revelation in a dream: "If this thief kills these five hundred bodhisattvas, he shall fall into hell;
you must employ skillful means to preserve each of their lives. Mahākāruṇika reflected: "By killing this one person... [five]...
"Those who preserved their lives have all escaped the suffering of hell and left the evil realms behind.

Having felt compassion, he immediately killed the wicked thief with his spear, enabling the merchants to return safely and securely. At that time, the one of great compassion was none other than myself;
the five hundred merchants were the five hundred bodhisattvas of the Bhadrakalpa. It was through my practice of skillful means that this occurred.

One attains transcendence from the hardships of birth and death for billions of kalpas. Thus, the following section concludes by providing an illustration. Regarding "entering a kalpa," the *Lotus Sūtra* states:
"Even if one were to carry dry grass into the conflagration at the end of a kalpa and not be burned, this would not yet be difficult.
Even if one were to place the entire great earth upon the tip of one's toenail and ascend to the Brahma Heaven, this too would not yet be difficult. Suppose there were a person..."
To walk about while grasping empty space with one’s hand is not yet difficult; nor is it difficult to move the great trichiliocosm with a toe and hurl it far away to another land.
Furthermore, [the Buddha said: "After my parinirvāṇa, who will be able to protect and uphold this sutra and expound it extensively?
Now, before the Buddha, he himself makes this vow (the first chant): "O sons of the Buddhas, who..."
One who is able to protect the Dharma should make a great vow so that it may endure for a long time (second recitation). O sons of good family, each of you should reflect with careful attention:

this is a difficult task; you should make a great vow (third recitation). Although other sūtras exist as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, even if one were to expound them all, it would not be considered difficult.
However, if one can uphold the eighty-four thousand treasuries of the Dharma and the twelve [fold teachings], [it is truly difficult].
To expound this section of the sutra for others and cause all listeners to attain the six supernormal powers—though such a benefit exists, it is not yet considered difficult.
(Text) By this we may infer that for those who possess the [right] mind, even what is difficult is not difficult. Regarding "no one is equal":
the *Lotus Sutra* states, "After the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, in the midst of a degenerate age, to read this sutra even briefly is indeed difficult; [it is difficult] before me..."
"After my parinirvāṇa, who will be able to receive, uphold, read, and recite this sutra? Now, before the Buddha, I shall personally utter a vow:

this sutra is difficult to uphold; if one upholds it even for a moment, I shall rejoice. (Text) By this we know that the absence of aspiration is not a difficulty to overcome, but rather a difficulty itself.

Regarding "upward propagation" and so forth: "attaining the sight of the sutra" and so on refer to the seven difficulties; "cultivating oneself" refers to the intermediate [practice]; "extensive study" refers to the lower [practice].
The "Seven Difficulties" (*sapta-durghaṭā*) refer to the upward guidance toward the Buddha-way. The "Three Difficulties according to Transformation" refer to the downward guidance of sentient beings.

If one does not even cultivate [the path] oneself, how could one propagate the transformation? Now, from the words "The Buddha descends," the objection is addressed. The objection asks: "If that is so, why speak only of 'difficulties'? Therefore, the present response says:
"If the difficulties were not raised, the aspiration for the mind would not arise. This is why the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* proclaims it three times.

△ Second, the specific explanation of mundane and supramundane practices. First, the explanation of the practice of cultivating the supramundane to attain purity (in three parts).
First, the elucidation of the dharma-gate of counteractive measures for awakening to conventional truth, in five parts.

First, purifying the mind to sever desire. A śramaṇa asked the Buddha: "By what causes and conditions can one know past lives and realize the ultimate Way? The Buddha said: "Purify the mind and maintain your resolve;
thus you may realize the ultimate Way. It is like polishing a mirror: when the grime is removed, the brightness remains. By severing desire and being without seeking, you shall attain it."

Past lives (*pūrvajanman*). [Commentary: Being born from one’s parents is the cause (*hetu*); that which assists in growth is the condition (*pratyaya*). Past lives are one of the six supernormal knowledges (*ṣaḍabhijñā*).

"Reaching the Way" refers to the principle of the Truths (*satya*). This is the nature of *tathatā*, and it is also the ultimate meaning (*paramārtha*) of all phenomena (*dharmas*). The passage beginning with "The Buddha said" is the answer. First...
The Way—the principle of True Suchness—pervades all places. Having no form or characteristics, it cannot be attained through deliberate mental effort;
it manifests solely in accordance with the minds of sentient beings. The mind of a sentient being is like a mirror: if the mirror is defiled by grime, its luminous colors do not appear;
if the mind is defiled by grime, the principle does not appear. One must therefore maintain one’s resolve and conduct, purifying the nature of the mind, and then one will see it.
The Way is true. It is like a mirror: when the grime is removed, the forms and images immediately appear. "Cutting off below" refers next to the command to sever desire;
when self and other are both empty, there is no seeking, and sensation and perception are extinguished. Then, none of the aggregates (*skandha*) or bases (*āyatana*) can act as an obstruction.
"In this way, throughout countless kalpas of the past, my successive abandonings of bodies and takings of bodies have all appeared before me;
therefore, the supernormal power of knowing past lives is also fully possessed by me. It is not something obtained from without. To claim that it is sought from without would be a false teaching."

[Commentary] There are two questions. First, regarding life; second, regarding the Way (*mārga*). The reason for this is that it is intended to show that both life and the Way are devoid of form or shadow such that they cannot be grasped through conjecture.
However, if there are causal dharmas (*pratyaya-dharma*) by which one may know past lives (*pūrvajanman*), then the Way may also be realized through them.
There are many meanings of "causal conditions" (*hetu-pratyaya*): first, explaining them in terms of the three worlds, wherein the seed is the cause and water [is the condition].

The soil, time, and so forth act as conditions for the sprout to arise. Furthermore, the lump of clay acts as the cause, while the wheel, cord, and potter act as conditions for the vessel to be completed;

this refers to the external world of vessels (*bhājana-loka*). Regarding defilement (*saṃkleśa*), ignorance is the cause and karmic formations (*saṃskāra*) are the condition for the arising of consciousness (*vijñāna*) and the rest.
Regarding purification (*vyavadāna*), the arousal of the bodhicitta is the cause and the Buddha’s teaching is the condition for attaining the Path.

The fruit [of this] refers to the mundane world of internal phenomena. Great Compassion serves as the cause, and sentient beings serve as the condition, whereby the manifestation of responsive transformation arises;
this refers to the mundane world of perfect enlightenment through wisdom. Regarding the explanation according to the five teachings and vehicles:

in the minor teaching of humans and devas, sentient beings’ capacity for resonance serves as the cause, and the responsive transformations of the Buddhas serve as the condition, whereby wholesome fruits [are attained].

It is accomplished as follows: in the Initial Teaching (*śākyadeśanā*), the cause is the spiritual lineage (*gotra*) and the condition is the permeation of hearing (*śrutavāsanā*), whereby Bodhi is realized.

In the Final and Sudden Teachings, the internal cause is original enlightenment (*prakṛti-āśraya-parāvṛtti*) and the external condition is the permeation of the teacher’s instruction, whereby ultimate enlightenment is attained.

In the Perfect Teaching, the cause is the mind-nature of the single true Dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*), and the conditions consist of universally visiting spiritual friends (*kalyāṇamitra*) and giving rise to the practices and vows of Samantabhadra; thus, the fruit of Buddhahood is accomplished. Now...
This refers to the world of sentient beings; it is the doctrine within the Lesser Initial Teaching (Hīnayāna).

In the answer, "the Way" is mentioned first and "past lives" (past karma) afterwards because the Way is fundamental and past lives are derivative. Since the Way can still be realized, how could past lives not be attainable? Thus, the Sūtra says:

Cutting off desire and maintaining emptiness, one immediately perceives the truth of the Path and knows past lives. Within the Path, the first two phrases represent the Dharma and the latter two are metaphors.
"Maintaining the will" refers to the tranquility of *samādhi*, like using a hand to hold something steady. "Purifying the mind" refers to the insight of *vipaśyanā*, like water washing and polishing.
Those who seek the external are proponents of heterodox teachings; these refer to the various non-Buddhist masters who claim to seek the Brahma Heaven for themselves.

Regarding those who claim that by [practicing] "Heavenly Arts" (*tian shu*) and so forth one immediately attains the power of recollecting past lives (*jatismara*), or who assert there are distinct magical arts (*dharmavidyā*) through which supernormal powers (*abhijñā*) can be achieved—all such claims are heterodox teachings that deceive the people.
These belong to the tainted fivefold supernatural powers (*sāsrava-pañcābhijñā*) of spirits and deities; they are not the untainted powers (*anāsrava-abhijñā*) taught by the Buddha.
△ Second, Guarding the Truth and Harmonizing with the Way.
A śramaṇa asked the Buddha, "What is good? What is greatest? The Buddha said, "To practice the Way and maintain the truth is good;
for one's will to be in harmony with the Way is greatest."

[Commentary] The question consists of two parts. First, regarding "goodness": there are the wholesome precepts and meditative concentrations of the mundane world, and the truths, bases of power, perfections, and practices of the supramundane.

It is not known which single dharma constitutes ultimate goodness. Second, regarding "greatness": there are the five great elements of the mundane world and the seven great elements of the supramundane.
It is not yet understood which dharma is the greatest. The Buddha answers below by first instructing him to well-guard his nature.

"True" (*zhen*) refers to the practice for one's own benefit; it distinguishes this from worldly meditations and the like. "Practicing the path of awakening" (*xing jue dao*) refers to the teaching for the benefit of others;
it distinguishes this from provisional teachings and the like. Because both nature and cultivation are fully present, it constitutes the ultimate good.

Regarding the term "aspiration" (*zhi*): it means a vow. It is the mind’s intent of seeking and longing; it is also a pledge. It is the mind’s intent of firm resolve. One dwells in seclusion to seek it.
Aspiration: To practice righteousness so as to realize the Way; aspiration manifests through the Way, and the Way is propagated through aspiration. Therefore, they are said to be "in harmony.
He dwells in the broad abode of the world and walks the Great Way of the world, thereby corresponding on high with the subtle transmission of the mind of all Buddhas.
The following covenant clarifies the propriety of the enlightened mind for all sentient beings. Within the realm there are four [destinies], and the Way and Principle (Dao-li) is the most supreme;
therefore, it is called "Great. This great goodness can only be realized through the human path. If one is human and yet does not practice it, I have no further recourse for such a person.

[Commentary] The five great elements (*mahābhūta*) are earth, water, fire, wind, and space. Regarding the seven greats (*mahādharmas*), the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* states: first, the Dharma; second, the arousal of the thought of enlightenment (*cittotpāda*);

third, faith and understanding (*adhimukti*); fourth, the superior intention (*adhyāśaya*); fifth, the provisions (*saṃbhāra*); sixth, time (*kāla*); and seventh, the perfect realization of the fruit (*phala-saṃpatti*).

The *Prajñāpāramitopadeśa* (Asaṅga’s commentary) also explains it in this same way. The *Abhidharmasamuccayavyākhyā* states: first, the object (*viṣaya*; namely, the vastness of the scriptural teachings); second...
1. Practice (the greatness of the practice for the dual benefit). 2. Wisdom. 3. Diligence. 4. Skillful Means. 5. Realization (the greatness of the fruit and virtue). 6.
Activity (the establishment of the great Buddha-work). 7. Guarding the Nature (which is concentration). Sentient beings are deluded regarding the truth and conjoin with the dust;

this is called distraction. The practitioner turns away from the dust and conjoins with the truth; this is called meditative concentration (*dhyāna*). Guishan said: "The original source, the mind-ground, is the principle of meditative concentration."

To forget emotions and accord with reality is the practice of *dhyāna-samādhi*. (Text) This is not the worldly *dhyāna*. The *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* states: "There are three kinds of concentration (*samādhi*):
the superior is Buddha-nature; the middling is the first *dhyāna* and so forth; the inferior is the mental factors of concentration. Guishan said:
"The *Tathatā-samādhi* transmitted by Bodhidharma refers to the four *dhyānas* and eight *samādhis*; those explained by various other schools [refer to something else]. (Text) Now...

This is the meditation of true nature (*bhūtatathatā-dhyāna*), which distinguishes it from other meditations involving effortful application. Qingliang says: "There are two kinds of concentration (*samādhi*): first, concentrating [the mind] on a single point so that nothing is not accomplished;
this is the gate of concentration on phenomena (*dharma-samādhi*). Second, being able to contemplate the nature of the mind and accords with principle without wavering;

this is the gate of concentration on principle (*tattva-samādhi*). (Text) Here, it belongs to concentration on principle, not concentration on phenomena. "Practice-awakening" (*xingjue*) refers to wisdom (*prajñā*). It exists...

The fundamental is the ultimate; the true mark (*dharmatā*) is the fundamental, while words and letters are the ultimate. Contemplative wisdom (*prajñā*) penetrates both the fundamental and the ultimate.

To clearly comprehend the characteristics of phenomena (*dharmalakṣaṇa*) is the contemplation of phenomena (*sadarśana*); to thoroughly understand non-arising (*anutpāda*) is the contemplation of principle (*tattvadarśana*).

Contemplating the non-arising of the true mark gives rise to all words, letters, and phenomenal characteristics, so that one first knows through understanding and subsequently knows through awakening. This is not the provisional teaching; it is by means of this Way...
To awaken the people is not to transform them through the minor teachings of other humans or devas. [The text] concludes with the nature [of the teaching]: if one maintains it, one perfects oneself;

if one practices it, one universally benefits the world. Therefore, it is called "good," and the term "ultimate" (*zhi*) is used because among all phenomena there are those that are good by nature, those that are not good by nature, those that are good through cultivation, and those that are not good through cultivation. [The distinction between] nature and cultivation is...
"Good. This refers to the cultivation of non-attachment, non-hatred, and so forth. Cultivating goodness that is not innate goodness refers to non-attachment and the like.

Innate and cultivated goodness together constitute the Way of True Suchness (*tathatā*), the principle of the Dharma-nature (*dharmatā*). Therefore, it is called "Ultimate. What is now termed "guarding the true" refers to guarding the ultimate goodness.
The *Vajrasamādhi Sūtra* states: "Guarding the One" means guarding the suchness of the one mind; this is practicing the Way, the practice of ultimate goodness. The *Vajra*... [text ends]
Gang Sanmei said: "Always use one awakening to awaken all sentient beings. This is the Great Learning’s reaching of ultimate goodness;
it is largely identical in meaning to Mencius’s teaching on the inherent goodness of human nature. Regarding the phrase "the will of the mind":

furthermore, may my resolve be fulfilled within my aspirations, and may my vow be realized through courageous and fierce intent within my prayers. Yunqi said: "That which is expected through one's resolve must be reached; this is what a vow provides."
He is the precursor. To strengthen one’s vow and not retreat is to pledge to act as his rear guard. (Text) "Seeking one's will" means to give rise to one's will based on the Way.
"Attaining the Way" means to practice the Way based on that will. As Mencius said: "If one attains their will, they share it with the people;
if they do not attain their will, they walk alone in their Way. Riches and honors cannot corrupt them; poverty and low status cannot shift them."
"Neither power nor majesty can humble him. This is what is called a great man. Regarding these four things within the realm, Laozi said:
"There was something formed in its entirety, born before heaven and earth. It is silent and vast, standing alone and unchanging;
it circulates everywhere without weariness and may serve as the mother of the world. I do not know its name; I designate it 'the Way' (Dào). I forcefully..."
That which is named "Great" is thus: the Way is great; Heaven is great; Earth is great; and the King is also great. Within this realm there are four greatnesses, and the King occupies one of them.
Man models himself after Earth; Earth models itself after Heaven; Heaven models itself after the Way; and the Way models itself after Nature.
The commentary states: As for "things," the Dao is the root of all things; thus it is called "Dao" (the Way), signifying its virtue through its capacity to penetrate and give birth.
It is named "Great" (Dai), designating its substance by its capacity to contain all. That the Dao is great means it can encompass Heaven, Earth, and humanity.
Heaven is great because there is nothing it does not cover. Earth is great because there is nothing it does not support and carry.
Furthermore, the Great King is one who can emulate the earth and follow the Way of Heaven. Man is the king; man is the spirit among the myriad things, and the king is the lord of the myriad people.
First, he should emulate the earth by being tranquil, still, gentle, and harmonious. Next, he should emulate Heaven by employing its power to bring about generation and completion.
Furthermore, he should emulate the Way by being pure and non-active, allowing all things to transform of their own accord. If...
This is precisely because it accords with the nature of the Way and the spontaneity of the Dharma. In the former sense, the Way is great and occupies the priority;
in the latter sense, the Way is the foundation of all dharmas. Thus we know that within heaven and earth, the principle of the Way is the greatest.

As for the five great elements and seven great elements, they all possess conditioned characteristics (*saṃskṛta-lakṣaṇa*) and are not like the Way and principle, which are great in being signless (*animitta*) and unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*). Therefore, they are not called "supreme. If...
As for those whose aspirations accord with his, they too are lofty beyond compare and pervasive without limit;
thus they are able to encompass the Way of Heaven and Earth—is this not magnificent? Only a person of such capacity can do so. Pei Xu said:

"That by which living beings come and go are the six realms of existence (*ṣaḍ-gati*). Ghosts and spirits suffer the bitterness of deep obscurity and sorrow; birds and beasts harbor the distress of flight and panic."
The asuras are currently in a state of rage, while the devas are in the midst of pleasure. Only by regulating the mind and inclining toward Bodhi can one do so;
this is possible only through the human path. (Text) These four lines are an exhortation. △ Third, enduring evil and extinguishing defilements.

A śramaṇa asked the Buddha, "What possesses great strength? What is most luminous? The Buddha said, "Patience possesses great strength, for it harbors no malice and is further endowed with peace and health.

One who practices patience is free from evil and will surely be honored by others. When the defilements of the mind are extinguished and purified until they are without blemish, this is what is called being most luminous.
From the time before heaven and earth existed until this very day, throughout all the ten directions, there has never been..."
He does not fail to see; there is nothing he does not know, nothing he does not hear. Having attained all-knowledge (*sarvajñatā*), he may be called "luminous.
[Commentary] In the question, first comes power, then luminosity. To be capable and without timidity is called power;
to penetrate thoroughly and without obscurity is called luminosity.

[Commentary] From the words "The Buddha said" below, the response follows in two parts. First, patience is of great power, which has two sub-sections. First, the heading: Patience is the foremost among the hundred practices.
If one lacks patience, it results in seven harms and three sufferings; if one possesses patience, it results in seven benefits and four joys.
Therefore, it possesses great power. The Āgamas state that there are six kinds of power: children have the power of crying; women have the power of anger;
kings have the power of arrogance; śramaṇas have the power of patience; arhats have the power of diligence; and the Buddhas have the power of compassion. This is what is meant.
Next, to explain "not inferior": patience is twofold. First is the patience of birth, which may be either adverse or favorable.
The "adverse" refers to not giving rise to anger, resentment, enmity, or vexation toward objects of malice, abuse, beating, or harm.
The "favorable" refers to not giving rise to craving, attachment, pride, or negligence toward objects of respect or offerings.

Regarding these two types of patience (*kṣānti*), there are those that are mental factors (*caitasika*) and those that are non-mental factors. Mental factors refer to sensual desire, ill-will, sorrow, doubt, and false views.
Regarding pride and so forth, those which are not mental factors refer to cold, heat, hunger, thirst, wind, rain, aging, illness, death, and so on.

To not harbor malice toward these now constitutes the "middle patience" (*madhyā-kṣānti*) regarding adverse conditions. To remain peaceful and healthy constitutes the "patience regarding phenomena" (*dharma-kṣānti*), which is not a mental factor.
Furthermore, the first is called "patience regarding harm from others," meaning that one should endure the afflictions caused by others without harboring a desire for retaliation in the mind.
It is also called "endurance of resentment. This refers to enduring the harm and affliction caused by enemies; it is the endurance of external obstacles.
Next is called "endurance of calmly accepting suffering," which means enduring such phenomena as gain and loss, defamation and praise, honor and insult, and pain and pleasure;

it is also called "endurance of peaceful acceptance," referring to enduring the sufferings of poverty, illness, and so forth; this is the endurance of internal obstacles. One who endures thus is without malice.

The *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* states: "There are three types of patience (*kṣānti*): namely, patience in enduring enmity and harm, patience in accepting suffering, and patience in the discernment of dharmas.
The commentary explains: "The latter one is the basis for the former two patiences, because it is capable of enduring the extremely profound and vast Dharma.
Furthermore, the *Prajñāpāramitā* states: "There are two types of patience: first, patience in acceptance, which refers to [enduring] the infliction of weapons and staves..."

When harmed, reviled, insulted, or humiliated, one does not give rise to a mind of retaliation. When afflicted by mosquitoes, gadflies, fleas, lice, cold, heat, or suffering, one does not give rise to a mind of resentment.
Second is the patience of observation: contemplating that all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) are like illusions and lack reality.
Who is it that reviles me? Who is it that harms me? Who is it that insults me? Who is it that suffers? It is only my own mind.
Regarding false conceptualization: "I should not now give rise to arbitrary attachment. This is the subsequent truth of contemplation.

Furthermore, not harboring a sense of security or well-being is the patience regarding phenomena with signs (*sanimitta-dharma-kṣānti*). This absence of malice is the patience regarding the non-arising of phenomena (*anutpatti-dharma-kṣānti*);

that is, by observing with right wisdom that the nature of arising phenomena is empty, one finds that neither insult nor harm can be apprehended—[realizing] they are suffering, empty, and without self.
Who is it that practices patience? Since the object of insult and the act of enduring it are both empty, non-arising manifests before one, and one thereby realizes nirvana.
What evil could there be? The *Śīla-sūtra* says: "Patience is the supreme path. The *Āgama* says: "This Dharma is worthy of veneration.
Therefore, those who abide in the three types of patience are the most honored among all people in the world.
[Commentary]: To maintain composure within and endure external circumstances of humiliation is called "patience" (kṣānti). Regarding the seven harms and seven benefits:
when Zizhang wished to depart and took leave of the Master, he requested that the Master grant him a single word to serve as the foundation for cultivating the person.
The Master said, "Of all the hundred practices, patience is supreme. Zizhang asked, "How does one practice patience? The Master—

The Master said, "If the Son of Heaven practices forbearance, his state will be free from harm. If the feudal lords practice forbearance, they will achieve greatness. If the officials and clerks practice forbearance, they will advance in their ranks.

If brothers practice forbearance, their family will enjoy wealth and honor. If husband and wife practice forbearance, they will endure for their entire lives. If friends practice forbearance, their reputation will not perish.
If one practices forbearance within oneself, one will be free from calamity. Zizhang asked, "What happens if one cannot practice forbearance?"
The Master said: "The Son of Heaven cannot bear for his state to be empty and desolate; the feudal lords cannot bear to lose their persons;
the officials cannot bear to execute punishments and laws; brothers cannot bear to live in separate households; and husbands and wives cannot bear to leave their children orphaned."
If one cannot endure for the sake of a friend, their affection will grow distant; if one cannot endure for oneself, one's afflictions will not be removed. Zizhang said: "Excellent!

It is not that one cannot endure toward non-humans, but rather that one cannot endure what is non-human. (Text) This clarifies the gains and losses regarding worldly patience. As for the three types of suffering:
The *Anāśraya-śāstra* states: "There are three kinds of suffering due to the inability to endure [the causes and conditions]:

namely, the suffering of transmigrating through birth and death (*saṃsāra*), the suffering of conflict with sentient beings, and the suffering of lacking resources for enjoyment. Regarding the four types of joy, the *Kuan-ting-chi* states: 1. Joy because patience has matured:
when the practice of patience is fully perfected, it is like a laborer who has long achieved his goal. 2. Joy of right concentration (*samyak-samādhi*)...
Therefore, there is joy. One constantly dwells in great meditative concentration (*samādhi*), which is quiescent and immovable. Third is joy through compassion for others;
it is like a child striking his father, whereby the father immediately experiences joy. Fourth is joy through self-benefit, as one uses this illusory form to easily attain a solid essence.
(Text) This clarifies that the worldly patience regarding suffering and joy is thus. Furthermore, the *Dharmasaṃgīti-sūtra* asks: "What is [it]?"
This is the power of patience of that bodhisattva: when reviled by others, they do not retaliate, because they have attained the power of wisdom regarding the equality of echoes;
when struck by others, they do not retaliate, because they have attained the power of wisdom regarding the equality of reflections in a mirror;
when troubled by others, they do not retaliate, because they have attained the power of wisdom regarding the equality of illusions.
When reviled by others, one does not retaliate, because one has attained the power of wisdom regarding internal purity and equanimity.
One cannot be defiled by the eight worldly concerns, because one has attained the power of time regarding the purity and equanimity of worldly phenomena.
One cannot be defiled or overcome by any afflictions, because one has attained the power of wisdom regarding the equality of the causes and conditions of their accumulation.
Therefore, it is said that patience possesses great power among all dharmas. "Peaceful and robust" means to endure suffering dharmas with composure;
it signifies being strong, powerful, immovable, and indestructible. A saying goes: "Patience is the treasure of the body; impatience is the calamity of the body.
When the tongue is supple, it remains forever in the mouth; when the teeth are rigid, they only break. This is precisely the meaning intended here.
Regarding "gain and loss, etc.," the *Commentary on the Awakening of Faith* states: "Gain" refers to wealth and prosperity that benefit oneself; "loss" refers to depletion and encroachment.

"Defamation" refers to slandering by transgressing against one's character; "praise" refers to extolling virtues beyond their actual measure. "Eulogy" refers to praising based on actual virtue; "ridicule" refers to discussing faults according to reality.
"Suffering" refers to oppression and physical affliction; "pleasure" refers to the mind and spirit being at ease and joyful.
(Commentary). To endure these eight is to remain unmoved by the eight winds (*aṣṭau vāyavaḥ*). There are three levels of endurance. Examining oneself, one says:

"Enduring resentment" refers to the patience toward sentient beings (*sattvākṣānti*); this is the cause for maturing sentient beings. "Accepting with equanimity" refers to the patience regarding phenomena (*dharmakṣānti*);

this is the cause for accomplishing the fruit of Buddhahood. (Commentary). The *Bishuo ji* states that there are two intentions behind enduring resentment without retaliating: first, to resolve the enmity; [second, to transform the mind].
Because of this bond. As stated in the verses of King Jīvaka in the Vinaya: "To repay enmity with enmity, the enmity never ceases; only by being without enmity does enmity naturally subside.
Second, it is for the sake of realizing the fruit of Buddhahood. By means of right wisdom, one knows that the objects of both self and other are empty and non-existent.
Unable to bear sinking into the cycle of birth and death, one practices patience, whereby one swiftly attains the Way of the Buddha and finds peace.
One experiences eight objects [of the senses], which do not transcend the categories of the adverse and the favorable. The adverse is easy to endure; the favorable is difficult to endure.
Tiantai describes these as the two thieves—the forceful and the soft. One who discerns the Dharma through the truths merely contemplates the objects of endurance:

that phenomena are essentially unborn, manifested solely by the mind, and that the three spheres are empty and quiescent—this alone is the single reality. As stated in the *Prajñāpāramitā*: "By means of right wisdom... [The text continues: "...there is no..."
