The three types of craving that pervade all places—namely, craving for the five sensory objects (*pañca-viṣaya*) that sustain life—are countered by means of the eight bases of mastery (*abhibhvāyatana*): (1) having the perception of internal forms, one perceives external forms as limited; (2) having the perception of internal forms, one perceives external forms as vast;

(3) being without the perception of internal forms, one perceives external forms as limited; (4) being without the perception of internal forms, one perceives external forms as vast; (5) the base of mastery of blue; (6) the base of mastery of yellow; (7) the base of mastery of red... [and so forth].

The spheres of mastery (abhibhvāyatana; specifically, the eight white spheres of mastery). Furthermore, there are four types of perceptions that counteract sensual desire (*rāga*): first, regarding color (*varṇa*), such as red or white, one forms the perception of a livid corpse (*vinīlaka*);
second, regarding shape (*saṃsthāna*), such as long or short, one forms the perception of a festering corpse (*vipūyaka*);

third, regarding exquisite touch (*sparśa*)—the softness, smoothness, and luster of one's own or another's body—one forms the perception of a worm-infested corpse (*vilohitaka*); fourth, regarding service and attendance that is pleasing to the mind, one uses the [perception of] a dead [corpse].

It is "equal" because it is used as an antidote for perception (*saṃjñā*). Thus, it is said to be "equal. Below, the *Siddhārthasādhana-sūtra* (or *Saddharmasmṛtyupasthāna-sūtra*) provides scriptural evidence for the word "equal.
"Pure contemplation" refers to the śamatha and vipaśyanā of the true mark (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*). Contemplative wisdom (*prajñā*) is able to cure all ailments, just like the agada medicine;
it is not merely that impurity removes greed. Question: Worldly beautiful forms and a bloated, rotting corpse are entirely two different appearances. How can [they be considered equal]?
View them as being of one substance. Answer: Suppose one were to die suddenly during the summer months; the body would immediately swell and rot, becoming terrifying to behold.
How could this be two separate things? Thus, the present body is false and unreal, like a sack of excrement, a walking latrine, or a bag of pus and blood.

A den of maggots, filled with all manner of impurities, it is utterly loathsome. When one’s contemplative practice is matured, the arising of aversion toward such objects makes them no different from a corpse.
History records that Xiao Chao detested seeing women; upon approaching within a few paces, he would smell their stench.
Xiao Chao was the reincarnation of Xu Xuan-du. Therefore, female beauty ruins people and obstructs the Path.
Just as when the crown of a tāla tree is cut off, its sprouts will never grow again; because it has been severed by the blade of a woman, the seeds of wisdom do not sprout.
Like a snake covered by flowers, like fire covered by ashes and dust, or like seeing a poisonous tree—the wise should abandon such things.
△ Second, abandoning defilement so that others may attain the fruit. This has two parts; first, directly clarifying the afflictions of desire. The Buddha said:
"A person of craving and desire is like one holding a torch while walking against the wind; there will inevitably be the affliction of burning their hands."
[Commentary: If a person harbors desire, the fire of lust blazes fiercely; how much more so when they act contrary to the wind of the state of liberation that is Perfect Enlightenment?
Within the body of Dharma-nature, the arms of Maitreya (Mudrā-bhuja)—how could they not be scorched and harmed? It is like traveling a perilous path in the dead of night;
though one encounters a headwind, because of a craving for the torch, one clutches it and refuses to let go, certain to burn one's hand.
It is a source of affliction. An ancient saying goes: "People call it the peony; the Buddha calls it the flower-arrow.
When it pierces a person to the very marrow, one dies without even knowing the resentment. For this reason, the Tathāgata designated sexual misconduct as the 'fire of desire.
When a Bodhisattva sees desire, they avoid it as if it were a pit of fire. If one can be like a vajra atop a flame, observing all the warmth within the hundred skeletal members."
When the breath of touch transforms a mind of excessive lust into the fire of wisdom, even if one enters a great conflagration, the fire will not be able to burn them;
how then could there be any affliction of the hands?
[Commentary] *Mudrā* means "seal" (or "hand-gesture"). When fire meets wind, it blazes; when lust meets ignorance, it becomes even more intense.
While alive, it burns the five viscera; at death, one must embrace the copper pillar. If the entire body is extinguished, how much more so the arms? As the Sūtra says:
"The habit of lustful intercourse arises from mutual friction. Grinding and rubbing without ceasing, within that [state], a great and fierce fire-light [arises]."
It is activated. It is for this reason that there are such things as the iron bedsteads and so forth. As for the "flower-arrows":

after Empress Wu Hui passed away, Emperor Xuanzong of the Tang dynasty had no one in the inner palace who met his heart's desire. He consequently fashioned fragrant arrows and lined up the palace women to shoot at them.
Those who are struck by it are fortunate. A song within the palace says: "The arrow of elegance and style—those struck by it are the objects of everyone's longing.
One does not realize that as soon as the fragrant arrow is released, the fire-arrow arrives immediately; the fragrant arrow is the cause, and the fire-arrow is the effect.

If one loses the cause and perishes with the effect, then the fire-arrow is not what is truly to be feared; what is to be feared is the fragrant arrow alone. Furthermore, the fire-arrow travels directly [to its mark].
Yet the harm [from the former] is slight; people keep their distance and avoid it, so that among those who die, one in ten thousand is not reached.
The fragrant arrow lurks in concealment yet its harm is profound; people become familiar with it and treat it with playfulness, so that eight or nine out of ten die.
That people do not fear the fragrant arrow but fear the fire-arrow—is this not a case of inverted perception? If one can act as described below, as the *Sūtra* says: "Ucchuṣma..."
He addressed the Buddha, saying, "I am one of great lustful desire. At that time, the Buddha, the King of Space, declared that those with excessive lust become a mass of fierce fire.

He instructed me to observe throughout my entire body—the hundred skeletal members, the four limbs, and all the sensations of cold and warmth. As the divine light coalesced within, it transformed my lustful mind into the fire of wisdom.
From this, the Buddhas named me Huotou (Fire-Head). By the power of the *Prabhāsvara-samādhi* (Light-Fire Samādhi),...
Thus, one becomes an Arhat. Furthermore, Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva knows that when perception and vision revolve back [to their source], one remains far removed from craving and desire.

This causes all sentient beings such that even if they enter a great fire, the fire cannot burn them. Therefore, we know that the departure from desire is the foremost dharma for escaping the dust of the world.
An alternate version states: "If a person holds a torch and walks against the wind, a fool who does not let go will surely..."

There is the affliction of burning one's hands. When the poisons of greed, lust, anger, and delusion reside within the human body, if one does not early on eliminate these calamities through the Way, there will inevitably be perilous disaster—just as a fool who greedily grasps a torch burns his own hand.

The commentary states: This original [verse] uses the metaphor of the poison of greed alone, whereas that original [verse] employs it as a general metaphor for the three poisons. Furthermore, those who study the Path must not fail to understand this.
△ Second, the realization of benefit through the very objects [of perception].
A celestial deity presented a jade maiden to the Buddha, desiring to disturb his resolve. The Buddha said, "A leather bag filled with various impurities—what is the purpose of your coming?

Depart; I have no use for you. The deity’s reverence increased all the more, and he consequently inquired about the meaning of the Path. The Buddha explained it for him, and the deity immediately attained the fruit of *srotāpanna*.

[Commentary: "Celestial deity" refers to Māra, the Lord of the Desire Realm. "The Buddha’s intention" refers to the mind of perfect awakening (*samyaksambodhi*). "Inquiring about the Way" refers to the path for extinguishing suffering.
"Explaining" refers to the Dharma of suffering and emptiness. The reason the celestial deity made this offering was, first of all, to test the Buddha’s intention.
Second, regarding the contemplation of the Buddha-way: one realizes that celestial maidens are merely capable of deceiving the mundane; they cannot disturb the Six Supernatural Powers (ṣaḍabhijñā).
How much less could the Honored One of Great Enlightenment be swayed by Māra? The *Buddhānusmṛtisamādhi-sūtra* states:

"When the Bodhisattva was about to attain the Way, Māra dispatched three daughters, adorned with seductive beauty, who came before him and said: 'We are celestial maidens, our loveliness is peerless.'"

She then entices him. When a mind of deceit arises, she feels slighted by any obstacle and gives rise to a mind of resentment. Her longing does not cease, and she gives rise to a mind of greedy attachment.
She seizes what another desires and gives rise to a mind of malice. She takes it as her own and gives rise to a mind of false views.
She turns against her husband and others, giving rise to a mind of enmity and hatred. This refers to a maiden, a girl living at home who is not yet married.
...as well. "A widow" refers to one who has no husband. The *Vinaya* says "inferior. The *Sudarsana-vibhasa* asks: "What is mindfulness (*smrti*) and reflection (*manasikara*)?
To first place the mind upon the object of observation is called mindfulness. To keep the mind fixed within the object of observation, causing it to hover there, is called reflection.
It is like the sound of a bell: at first it is loud, like mindfulness; later it is faint, like reflection. It is like a bird soaring through the sky: at first..."

Movement is like *smṛti* (mindfulness); subsequent concentration is like *cetanā* (volition). It is like a bee gathering nectar from flowers: the initial arrival is like *smṛti*, while the subsequent selection is like *cetanā*.

(Text) To look up at those below is the opposite of this; to gaze at women is an evil of the body; to converse with them is an evil of the mouth; and to harbor perverse thoughts is an evil of the mind.
The mind is evil. When the day possesses three evils, one is called a "malignant person" (*xiōng rén*). Malignant deities follow such a person, and calamities and misfortunes arrive. As for Li Tuifu:
Tuifu lived in seclusion on Mount Nanyue seeking a teacher but could not find one. Suddenly, he heard the sound of *tanqi* (a board game) from the air.
Raising his head to look, he saw two divine immortals playing at the tree’s edge. Tuifu hurried over to pay his respects.
Just as he was inquiring about the way, a field-woman suddenly emerged from the side; he unconsciously looked back, and the two chess players had already vanished.
Regarding the five hundred immortals, the *Vibhāṣā-śāstra* states that King Udayana took his palace ladies with him.
He went to the forest of Uddapāda to enjoy himself with the five sensual pleasures. At that time, five hundred seers were flying over that place by means of their supernormal power (*ṛddhi*).
Upon seeing forms, hearing sounds, smelling scents, and forming mental conceptions, they lost their supernormal powers and fell into that forest.
The king asked them, "Have you attained the first dhyāna? They replied, "We once attained it, but have now lost it. Or...
Some remained in the eye-consciousness and regressed; some remained in the ear-consciousness and regressed; some remained in the nose-consciousness and regressed;
others remained in the mind-consciousness and regressed. The king then became enraged. Seeing my palace women, the lustful man acted improperly;
he drew a sharp sword and severed the hands and feet of the seer. "Kali-yuga" (the age of turbulence) is a Sanskrit term for *kalpa*.

*Pāpa*. This is translated as "time-period" (*kāla*). It is so named because the four turbidities converge therein. The *Karunāpuṇḍarīka-sūtra* states that when the human lifespan decreases to twenty thousand years, one enters the *kalpa-kaṣāya* (turbidity of the eon).

Regarding the *dṛṣṭi-kaṣāya* (turbidity of views), its essence consists of the five sharp afflictions (*kleśa*)—namely, the view of a self-body (*satkāya-dṛṣṭi*), extreme views (*antagrāha-dṛṣṭi*), attachment to precepts and rituals (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*), attachment to views (*dṛṣṭiparāmarśa*), and false views (*mithyādṛṣṭi*)—because these various views are intensely active.

Regarding the *kleśa-kaṣāya* (turbidity of afflictions), its essence consists of the five dull afflictions (*kleśa*)—namely, greed (*rāga*), hatred (*dveṣa*), [delusion (*moha*), pride (*māna*), and doubt (*vicikitsā*)].

[The afflictions of] delusion, pride, and doubt. Because of the stubbornness of strife, the *sattva-kaṣāya* (defilement of sentient beings) takes as its essence the grasping at the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*) and the fruits of views and pride;
because foul reputations and ignoble names fill the world, the *āyuḥ-kaṣāya* (defilement of lifespan) takes as its essence the continuous maintenance of form and mind.
Because it destroys years and diminishes lifespan. The *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* explains this in terms of causes, whereas the present sutra explains it in terms of effects.

The presence of these five turbidities is what defines an "evil world," while their absence defines a "virtuous world. One should know that the turbidity of the world arises from the turbidity of the mind;

when the mind is pure, the Buddha-land is pure. If one can shatter the five aggregates and transcend the five turbidities—exceeding the kalpa by exhausting form, exceeding views by exhausting sensation, and exhausting perception...

Transcending afflictions; through the exhaustion of formations, one transcends sentient beings; through the exhaustion of consciousness, one transcends life. By severing the five desires, one achieves the five fruits (ranging from the four fruits and the Pratyekabuddha at the lower level, to the stages of faith, abiding, practice, and penetration at the higher level).
Just as a lotus flower, though emerging from the mud, remains untainted by it, so too does the nature below remain pure and transcend life.
Like the essence of the lotus, it is pure and wondrous; like its color, form, fragrance, and radiance, it is lofty and pure, transcending all sentient beings, and is not defiled by afflictions.

Transcending the *kalpa* of affliction (*kleśa-kalpa*) is like not fearing the scorching sun; it corresponds to the *Avataṃsaka*, whereby one attains liberation from worldly paths and is not defiled by desire.
Transcending the turbidity of the *kalpa* (*kalpa-kaṣāya*) is like not being stained by mud; it corresponds to the *Avataṃsaka*, whereby one attains liberation from the realms of Māra.
Transcending views is like not dreading wind and rain; it corresponds to the *Avataṃsaka*, whereby one attains resolution regarding all delusions and is not bound by the confusion of craving.

Transcending afflictions. Like washing ripples so they do not stain the heavens; this combines with the *Avataṃsaka* to explain that all karmas attain liberation. Regarding the first line of the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya*:
it proves that while the śramaṇa dwells in turbidity, the lotus flower emerges from the mud. The subsequent three lines prove that one is not defiled by turbid evil, nor stained by the mud.
Regarding the *Brahmajāla-sūtra*: it cites an internal scripture. Regarding the *Liji*: it cites an external classic. "In the past there was... [and so forth].
The citation of the precedent serves as a conclusion and praise for what follows. Regarding the passage "In the Sūtras and Vinaya," there are likewise two contemplations as antidotes;
this citation now serves as proof for the latter one. The phrase "Thus we know" concludes the summary of the skillful application of provisional conceptualizations as an antidote.
"Adorned with makeup": when applying powder and rouge. "Tears and disheveled hair": when one has not yet washed or combed oneself.
"Bright and pure": the years of youth and vigor. "Cranes and chickens": the years of decline and old age. "Light and soft": days of physical strength and health.

"Ulcers and toxins": days of illness and suffering. "Wasp-like and moth-like": the appearance before death. "Dead and putrid": the appearance after passing away. Below "Holding the World," it says in full: [text follows].
The speech was welcoming. Although one may possess the fruits of merit, one should not indulge in self-indulgence;

rather, one should contemplate the impermanence of the five desires in order to seek the root of goodness, and cultivate the firm Dharma regarding body, life, and wealth. In the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa*, it further says: "O virtuous ones!"
This body is impermanent and lacks strength; it is powerless and unsubstantial, a thing subject to rapid decay that cannot be relied upon.
It is suffering and affliction, a gathering place for manifold diseases. This body is impure, filled with filth and evil; this body is false and deceptive.
Although one may provisionally provide it with bathing, clothing, and food, it will inevitably return to decay and extinction. This body is a calamity;

the arising of the one hundred and one diseases and so forth—all these are methods for transcending others. Regarding "not seeing what is desirable," there are two kinds of the desirable: first, beautiful appearance.
Second, on physical appearance. The *Sūtra of Yaśodharā* says: "What is meant by being upright and handsome?

To eliminate eighty-four defilements and perverse dispositions, and to maintain a concentrated mind and single-mindedness—this is what constitutes being upright and handsome; it is not by means of one's complexion.
Herein, the text clarifies that not seeing what is desirable also opens up two meanings. First, regarding all women, one should perform the contemplation of impurity (*aśubha-bhāvanā*), as follows:
The aforementioned sūtras state: "The body is filled with various impure substances that constantly flow out, like a leaking bag containing filth. Second, one should view all women as unattractive;
there are eight major faults in women that are loathed by the wise: first, jealousy; second, false anger; third..."

First is reviling; second is slandering; third is cursing; fourth is incantations; fifth is suppression; sixth is stinginess and greed; seventh is fondness for ornamentation; eighth is harboring poison.
These are the eight great perverse dispositions. The *Piyu jing* (Sutra of Similes) says: "In the past, there was a Brahmin who had two daughters of exquisite beauty.
He hung up gold as a prize, setting a condition that whoever could denounce his daughters as ugly would receive the gold. Ten days passed..."
In the end, there was no one who accepted the invitation. As they were about to arrive at the Buddha’s dwelling, the Buddha rebuked them, saying, "These women are all ugly;
not one is beautiful. Ānanda asked the Buddha, "What is it about these women that is not beautiful? The Buddha said, "When the eyes do not gaze upon forms, that is a beautiful eye.
It is the same for the ears, the nose, and the mouth. When the body does not cling to smooth textures, that is a beautiful body."

The body: when one’s hands do not steal the wealth of others, these are called "good hands. Now, if the eyes crave beautiful forms, and so on, up to the body delighting in smooth textures, and the hands delighting in stealing wealth—those who act in such ways as these all possess what is not good. The *Saptakumārikā-sūtra* says:
A householder had seven daughters whose beauty was peerless; no one in the country dared to say they were not beautiful. He took them...
The Buddha said, "To be without craving for the worldly objects of form, sound, smell, taste, touch, and mental phenomena is what is truly excellent. What is it that this woman craves?
[He continued,] "In the time of Kāśyapa Buddha, seven daughters of a king did not cling to pleasure and amusement; they entered the Śītavana cemetery."
They observed the corpses and each explained their reasons, saying, "Such as these are excellent; which of them is excellent in your daughter? [The Buddha said:

"Since her body is impure and her conduct is not upright, what is there to love that could give rise to desire? These two [contemplations] are the foundation for the mind of concentration free from desire."
