△ Third, distancing oneself from desire.
The Buddha said: "One who practices the Way is like dry grass; when fire approaches, it must be avoided. When a practitioner of the Way encounters desire, he must certainly distance himself from it."
[Commentary: Sentient beings give rise to deluded sentiments, which can produce the springs of greed and the waters of craving—like weeds in a field that flourish with moisture.
For those who cultivate the Way, when the faculties and their objects do not encounter one another, greed and craving dry up like parched grass.

When the habituation of craving has only just begun to dry, it has not yet connected with the flowing water of the Tathāgata’s Dharma; therefore, it encounters the fires of desire and the smoke of lust.

One must urgently avoid [these afflictions] from afar. Should one approach them, not only will one lose the path and find it difficult to return, but one’s body will become ulcerated and fall into hell.

Question: Since lust, anger, and ignorance are all part of the Brahma-faring (brahmacarya), and both the attainment and loss of mindfulness are non-different from liberation, why is there such a need for specific antidotes?
Such traces seem to resemble those of the Hīnayāna. Answer: This is the practice of those with the faculties of the Mahāyāna.
This is the place where one treads. Yet, it has been cultivated through many kalpas; thus, one can enter the pure and enter the defiled, remaining unimpeded everywhere.

For those of middling or inferior capacity, their habitual impurities remain strong and the burdens of desire are not yet exhausted; how could they make every step the Way and find perfect penetration in every phenomenon?
To speak of emptiness while failing to practice accordingly is a fault that is no small matter. Therefore, it is said that the profound Dharma of the Buddhas cannot be [attained]...
If one says this to a beginner practitioner, they may well not believe it.

[Commentary] Regarding "the faculties do not encounter their objects": the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* states that for a person who maintains the prohibitive precepts, the mind is free from greed and lust, and does not flow excessively toward the six external sense-objects (*viṣaya*).
Since the objects are no longer taken as conditions, the faculties have nothing to encounter. This refers to the two phrases concerning "affection" and "habitual tendencies."
To clarify by means of a dharma-illustration: it is like dry grass on high ground that, when encountering the Dharma-rain of ambrosia, does not avoid fire.
Regarding "having lost what is common, it is difficult to return": once, the Rishi Kalpa flew back and forth using the five supernormal powers (*pañcābhijñā*).
At that time, a king paid him homage for many years. One day, having business requiring a long journey, he ordered his daughter to attend to the flying seer. That flying seer—
Upon his arrival, the woman supported him with her hands and placed him upon a table. As he touched her softness, a desire immediately arose within him.

Once his mind was stirred by lust, he lost his supernormal powers and could no longer fly back. Regarding the "one with the ulcerated body," the *Śatapañcāśatkathā* (The Sutra of a Hundred Causes) states:
During the time of Krakucchanda Buddha, there was the son of an elder who was fond of beauty. Upon seeing a courtesan, his heart became deeply attached to her; he had nothing [he would not give].
"I can give it to you. He then went into the stupa and stole some flowers to give him. That night they slept together, but at dawn the youth broke out with malignant sores;
the pain was beyond description, and no physician could cure them. Someone said that if sandalwood were applied to the sores, they could be healed.
Thereupon, the son of the elder sold his house and estate, obtaining six hundred thousand gold coins, with which he purchased ox-head sandalwood (*gośīrṣa-candana*).
[He took] six *liang* [of incense], pounded it into a powder, and placed it inside the stūpa. He then made a vow, saying: "The ailment I now suffer is a disease of the mind.
By using this incense to smear the stūpa and providing the price for these flowers, I pray that you will, out of your great compassion, accept my repentance."
"Quickly remove this affliction. The ulcer was immediately healed. Regarding the fragrant scent from the pores for those falling into hell, the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* states:

"Ānanda, you should know that these ten kinds of demons—*guài*, *bò*, *mèi*, *gǔdú*, *yànshèng*, *lì*, *dàlì*, *chuānlín*, *shānhǎi jīng*, *zhīcǎo*, and *zìzàitiān*—in the age of the final dharma, within my teaching, will praise sexual desire and violate the Buddha’s disciplinary code; they are the demonic teachers and their disciples who engage in lust."

The tradition regarding lustful signs states that such perverse spirits possess the heart and viscera; at the very least for nine lifetimes, and often for more than a hundred generations, they cause those who practice true cultivation to become entirely part of the demonic retinue.
After their lives end, they will surely become subjects of Māra, lose right and universal knowledge, and fall into the Avīci Hell.
Yunqi said: "Do not greedily become stained by objects of desire, for this is the root of hell. Question:

[The character] "lower" (xià) serves to address a potential objection. Regarding the phrase "every dharma, every instance": the *Vimalakīrtinirdeśa-sūtra* states, "Though dwelling in a household, he is not attached to the triple world;
though manifesting a wife and children, he constantly cultivates pure conduct (*brahmacarya*); though manifesting kinsmen, he always delights in seclusion.
This is the family tradition of the Bodhisattvas and the realm of the Tathāgata. If one is a beginner, one must first develop a profound sense of weary detachment toward the household.

The household. One attains it only by departing from desire and purifying oneself. Question: If everyone were to practice the holy life (*brahmacarya*) to its full extent, would not the human race soon be extinguished?
Answer: If every person, despite having desires, were to dwell in purity, this world would become a blissful land like *Sukhāvatī*, where beings are born through transformation from lotus flowers.
Why then worry about the extinction of the human race? It is simply that people lack the resolve to seek the Way. Truly.
This is for the sake of transcending the world. That you worry about this—how is it different from a wooden man? △ Fourth, severing the mind. The Buddha said:
"There was a man who suffered from unrestrained lust and wished to remove his own genitals himself. The Buddha said to him: 'If one were to cause the genitals to be severed...'"
"It is better to sever the mind. The mind is like a chief minister; if the chief minister stops, his followers all cease.
If the deviant mind does not stop, what benefit is there in severing the aggregates? The Buddha spoke this verse for him: 'Desire arises within your thought;
thought arises from mental ideation. When both minds are each stilled, they are neither form nor formations. The Buddha said: 'This verse was spoken by Kāśyapa Buddha.'"
[Commentary] "There are [the following]" and below first clarify the root: "sexual misconduct" refers to lustful acts. "Not ceasing" means excessive indulgence.
As for "affliction," there are ten causes: 1. Evil thoughts (such as violating precepts or slandering the Dharma); 2. Agitating the fire (giving rise to fever, dry mouth, a bitter tongue, etc.); 3.

Depleting the essence (causing the spirit to sink and strength to be lost, twitching of the tendons, fear of cold, dread of heat, aversion to wind, suffering from rain, etc.); 4. Damaging the body (yellowish skin, emaciation, soreness of the waist, weakness of the legs, etc.); 5. Inviting disease (consumption and timidity...).

Thirsting consumption (such as developing sores and erupting toxins); sixth, neglect of duties (such as fondness for sleep and laziness in practice); seventh, arrogance toward others (such as being haughty toward teachers and disparaging friends);

eighth, susceptibility to aging (such as the fading of complexion and the decline of blood); ninth, shortening of lifespan (such as slighting the heavens and profaning the deities); tenth, anxiety over death (such as punishments for offenses and retribution for suffering).

[These are] briefly ten, but expanded they are forty. "The *yin*" refers to the male organ, an object of the private parts. It is not like severing the mind; for the *yin* is the secondary, while the mind is the primary.

This is the fundamental principle. "Gongcao" (Merit Official) refers to the office of the official who examines merit. "Followers" refers to those officials in charge of recording blessings, goodness, calamity, and evil.
A lustful mind serves as the cause; it is likened to the Gongcao. Lustful objects serve as the conditions; the direction of lust serves as the method;

and the root of lust serves as the equipment; these are likened to the followers. Just as soldiers follow the general’s movements and companions travel according to their leader's lead, such is the case here.

When the mind is at peace, the *yin* is still; when the mind arises, the *yin* moves. As the Sutra says: "If the mind clings to sexual conduct, the fluids of the male and female organs naturally flow.
Thus, one can see that by severing the *yin* and preserving the mind, one avoids being a foolish person of the secular world who possesses inverted knowledge.

The Buddha descends. Next, he cites scriptural evidence regarding desire (*chanda*), thought (*vitarka*), and perception (*saṃjñā*). Desire is the longing for an object of pleasure. Thought is that which causes the mind to engage in formative activity (*karma*).
Perception is the grasping of the distinct features of an object. "Mind" (*manas*) refers to the sixth consciousness, the sovereign.

If these are correlated with the five aggregates (*skandha*), they correspond to sensation (*vedanā*): it is the experiencing of the preceding object that gives rise to craving and desire. Thought is... [as defined above].

It is action (*saṃskāra*). It is the driving and employing of one's own mind; it is the performance of karmic deeds. "Mind" (*manas*) refers to consciousness (*vijñāna*). "Mind" here specifically denotes the *vibhava-vijñāna* (the consciousness that discriminates phenomena).
Its conceptualization of form (*rūpa-saṃjñā*) can be understood as that which is able to move the substance of form. It arises from desire and thought, hoping for and longing after objects of desire.

It is rooted in the mental consciousness (*mano-vijñāna*) and is associated with the mind. It takes on various images, produced solely by the two mental factors of ideation (*saṃjñā*) and volition (*cetanā*).

Thus, that which is the object of the King’s mind is the root of desire. When both the mind-king and its mental factors are stilled, the physical substance of the aggregates and faculties likewise becomes tranquil.
Upon reaching this state, the five aggregates are all empty; what then remains of form or action?
The affliction of lust shall cease from this point on. When the Buddha descended, he first cited the verse; this identifies the speaker.

In Sanskrit he is called Kāśyapa, which here means "Drinker of Light" (Drinking Radiance). He was a Buddha of the past. To eliminate desire and to eliminate the mind—this is the path shared by all Buddhas.
If you practice abandonment, this dharma is the most supreme. [Commentary]:

"The mind is the root and the aggregates are the branches" means that the mind encompasses the four aggregates of feeling and so forth, while the aggregates refer specifically to the aggregate of form. Below, regarding "merit":

Furthermore, the officials who transmit [these matters] are named *gongcao* (merit-officials) and are the masters. Those who share the same task are called *congzhě* (attendants) and are the companions.
As for "the cause of lustful intent," this refers to the arising of thoughts of desire below. As for "the realm of lust," this refers to the descent of sensual desire. The *Brahmajāla Sūtra* states:
"The cause of lust, the condition of lust, the dharma of lust, and the karma of lust. A single thought that fundamentally gives rise to a defiled mind constitutes [this].
The causes include acts such as gazing and following after [the object]. Various factors that assist and complete the act of lust serve as conditions (*pratyaya*).

Within the act of lust, the preparatory stages consist of providing the necessary implements, physical contact, and expressions of praise; these constitute the formal method (*dharma*). The actual functioning consists of the mutual union of the two parties, which constitutes the completion of the act of lust as its function (*karma*).
The Vinaya states: "This precept is established as a grave offense through five conditions: first, the lustful mind; second, the sentient being..."
First, birth; second, the perception of sentient beings and so forth; third, the path; fourth, the fulfillment of the objective.

Thus, one knows that the commission of impure conduct depends solely upon the mind of sexual misconduct. As for the statement that "severing the aggregates is of no benefit," it is like a eunuch who still takes a wife;
being neither male nor female, he still clings to matters of desire. Therefore, the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* says: "One must ensure that the mechanism of lust is severed in both body and mind."
Even the nature of cessation does not exist; regarding the Bodhi of the Buddha, one may indeed hope for it. Mahāmati said:

"When consciousness breaks through the place where its own mind arises, boundless karmic obstacles are purified all at once; various kinds of excellence arrive spontaneously without being sought. This is precisely that meaning.
As for "the two minds are tranquil, neither form nor action," this refers to how only by practicing the foundations of mindfulness (smṛtyupasthāna) can one [attain] such [a state].

Such persons give rise to four perversions regarding the five aggregates: they frequently give rise to the perversion of purity regarding form; they frequently give rise to the perversion of pleasure regarding feeling;
they frequently give rise to the perversion of self regarding perception and mental formations; and they frequently give rise to the perversion of permanence regarding consciousness.

To eliminate these four perversions, the Tathāgata taught the contemplation of the four foundations of mindfulness: first, by contemplating the impurity of the body, one destroys the perversion of purity regarding form; second, by contemplating...

One contemplates that sensation is suffering, thereby subverting the perversion of perceiving pleasure in sensation. Third, one contemplates that the mind is impermanent, thereby subverting the perversion of perceiving consciousness as permanent.

Fourth, one contemplates that phenomena are without self, thereby subverting the perversions of perceiving perception and formations as a self. Once these four perversions are empty, the five aggregates do not exist;
from where, then, could affliction arise? Furthermore, Yongjia said: "Regarding all female forms, the mind has no defiled attachment. This is because ordinary people are deluded.
Inverted, intoxicated by desire, they are addicted, debauched, and deluded, unaware of their transgression. It is like grasping the stem of a flower while failing to realize it is a venomous serpent.
To the wise, the mouth of a venomous serpent, the paws of a bear or leopard, fierce fire, or glowing iron are not even fit for comparison.

[The sufferings of] the copper pillar and the iron bed cause the back to char and the intestines to rot; flesh and blood are crushed and disintegrated, with pain piercing to the very marrow of the heart.
Contemplate it in this way: its nature is suffering and devoid of pleasure; it is like a leather bag filled with excrement, a mass of pus and blood.

Though the exterior is falsely adorned with perfumes and ointments, within there is only foulness and impurity overflowing. It is a dwelling place for maggots and worms, surpassing even a fish-market stall or a latrine hole.
When the wise contemplate it, they see only hair, body hair, nails, teeth, skin, flesh, blood, fluids, tears, mucus, and [saliva].

Saliva, pus, fat, excrement, urine, and such foul-smelling substances—each of these is a non-human being. Stirred and struck by the winds of consciousness (*vijñāna-vāyu*), they falsely produce speech and feign intimacy;
yet in reality, they are envious and hostile. They ruin one’s virtue and obstruct the Path, constituting an exceedingly grave transgression.
One should distance oneself from them as one would avoid enemies or bandits. When the wise contemplate them, they regard them as venomous snakes; how could one ever draw near to them?
A venomous serpent does not compare to the attachment to female form. Why is this? A venomous serpent kills a person, resulting in death once;

the fetters of female form bind one for thousands of births and myriad kalpas, with various forms of torment and suffering that are inexhaustible. Examine this with discernment and reflect deeply upon it.
It is difficult to draw near. This, too, is a method of contemplation for stilling the mind and detaching from form; one should practice it with earnest dedication.
△ Five: Detachment from Craving.
The Buddha said: "From craving arises sorrow; from sorrow arises fear. If one is detached from craving, what sorrow and what fear can there be?"
[Commentary: The first two phrases mean that when the root arises, the branches arise; the latter two phrases mean that when the root ceases, the branches cease.
When an object first accords with one's feelings, desire arises; after desire persists for a long time, attachment arises. When attachment first encounters separation, sorrow arises;
when pleasure departs and suffering arrives, fear arises. Vimalakīrti said: "From delusion comes craving, and from this my illness arises. Thus, one does not give rise to craving or views.

Severing all攀緣 (pān-yuán, clinging to objects), one forgets both hatred and affection. Departing from the notions of "self" and "what belongs to the self," even the concepts of "I" and "person" are empty;
how, then, could any external object give rise to sorrow or fear?

[Commentary] "Lustful desire" refers to delusion and karma. "Sorrow and fear" refer to the retribution of suffering. Happiness is not permanent; after a long time, it must inevitably decay and perish.

Therefore, there are seven kinds of sorrow: first, the sorrow of physical weakness; second, the sorrow of illness (humans have five desires and seven emotions, and illnesses consist of five wasting diseases and seven injuries, as well as the four hundred and four ailments, most of which arise from lust);

third, the sorrow of the end of life (as vital essence is depleted and the body loses its life-force with each passing year; Guǎngchéngzǐ said: "Do not agitate your essence, and you may attain longevity"); fourth, the sorrow of evil deeds (for among all evils, lust is the foremost);
fifth, the sorrow of calamities (for according to the Way of Heaven, blessings follow goodness while calamities follow lust); sixth, the sorrow of separation.

Anxiety (such as when one falls asleep for a moment and family members, both male and female, depart without taking [one's belongings], leaving them unused; how much more so after death—how could there be mutual joy then? Furthermore, there are those whose love turns into enmity).

Seventh, the anxiety of death (neglecting one’s own person in pursuit of dog-like desires, yet death stands imminent. The *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* says: "If one indulges excessively in greed and desire, before even a year has passed, the liver and brain will wither away until one dies and falls into the Avīci Hell").
There are five fears: first, the fear of not being able to subsist; second, the fear of ill repute; third, the fear of the majesty and power of the great assembly; fourth, the fear of death.

Fifth is the fear of falling into the evil realms. Superior desire is an object that accords with one's emotions and brings pleasure; this anxiety and fear are objects that oppose one's emotions and bring suffering.
Thus, one knows that pleasure is the cause of suffering, for enmity arises from intimacy. If things were situated in separate places, what would there be to hate and what to love?
Upon entering the equality of emptiness, there is neither opposition nor accord. It is like a beautiful woman: a lustful man perceives her as beautiful.
Craving gives rise to desire; the jealous wife views it as suffering and does not wish to see it with her eyes. An ordinary person views it with indifference, neither favoring nor rejecting it.
A practitioner of the Way views it as the contemplation of impurity. Therefore, suffering and pleasure, opposition and compliance—the objects are fundamentally empty from the start.
Joy, anger, sorrow, and happiness—these emotions likewise do not exist. Yet, within ultimate quiescence, one gives rise to grief.
To fear inverted false imaginings—is this not the mark of a fool? △ Second, the fourfold cultivation of truth.
First, clarifying the method of cultivation in three parts. First, attaining the fruit through firm resolve.
The Buddha said: "One who practices the Way is like a single person going out to battle ten thousand men.
Having donned his armor and stepped forth, his mind may become timid and weak, he may retreat halfway, or he may die in the fray. If his mind is free from fear, he may emerge victorious and return.
A śramaṇa studying the Way should likewise firmly maintain his resolve, practicing with vigor and courage, fearing no external objects, and shattering [all obstacles]."
He extinguishes all demons and attains the fruit of the Way.
[Commentary] First, the analogy: one person represents the śramaṇa practicing the Way; ten thousand people represent the armies of the various demons. Donning armor represents the pure precepts;
riding a mount represents meditative concentration (dhyāna); sharp weapons represent wisdom; leaving the gate represents departing from the gateway of the teachings; cowardice...
"Feeble" is a metaphor for being fearful and failing to advance. "Half-retreated" is a metaphor for abandoning one's path midway.
"Dying in battle" is a metaphor for being bound by Māra and destroying the jewel-like body of awakening. "Fearless" is a metaphor for directly penetrating birth and death;
it is like the courage cultivated by Meng Sheshe, who said, "The son of Long has his entire person composed of gall. "Victorious" is a metaphor for attaining the fruit of the Way. Dharma...
Huā said: "The army of the worthy and holy ones battles against the demon of the five aggregates (skandha-māra), the demon of afflictions (kleśa-māra), and the demon of death (mṛtyu-māra).

They have achieved great merit and renown; they extinguish the three poisons, transcend the three realms, and shatter the net of Māra. This is it. As for the 'Sands' (sa) below, it signifies the Dharma of subsequent study.

To learn the Way, one must join in battle with firm progress and fearlessness; one must possess the power of being without dread and be strong. By destroying Māra, one attains the fruits [of the path]; by joining in victory, one attains loftiness."

"Transference" refers to abiding in principle with a firm mind. "Vigorous courage" refers to spiritual cultivation. "Fearlessness" refers to clarifying the teachings. "Extinguishing demons" refers to realizing the fruits [of the path].
[Commentary] As for the various Māras, they are briefly fourfold: first, the Devaputra, who is the Māra-king at the summit of the Desire Realm (*kāmadhātu*).

Because he is deeply attached to worldly pleasures and harbors hatred and jealousy toward the Buddha-dharma, he is a condition for birth and death (*saṃsāra*). Second, the Afflictions (*kleśa*), which defile and transform the three realms.
There is the Māra of View and Attachment, which purifies the three realms; there is the Māra of the Two Obstructions, which enjoys the three realms;
there is the Māra of the Obstructions of the Various [Seeds], which is the dharma-nature of the three realms;
there is the Māra of the Obstructions of Habitual Tendencies within the land of the dharma-realm, which is the cause of birth and death—the five aggregates and the four great elements.
The six sense faculties and so forth are the māras of form (*rūpa-skandha*). Adverse and favorable conditions, suffering and pleasure, and so forth, are the māras of feeling (*vedanā-skandha*).
Immeasurable thoughts and considerations are the māras of perception (*saṃjñā-skandha*). The arising of various greed, anger, and so forth, are the māras of mental formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*).

The various discernments of consciousness and so forth are the māras of consciousness (*vijñāna-skandha*). The four māras of death are the impermanent causes and conditions that destroy the continuity of the five aggregates and depart from warmth.

Because consciousness is stilled, the latter two are the fruits of birth and death. They are extensively eighty-four thousand in number; that is to say, the ten afflictive propensities (*anuśaya*) mutually combine to form one hundred.
When these are multiplied by the five faculties and the five sense objects, they total one thousand. The *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* states:
"Regarding the eyes and so forth with respect to the objects of form, sound, smell, taste, and touch, there are five hundred afflictions within and likewise five hundred afflictions without."
The seven branches of body and speech constitute seven thousand; together with those of the three times, they total twenty-one thousand.
Greed, hatred, delusion, and their equal distribution constitute four types of mind; each possesses twenty-one thousand, totaling eighty-four thousand demonic forces. Hanging down.

Armor is a metaphor for ethical discipline (*śīla*), because it protects and sustains the body. A vehicle is a metaphor for meditative concentration (*samādhi*), because one mounts the correct vehicle. A vessel is a metaphor for wisdom (*prajñā*).

Because they destroy various things, these three [stages] and their teachings apply equally to both the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna. "Non-advancement" refers to those of middling or inferior faculties whose minds are timid and whose courage is weak;

they regress midway. At the minimum, this occurs at the stage of *uṣmagata* (Heat); initially, it may occur at the stage of *gotrabhū* (Lineage), and finally, even at the ten levels of faith (*śraddhā*).

This is like the case of the monk who lacked learning in the fourth dhyāna, or Śāriputra’s regression from six moments of mind, and so forth. Below the section on "Death in Battle," the *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra*...
Yan said: "If you maintain meditative concentration (*dhyāna*) in this very place and awaken to it without delusion, then those demonic affairs will be powerless against you.
If you do not attain clear awakening, you will be deluded by those demons; then, Ānanda, you will surely become a child of Māra.

This would utterly destroy your entire body of precious awakening, like a high minister’s family suddenly being subjected to confiscation of their property—reduced to ruin and decay beyond all hope of pity."
Regarding Jiu Mengsheshe, Mencius said: "As for the way Mengsheshe cultivated his courage, he said: 'I regard not being victorious as being the same as being victorious.
To measure the enemy before advancing and to deliberate on victory before engaging is to stand in awe of the three armies.
Could Sheshe truly ensure victory? He was simply able to remain without fear. As for Zilongdan, [it refers to] Wei...
When King Cao approached Hanzhong, Zhao Yun led several dozen horsemen to scout it. Just as they encountered Cao’s troops making a major sortie, Yun fought while gradually retreating.
Cao pursued them to the camp gates; Yun entered the camp and threw the gates wide open. Suspecting an ambush, Cao withdrew.
The following morning, Liu Bei went to Zhao Yun’s camp and looked about, saying, "Zi Long, every inch of you is filled with [the enemy]."

It is the gallbladder. As for the army of the worthy and sages: on a small scale, it consists of the various generals such as the Seven Sages and the Four Fruits; on a large scale, it consists of generals such as the Ten Sages and the Three Worthies.

"Dying from internal afflictions" refers, on a small scale, to the five tainted aggregates (*skandhas*) within the realm, which are the fruit-demons (*phala-māra*) of birth-and-death with fixed limits (*paricchinna-jāti-maraṇa*);
their causes are the demons of views and craving. On a large scale, it refers to those beyond the realm, which are untainted (*anāsrava*).
The five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*) and the cycle of birth and death through transformation are the fruit-demons (*phala-māra*).

As for the dust-like sands of [phenomena] being non-existent, up to the solid false conceptualization regarding form (*rūpa*), the pervasive false conceptualization regarding sensation (*vedanā*), the false conceptualization regarding perception (*saṃjñā*) as it integrates [objects], the subtle and hidden false conceptualization regarding mental formations (*saṃskāra*), and the illusory false conceptualization regarding consciousness (*vijñāna*)—all these are due to demons.

There are three kinds of merit: first, the extinction of poison, whereby the demon of affliction (*kleśa-māra*) is departed from; second, the transcendence of realms, whereby the demon of death (*mṛtyu-māra*) is departed from.

Thus, the three nets are shattered and the *skandha-māra* (aggregate demon) is cast off; hence it is called "Great Accomplishment. The *Mahāsaṃnipāta Sūtra* states: "By knowing suffering, one destroys the *skandha-māra*;
by severing the origin [of suffering], one distances oneself from the *kleśa-māra* (affliction demon); by realizing cessation, one eliminates the *mṛtyu-māra* (death demon);

and by cultivating the path, one subdues the *devaputra-māra* (heavenly son demon). The "Chapter on the Four Reliances" in the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* says: "If the heavenly demon Pāpīyān should come again, you shall bind him with the five fetters. [End of] Exegesis.
It is said: The five fetters are precisely the gates of the five *sthāpanā-citta* contemplations (*pañca-viśrāma-citta-vidarśana*), which counteract those five kinds of Māras.

The three phrases beginning with "extinguishing" refer to severing the seeds and habitual tendencies of greed; this is to transcend the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) and break the net of the *skandha-māra*, transforming the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*) into the *dharmakāya*.
Severing the seeds and habitual tendencies of hatred is to transcend the form realm (*rūpadhātu*) and break the net of the *kleśa-māra*, transforming afflictions into... [the *anāsrava-kāya*].
Bodhi is the severing of the seeds and habitual tendencies of delusion; it is emerging from the formless realm and breaking the net of the Lord of Death.

When sentient beings die, they thereby attain nirvāṇa. As for those who possess powerful strength and are fearless, this refers to the powers of precepts, patience, firm diligence, compassion, meditative concentration, and wisdom.

Regarding those who have attained high advancement: the *Lotus Sūtra* states that when a king sees his soldiers who have performed meritorious service in battle, he is filled with great joy and bestows rewards according to their merit.
He may grant them fields, houses, villages, or towns; or he may grant them clothing and articles for adorning the body.
Or he may bestow upon them various kinds of rare treasures, elephants, horses, chariots, servants, and subjects;

if there is one who is brave and capable of performing difficult deeds, the king unties the bright jewel from within his topknot and grants it to him. The Tathāgata is likewise: seeing the army of the noble ones, he bestows such rewards.
He fights alongside them; when they achieve merit, his heart is filled with joy.
Among the fourfold assembly, he preaches various sutras for them, bestowing upon them the wealth of the dharmas—dhyāna, samādhi, liberation, and the faculties and powers free from outflows.
He further grants them the city of nirvāṇa, and finally, he preaches this Lotus Sutra, enabling sentient beings to reach the ultimate goal.

Wisdom. The commentary explains: the field is a metaphor for meditative concentration (*dhyāna*); the house is a metaphor for liberation (*vimukti*); the village is a metaphor for the four fruits of the Śrāvaka;

the city is a metaphor for the *pratyekabuddha*'s nirvāṇa; the town is a metaphor for the pure land of the Bodhisattva; clothing is a metaphor for the wholesome dharmas of shame (*hrī*) and patience (*kṣānti*);

ornaments are a metaphor for all the factors conducive to enlightenment (*bodhipakṣadharma*); precious jewels are a metaphor for the seven limbs of awakening (*saptabodhyaṅga*); and oxen, horses, elephants, and chariots are metaphors for the three vehicles (*triyāna*).

Contemplative wisdom is likened to servants; supernatural powers (*abhijñā*) are likened to subjects; knowledge and vision (*jñāna-darśana*) are likened to the populace; and the bright jewel within the topknot is likened to the Tathāgata’s knowledge of all modes (*sarvākārajñatā*).

Thus, one knows that within the process of transformation, there are differences among the fruits of the paths and stages of the various noble ones (*ārya*), whether small or great. [The section on] "Firmness" follows below.

The teachings, practices, principles, and fruits encompass both the Small and Great Vehicles. In the Small Vehicle, they consist of the six consciousnesses, the contemplation of the emptiness of persons, the teaching on the cessation of suffering, and the fruit of the Two Vehicles.
In the Great Vehicle, they consist of the eight consciousnesses and so forth, the contemplation of the emptiness of all phenomena, the adornment of the lands, and the salvation of sentient beings;

these constitute the teaching of the Great Vehicle and the fruit of wondrous enlightenment. Thus, one knows that firm progress and courageous penetration are the essential tasks for the Way. Question: Why?
Since this is known to be so, why was this analogy composed? Answer: A certain version of the text states:

"If a person can firmly maintain their mind and advance with vigor and acuity, undeluded by the words of the worldly and the madly ignorant, and desires to extinguish and exhaust evil, they will surely attain the Way.
Therefore, there is a basis for composing this analogy. II. Proving the Principle through the Middle Way.
A śramaṇa was reciting the *Kāśyapa-buddha-avaivartika-śāsana-sūtra* at night; his voice was neither too tight nor too loose, yet he felt regret and wished to withdraw from his practice.
The Buddha asked him, "When you were formerly a householder, what was your profession? He replied, "I loved playing the lute. The Buddha said, "If the strings are too slack, what happens?
He replied, "They do not sound. "If the strings are too tight, what happens? He replied, "The sound is broken. "When they are adjusted to the middle between tight and slack—"

"What is it? he asked. He replied, "All the notes were perfectly tuned. The Buddha said, "The śramaṇa who studies the Way is likewise so. If the mind is harmonious and well-adjusted, the Way can be attained.
If one is violent toward the Way, that violence leads to physical exhaustion. When the body is exhausted, the mind gives rise to affliction.
When the mind gives rise to affliction, one's practice regresses. Once practice has regressed, retribution must surely follow. Only through purity and tranquility is there true peace and happiness."
"The Way will not be lost.
[Commentary] First, the text describes the improper application of the mind. Regarding "reciting at night": as for the *saṃgha*, during the day they attend to their regular duties;

at night, they cultivate their own practice, disciplining the mind at every moment without the slightest laxity. This refers to the Buddha’s *Śāsanānuśāsana* (The Teaching Left Behind by the Buddha). It is...
This is the scriptural teaching left behind by the third Buddha of the Bhadrakalpa. "Pity" refers to the lack of proficiency in the faculties of compassion.

"Tightness" refers to the immaturity of the sutras of suffering. "Regret" refers to lamenting that the Sangha is difficult to serve. "Retreat" refers to the thought that the Way is difficult to attain. As Mengzi said:
"He who advances with excessive vigor will retreat with equal speed. Therefore, the mouth is tight while the heart feels regret. Thus spoke the Buddha.
Questioning the Lower [Extreme]. Next, showing the path of the Middle Way in two parts. First, raising the question so that it may be understood. The lute-playing analogy applies to both cases:

in contrast to the upper metaphor, it refers to reciting the sutras; in contrast to the lower metaphor, it refers to practicing the Path. The tuning of the strings also has two aspects: it is a metaphor for tuning the voice and tuning the mind.
"Tight" and "slack" are metaphors for haste and laxity, or diligence and indolence. "Middle" is a metaphor for being neither slow nor fast. "The sound ceases and does not ring" is a metaphor for...

The words and meanings were not yet matured; the principle and nature were not yet penetrated. Pútíáo remarked, "This is like a metaphor for when the words are clear and the meaning is manifest, the principle is exhausted and the nature is fully realized.
The *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* says: "For example, although lutes, harps, *huqiu*, and *pipa* have wondrous sounds, if there are no skillful fingers, they can never produce music.
Yet, when the Great Tree Kinnara King moves his strings and sings, the sound vibrates throughout the great trichiliocosm."
As Mount Sumeru, the King of Mountains, surges and subsides, rises and falls, all the śrāvakas dance and play;
this truly accords with the Way of holding fast to the Mean. It can truly be called the unalterable Dharma transmitted from sage to sage.

Following the words of the Buddha, there are two examples that clarify the method of training. First, the brief example: if one is too tense, the ailment of agitation is removed; if one is just right, one is not lax.
Scattered ailments depart. Furthermore, through regulation, one advances toward physical purity; this is not abrupt violence. Through adaptation, one follows toward mental joy;
this is not indolent laxity. Being neither restless nor weary, how could there be anything that cannot be attained on the Way?
At the assembly of the *Āgama*, the Buddha told Kātyāyana: "Excessive diligence is like mere play; if one is lax..."
The indolent fall into false views; those who abide in the middle proceed upward.
Thus, before long, for one whose precepts are free from outflows, the *Perfect Enlightenment Sūtra* also says: "That which can realize is without action and without effort; that which is realized..."
Without grasping and without abandoning, those who seek to enter the Buddha-way should practice in this manner.

Regarding the section on "The Lower Path," the following provides a detailed explanation: As for the "violent" practitioner, it is because their resolve is excessively high and their efforts are too hurried.

As for the "exhausted" practitioner, their spirit of exertion is overly intense, causing their mental energy to easily decline; once their strength is spent, it is difficult to sustain, and indolence follows.
One who gives rise to mental affliction acts with haste and disorder, ultimately falling back into negligence; therefore, retribution will surely be added.

This is because such a person does not blame their own unwholesome state of mind, but instead slanders the recitation of sutras as being fruitless and the study of the Way as being of no benefit, thereby giving rise to great false views and committing various evil karmas.
This is like a lute whose strings are too tight, causing the sound to snap; so it is with the Way.
One follows along with indolence; through such laziness, the body becomes exhausted and dull, while the mind becomes distracted and difficult to restrain, leading to distress.

Consequently, one ruins the Path and finds it difficult to progress; one comes to resent the scriptures and find them difficult to study, giving rise to great hatred and delusion, and committing various karmic obstacles.
This is like a lute whose strings are too slack and thus do not sound. Through purity, one adjusts the body so that it does not fall into haste or violence;
the Way will advance of its own accord. Through tranquility, one comports the mind so that it does not fall into laxity; the Way will be accomplished of its own accord.
This is like playing the lute: when the tension is adjusted between too tight and too loose, all the notes are harmonized.
Thus, one who studies the Way should emulate Boya’s skillful tuning.
[Commentary] Regarding the phrase "reciting at night," the *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra* states: "One should avoid crowds, worldly customs, and sleep during the first, middle, and last watches of the night."
One should constantly awaken oneself to the practice of skillful means. The *Śāriputra-parivarta* (The Sutra of the Bequeathed Teaching) says:

"You bhikṣus, during the day you should diligently cultivate wholesome dharmas so as not to let the time pass in vain. During the first and last watches of the night, do not allow them to be neglected either.
During the middle watch, recite the sūtras to refresh yourself. Do not, for the sake of sleep, allow this one life to pass in emptiness, achieving nothing."
It is so. You should contemplate that the fire of impermanence burns all worlds; seek early deliverance for yourself and do not indulge in sleep.
Let your voice be sorrowful and directed toward the mouth; let your thoughts be remorseful and directed toward the mind.

At the beginning of the day, when a person studies the Way, they must certainly not fail to apply their mind, yet they must also not apply their mind too intensely. If one advances with excessive vigor and sharpness, then their vital energy will easily decline.

Yet his regression will necessarily be swift; this is because he overuses his mind, and thus his merit will not be accomplished. Being insufficient is as much a fault as being excessive; each has its own drawback.
"Advancing" (*jin*) refers to gradually treading forward without haste. "Following" (*xun*) means to comply; it refers to maintaining [the mind] with composure and ease.
Regarding the Buddha below, the *Āgama* Sūtras state: There was a venerable one named Śroṇakoṭīviṃśa. By day...
He practiced at night with diligent effort without ceasing, yet his mind was unable to be liberated from the outflows of sensual desire (*kāma-āsrava*).
He then addressed the Buddha, saying: "The life of a śramaṇa is extremely difficult. I now wish to cast off my robes, return to being a layman, and provide extensive offerings of material goods.

The Buddha asked: "Are you skilled at playing the lute while living as a householder? He replied: "I am. The Buddha asked: "If the strings are too tight, can the sound be heard? He replied: [It cannot.]
[He] said, "No. He asked again, "If the strings were somewhat loose, could they be played? [He] replied again, "No.
He asked once more, "If they were neither too tight nor too loose, could they be played? [He] replied, "They could be played. The World-Honored One told him: "It is just like this.
One who exerts excessive diligence is like one who is frivolous; if one is indolent, one falls into wrong views. If one is..."
Those of middling capacity will then proceed upward; before long, they will become persons free from outflows (*anāsrava*).

At that time, the twenty *koṭis* of ears contemplated the Buddha’s teaching and, dwelling in a secluded place, practiced its Dharma. Knowing it as it truly is, they realized arhatship. The commentary states:
"Distracted playfulness is like a person chasing after others on the road; wrong views are like a person hiding in a cave. Thus, [it is said in] the *Perfect Enlightenment Sūtra*.
It is said: In cultivating and realizing the wondrous Dharma, one should avoid two types of illness. The first is the illness of effort (*kriyā-roga*), which means:
"I shall perform various practices in order to seek perfect enlightenment (*pariniṣpanna-avabodha*). This is because that nature of perfect enlightenment cannot be attained through effort.

The second is the illness of indifference (*anābhoga-roga*), which means: "I shall now neither sever birth-and-death (*saṃsāra*) nor seek nirvāṇa; I will leave everything as it is, following the nature of all phenomena (*dharmatā*)," while desiring to seek [enlightenment].
Regarding that nature of perfect enlightenment, it does not exist merely by chance. Guishan said:

"If you set your mind upon the teachings and study the palm-leaf scriptures, diligently searching out their principles and meanings, then your time will not be spent in vain, and you will become a vessel for the Dharma among the monastics.
Thus we know that those who remain complacent in decline are utterly incapable of purposeful action, and those who are restless and disorderly will find it difficult to achieve perfection.

Thus its function is fulfilled; whether in urgency or relaxation, it is appropriate, and the task is completed from beginning to end. Regarding the path, "if one is below" refers to making up for deficiencies.

As for the fact that the *Sūtra* does not clarify this, the error lies in over-exerting one's efforts. The commentary provides both [alternatives] because being either too urgent or too relaxed is equally a fault.

Regarding "Pure and Tranquil" (*qingjing*): above, there is no seeking with longing; this is called "pure" (*qing*). Below, there is no abandoning through weariness; this is called "tranquil" (*jing*).
Not being attached to existence externally is called "peaceful" (*an*). Not being indulgent in emptiness internally is called "blissful" (*le*). These are all the Middle Way that avoids extremes.
If one conducts oneself and halts in such a manner, the fruit of the Way can be attained. Regarding "Boya was skilled at tuning": Boya studied the *qin* lute under...
Cheng Lian had been practicing for three years without success. Cheng Lian said, "My teacher is Fang Zichun;
he is currently on the Eastern Sea and can move the hearts of men. He then went with Bo Ya there. Upon reaching the mountain, he left Bo Ya behind, saying, "You stay here and practice;
I shall go to fetch you. Bo Ya looked around but saw no one, hearing only the surging roar of the sea. He sighed and said, "Master..."

"It has moved my feelings," he said, and thereupon composed the "Water Immortal" (Suixian) piece. When the music ended, Chenglian welcomed him back. Boya subsequently became the most marvelous player in the world.
Later, he met Zhong Ziqi, who was skilled at listening. When Boya played the zither with his mind set upon lofty mountains, Ziqi said, "How excellent!
How majestic, like Mount Tai! When his mind was set upon flowing water, Ziqi immediately said, "How excellent!"
How vast it is! It is like the Yangtze and the Yellow River. Whatever Bo Ya contemplates, Ziqi invariably and skillfully captures its essence.

Furthermore, while Bo Ya was traveling on the northern slope of Mount Tai, he encountered a torrential rain and took shelter beneath a cliff. His heart was filled with sorrow, so he took up his *qin* and began to play.
At first, he composed a melody of lingering rain; then, he created the sounds of a collapsing mountain. Such was the music.
Every time Ziqi played, Boya would invariably fathom its essence. Boya then set aside his lute and sighed, saying, "How excellent!
Your listening—your will and imagination are as if they were my own heart. How could I have escaped from such sounds?
Had Boya not been skilled at tuning the strings, Ziqi likewise would not have been able to understand the intent behind the flowing water and the lofty mountain."
△ Third, removing defilements to perfect practice.
The Buddha said: "It is like a person forging iron; by removing the dross, the vessel is made, and the vessel is then refined and excellent. So too for one who studies the Way:
by removing the defilements of the mind, their practice becomes pure."

[Commentary] First, an analogy is presented. "Person" refers to one who studies the Way. "Smelting" means heating and refining; it refers to cultivation and severance (*bhāvanā-prahāṇa*). "Iron" refers to the mind of the Way.

"Dross" means refuse and impurities; it refers to defilements. "Vessel" refers to the practice of the Way. "Exquisite and fine" refers to purity. Following "studies the Way," the analogy is next applied to the Dharma. "Defilement" refers to delusion.
"Coarse defilement" refers to the afflictions of views and thought (*dṛṣṭi-kleśa* and *saṃjñā-kleśa*). "Subtle defilement" refers to the dust [of sensory objects].
It is like sand and ignorance. When the mind is defiled, one creates karma in accordance with emotional attachments; the retribution of suffering is immeasurable, and birth and death do not cease.
When conduct is pure, one accords with principle and realizes the truth, abiding in the realm of nirvana and constantly experiencing peace and bliss.
Therefore, by removing the defilements of the mind, one accomplishes the practice of ultimate purity. The remainder is as explained in the *Nirviśeṣa-śāstra*.

[Commentary] Iron first burns away coarse dross to form a fine vessel; the mind first severs the coarse defilements of affliction (*kleśa*) to achieve the clear and pure contemplative practice of the emptiness of self (*pudgala-śūnyatā*). Iron next refines subtle impurities to form a refined vessel;

the mind next eliminates the subtle stains of the knowable (*jñeya*) to achieve the pure contemplative practice of the emptiness of phenomena (*dharma-śūnyatā*). According to the teachings, this pertains to the Hīnayāna.

Coarse defilements are removed; initially, subtle stains are partially eliminated; finally, they are realized as identical and suddenly both vanish. Perfectly interfused and unimpeded. In terms of stages:
impure sentient beings, those who are pure within the midst of defilement (Bodhisattvas and Śrāvakas/Pratyekabuddhas being included), and those who are supremely pure.
He is called the Tathāgata. The proponents of non-differentiation say:

"Śāriputra, this very dharmakāya, when enveloped by the storehouse of boundless afflictions since beginningless time, circulating through birth and death within the realms of saṃsāra, is called the 'realm of sentient beings' (sattvadhātu). Furthermore, Śāriputra, this very dharmakāya, when [possessed of] revulsion..."

Suffering from drifting through birth and death, they renounce all realms of sensual desire and cultivate various practices for the sake of seeking Bodhi within the ten *pāramitās* and the eighty-four thousand dharma-gates; these are called Bodhisattvas.
Furthermore, Śāriputra, this very *dharmakāya* is far removed from all suffering and has eternally eliminated all [afflictions].
The afflictions, secondary afflictions, and stains are purified, utterly purified, and supremely purified;

abiding in the *dharmatā* and attaining non-obstruction, one is called a Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha. The commentary states: regarding the passage on the realm of sentient beings (*sattvadhātu*), it refers to the purification of the upper mental stains.
For Bodhisattvas and Tathāgatas, this refers to the purification of the upper practices. The *dharmakāya* is simply another name for the mind.
When defilements depart from the mind, the pure *dharmakāya* is realized. II. Citing Evidence for the Difficulty of the Result. The Buddha said:
"It is difficult for a person to escape the evil realms and obtain human birth. Having obtained human birth, it is difficult for a woman to become a man.

Having become a man, it is difficult for one's six sense faculties (*ṣaḍindriya*) to be complete. Once the six faculties are complete, it is difficult to be born in a central land (*madhyadeśa*). Having been born in a central land..."
It is difficult to encounter the era of a Buddha. Having encountered the era of a Buddha, it is difficult to meet a path-attainer. Having met a path-attainer, it is difficult to give rise to faith.
Having given rise to faith, it is difficult to resolve upon bodhicitta. Having resolved upon bodhicitta, it is difficult to practice without cultivation and realize without realization.

[Commentary] From "The Buddha" onwards, the first section raises the difficulty by illustrating it through worldly results. There are five points: for one hundred and eighty kalpas, time passed in vain without a Buddha;
beings constantly practiced unwholesome deeds and frequently fell into the evil realms. Therefore, it is difficult to escape the three evil realms.

The Buddha asked the bhikṣus: "Which is more: the dust on my fingernail or the dust upon the earth? The bhikṣus replied: "The dust upon the earth is far more numerous. The Buddha said: [the remainder of this passage follows].
Those who pass away from the heavens and are reborn among humans are like the soil on a fingernail; those who fall into hell are like the soil upon the earth.
Just as with Śakra, the gods of Yāma, and the Ṛṣi Udraka, one knows that a human body is difficult to obtain.
Once a human body is lost, it will not be regained for ten thousand kalpas. A woman has five obstacles and ten evils, and may encounter her father-in-law or mother-in-law.
How tragic! A husband may be cruel and tyrannical, or one may encounter meager parental affection, or have children and daughters-in-law who are obstinate and rebellious;
even within the seclusion of the inner chambers, there may be restrictions that make childbirth difficult. Men do not experience this.

One must possess the four dharmas of practice, as exemplified by Shanmin, who was the daughter of District Magistrate Dong, and Haiyin, who was the daughter of Defense Commissioner Zhu; such was the case with the nun Fahua’s subsequent incarnation.
As for courtesans, it is difficult to see one who has been transformed from female to male and possesses the marks of a man.
Even if one obtains a male body, it is not easy to have all faculties complete and the five limbs dignified, free from such afflictions as being crippled, maimed, blind, deaf, mute, hunched, or lame.
Although the six sense organs may be complete and free from various ailments, it is still difficult to avoid being born in a frontier region.
Alternatively, those dwelling in the Northern Continent (Uttarakuru) do not know benevolence and righteousness, nor do they believe in cause and effect;

even if some *pāraloka* masters with their disciples reside there, they are difficult to transform and guide. This is unlike the Middle Kingdom (Jambudvīpa), where one can sever lustful consciousness and thoughts, and practice with vigorous diligence.
Having been born there, [the text] presents four points illustrating the difficulty of attaining the fruits of world-transcendence. First, residing in the Central Land (*madhyadeśa*).
The retribution lies within Jambudvīpa; yet, how can one avoid being born before or after a Buddha and thus fail to behold his physical form?
Only after passing through one hundred and thirty kalpas can one obtain a single vision of him, for he appears but once in an age, like the udumbara flower. As the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* says:
"The appearance of Buddhas in the world is remote and difficult to encounter. Truly, these words are so! Even if one encounters the era of a Buddha, if one lacks merit...
If one has a friend who guides them, yet they are unable to see the Buddha or hear the Dharma, it is likewise in vain.

Consider, for example, King Ajātaśatru of *Sudarśana*, whose worldly wisdom and eloquence gave rise to great false views; or the three hundred million households in Śrāvastī and all those who were unwilling to see or hear [the teaching].
Is this not truly lamentable? Though they may encounter a spiritual friend (*kalyāṇamitra*) and have the opportunity to hear the Buddha-dharma, they are unable [to practice it].
Having given rise to the fourfold faith and practiced the ten wholesome deeds, one may immediately fall away upon encountering adverse conditions.

Or, even if one attains the fulfillment of faith—which is not like a swan’s down feather that rises and falls—one may still be unable to give rise to the three minds, establish the four vows, and cultivate the five practices.
[The text] attests to the two fruits. The *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* says: "The initial resolve and the ultimate [attainment] are not different;
yet between these two states of mind, the former is more difficult. To seek first to deliver others before one has delivered oneself—therefore, I prostrate to the initial resolve.

Thus we know that the resolve to transform and deliver beings through cultivation and realization is truly most rare. Having spoken of the lower [resolve], [the text] next cites three points regarding the mundane and supramundane.

The supreme fruit is difficult to clarify. Once the great resolve has been awakened and the myriad practices have been cultivated, if one allows even a hair’s breadth of attachment to remain in the mind, one falls back into the realm of conditioned phenomena;
if a fleeting emotion arises, one immediately deviates from the essence of the Dharma-nature (*dharmatā*). With effortful cultivation and realization, one may spend many kalpas only to end in ruin;
yet through mindless realization, one attains sudden accord with the Buddha-family in a single thought-moment. As the *Prajñāpāramitā* says:
Do not give rise to the mind dwelling on form; practice giving without the mark of dwelling. The *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* says:
"When delivering sentient beings, one should eliminate the mark of delivering them," and so on, until "perfecting Bodhi and returning to non-attainment.

This is the path of effortless action (*anābhoga-mārga*), which is truly the most difficult among difficulties. Nevertheless, these ten difficulties are not difficult at all. As the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* says: "Though dwelling in the ocean..."
Even amidst the calamities of water and fire, those capable of receiving this Dharma will surely hear it; how much more so now that you have escaped the three miserable realms,

attained birth in the human path as great beings, possess complete physical faculties, dwell in the Central Land, encountered a sovereign of the Way, beheld the Honored Image, partaken of the nectar of the sublime teachings,
drawn near to virtuous friends, distanced yourselves from evil associates, and have given rise to the Mahāyāna mind?
Faith eliminates doubt and abandons false attachments, while further establishing wholesome causes and generating great vows for the salvation of sentient beings.
It gives rise to the meritorious karma of humans; it is the very nature of all phenomena, yet free from all marks. Thus, there is non-attachment to both "identity" and "separation."
Inferring from this, you should rejoice in yourself. You ought to know that if one can take single-minded devotion as the Way, what difficulty could there be?
If one cannot take the Way as one's mind, then even in the absence of difficulties, what can be done?
[Commentary] The *Śāstra* contains two intentions. The first is a direct explanation of the difficulty to serve as an admonition.

Among the five difficulties regarding the fruits of the world, the first is "avoiding the difficulty of evil," which refers to the three miserable realms (*trāya*) within the eight difficulties (*aṣṭākṣaṇa*).

Regarding the two lines of the one hundred and eight [verses], the various Brahmās to the southeast of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* recite in verse: "For one hundred and eighty kalpas, time passed in vain without a Buddha; the three evil paths were filled."
The [world] is filled; the hosts of devas are diminishing. They constantly recite two verses. A Brahma hymn from above says:
"In the past, throughout immeasurable kalpas, time passed in vain without a Buddha. The three evil realms increased, and the asuras were likewise flourishing.
The hosts of devas steadily diminished; many who died fell into the evil realms. Not hearing the Dharma from a Buddha, they constantly practiced unwholesome deeds. Furthermore—
A sutra states: "Ants have not shed their ant-bodies since the time of the seven Buddhas; how can one know on what day they will obtain a human body?
Thus, it is truly difficult to escape the three evil realms. The passage beginning with "The Buddha asked" concerns the second difficulty: being born as a human.

Even when celestial beings fall from their heavenly states, they do not even attain human birth; how much less can humans, once fallen, return to being humans again? Furthermore, another sutra states:
The World-Honored One took a small amount of earth from the ground, placed it upon his fingernail, and said to Kāśyapa:

"There may be someone who, having abandoned their body, regains a human body; having abandoned the bodies of the three evil realms, they receive a human body with all faculties intact, born in a central land."

Those who possess perfect faith are able to cultivate the Path; having cultivated the Right Path, they are able to attain liberation and enter parinirvāṇa—such as the particles of earth on a fingernail.
Those who, after discarding a human body, obtain the bodies of the three evil realms; or, after discarding the bodies of the three evil realms, obtain yet another body within the three evil realms;
those with deficient faculties; those born in border regions; those who believe in false and inverted views; and those who cultivate false paths—[these are few].

One attains liberation, the eternal bliss of *nirvāṇa*. Regarding the amount of earth and soil found throughout the worlds of the ten directions, as explained below in the *Saddharmasmṛtyupasthāna-sūtra*:
"Indra is named Aṃśumān; having ruled over the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven, when his merit was exhausted, he fell and became a large-bodied fish in the Mahāgara Ocean.
Furthermore, there have been three or four Indras who fell into the three evil realms."
On the way, the King of the Yāma Heaven fell into the Raurava Hell because his merit was exhausted.

The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states that the seer Udraka attained the four formless absorptions and was reborn in the Heaven of Neither Perception nor Non-perception; there, his lifespan came to an end.
As a karmic retribution, they become flying weasels; by killing various fish and birds, they commit immeasurable sins and fall into the three evil realms.
The devas of the formless realm, being deeply attached to their concentrated minds, do not realize their lives have ended; they fall into the desire realm and receive the forms of birds and beasts.
The various devas of the form realm fall into the desire realm, and when the merit of the six heavens is exhausted, they regress and fall into hell. Women may be reborn in the three lower states.

Regarding the five obstructions (*pañca-āvaraṇāni*), the *Candrāditya-vyūha-sūtra* states: First, one cannot become a Brahmā King, because purity and defilement are incompatible. Second, one cannot become Śakra, because few desires and many desires are mutually exclusive. Third, one cannot become a Māra King, because ferocity and meekness are contrary to one another. Fourth, one cannot... [become a Cakravartin King]. Fifth, one cannot become a Buddha, because the nature of a woman is inherently inferior. Thus it is said. Furthermore, the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states: "If a woman were to attain Buddhahood, she would have to undergo the transformations of a man; if she were to become a Bodhisattva, she would likewise have to undergo the transformations of a man. He becomes a Wheel-Turning King because his benevolence is free from all jealousy. Fifth, he cannot become a Buddha-body because the myriad virtues and afflictions are distinct from one another.
Regarding the ten evils, the *Yujie jing* (Sutra of Yujie) states: First, at birth, his parents do not rejoice;
second, when raised and nourished, they find no pleasure in him; third, his mind is constantly fearful of others; fourth, his father...
Five: being separated from one's parents while they are still alive. Six: fearing the joy and anger of one’s husband. Seven: experiencing great difficulty in childbirth.
Eight: being constrained by one’s parents in youth. Nine: being restricted by one’s husband in middle age. Ten:
being rebuked by one’s children and grandchildren in old age. Regarding those who possess four qualities, the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* states: "Endowed with four dharmas..."
He is called a "true man" (puruṣa) for four reasons: first, approaching virtuous friends; second, hearing the true Dharma; third, contemplating its meaning;

and fourth, practicing according to the teachings. Shan Min and Hai Yin were both names of śramaṇas; their biographies are fully recorded in the six volumes of the *Lèbāng wénlèi* (Classified Writings on the Land of Bliss).
As for the nun Fahua: when Ou Yang Yongshu was serving as the Governor of Yingzhou, he encountered a courtesan whose breath [was foul].
She was made into a lotus-scented woman. There was a monk who knew past lives; he said, "This courtesan was a nun in a previous life.

She recited the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra* for thirty years, yet due to a single moment of negligence, she has come to this state. He asked the courtesan, "Have you ever read the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra?
She replied, "Having lost my body to this life, what leisure have I had to recite the sutra? He then gave her the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*, and she praised and recited it as follows:
[The Master] said: "If one gives them other sutras, they will be unable to read them. Question: "It is true that women are inherently inferior to men.

However, if one falls into their category [of being female], how can one transform and abandon it? Answer: The *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* states: "This Mahāyāna sūtra possesses the characteristics of a man (*puruṣa*).
That is to say, it is to have faith and know that within one's own body there is Buddha-nature (*tathāgatagarbha*). If a man does not know this, he is a woman; a woman [who knows this] is a man."
If one knows that one is indeed a male man and is further able to practice the mindfulness of the Buddha, one may likewise transform from female to male.

For instance, Lady Yang of Guanxu in Taiping Prefecture gave birth to only a posthumous daughter; both mother and daughter lived as widows, and they devoted themselves single-mindedly to the ritual recitation of Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva.
After four months, the girl transformed into a boy. Furthermore, there was the case of Longshi’s daughter.
The Sūtra states: "There was a wealthy elder whose daughter was named Nāgadattā. Seeing the Buddha from atop a high tower, she gave rise to the bodhicitta;
she was transformed into a male and left the household life to practice the Way. Regarding the woman in the womb who hears the Dharma, the Sūtra says:

"A woman in the womb who hears the Dharma transforms her body into the form of a man, leaves the household life, and realizes the fruit [of the path]. As for this "form of a man," the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* [states]:...
There are seven meanings: first, a long lifespan; second, exquisite and dignified appearance; third, freedom from illness and few afflictions;
fourth, being neither a servant nor a woman; fifth, sharp and keen wisdom; sixth, a majestic and solemn presence when speaking; and seventh, possessing a great and flourishing lineage.
One who possesses these seven dharmas is called a "great man" (*puruṣa*). Mencius said: "Riches and honors cannot corrupt him;
poverty and lowliness cannot move him; power and authority cannot subdue him. This is what is meant by a great man. Question:
According to the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*, even if one is a woman, if she can believe that she possesses Buddha-nature, she is a great man. How is this so according to this sutra?
"Is it that one must leave the female state to become male? He replied: "The female body is a vessel of lust and impurity; it is the root of procreation.

Although one may perform virtuous deeds, one cannot attain Buddhahood [in this form]. If a man practices, he realizes Bodhi in the present life. Therefore, Śāriputra said: 'The female body is filthy and impure;
it is not a vessel for the Dharma. How could it attain unsurpassed Bodhi? This is as stated in the *Sumati-sūtra*."
An eight-year-old girl transformed her body into that of a man, left the household life, and preached the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*.

A dragon girl likewise transformed into a male and went to the realm of Vimalā to attain *samyak-saṃbodhi*. This clearly demonstrates that a female body cannot achieve Buddhahood and ascend the seat to preach the Dharma.

Question: The *Tāi jīng* (Womb Sutra) states that the four types of women—those born from the womb, those born from eggs, those born from moisture, and those born by transformation—all do not abandon the *pariccheda-śarīra* (the body of segmented existence).
They do not receive a physical body, nor do they receive a true recompense *dharmakāya*; rather, they all attain the Buddha-way within their current bodies.
A verse says: "The nature of phenomena is like a great ocean; it does not speak of right or wrong. Whether ordinary person or sage, there is equality without high or low.
It depends solely on the extinction of mental defilements; to realize the truth is as easy as turning over one's palm. In the *Vimalakīrti Sūtra*, the heavenly maiden answers Śāriputra...
"Reverend Śāriputra, male and female illusions have no fixed characteristics; that they now transform from male to become Buddhas—how is this principle to be understood?

Answer: Nirvāṇa is itself 'male. This refers to the ultimate realization of the supramundane rational nature (*dharmatā*). In this present sutra, the 'female' is removed; this refers to the conventional teaching regarding the phenomenal characteristics of human affairs.
The *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra* and the *T'ai-ch'ing ching* do not undergo such change; these speak from the perspective of one's own practice realizing the nature of True Suchness (*tathatā*)."

The "Real" (shí) is the fundamental essence; the *Lotus Sūtra*’s transformation of the male form is explained in terms of the Eightfold Path to Enlightenment for the sake of transforming others—it is the provisional trace (*quán*).

If one synthesizes these two, the provisional and the real are mutually fused, and principle and phenomena are without obstruction. Teaching is established according to the capacities of beings, such that there are none who do not derive benefit.

Regarding the phrase "although [one] obtains [the opportunity]," it refers to the difficulty of possessing the four faculties (*sì gēn*). This refers to those among the eight difficulties (*bā nàn*) who lack the six sense organs (*liù gēn*), being crippled, deformed, or impaired.

"Disease" refers to the difficulty [of being born]. Regarding the "six faculties" below: the five difficulties of the central lands (*madhyadeśa*) are, in fact, the two difficulties of the borderlands (*pratyanta*) and the long-lived heavens.

Among humans, this includes the northern continent of Uttarakuru and the small kingdoms of the borders; among the gods, it includes the Heaven of No-Thought (*asaṃjñisattva*) or the long-lived heavens.
In these places, one cannot encounter a Buddha or receive the transformation of a sage. The Buddha told Mañjuśrī: "This *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra* [is rare] in immeasurable lands."
In the middle [continent], even their names cannot be heard, let alone being seen, received, upheld, read, or recited. The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states:
"The Southern Continent (Jambudvīpa) surpasses all the heavens for three reasons; how much more so the Northern Continent (Uttarakuru)?
First, the ability to sever sexual desire; second, the power of mindfulness and awareness; third, valorous diligence. The *Mūlasūtra* states: "The various heavens and the three [heavens]..."
Below, each has three kinds of excellence that surpass Jambudvīpa: first, longevity; second, superior physical form; and third, superior land.
Southern Jambudvīpa possesses five kinds of excellence that surpass the other three continents as well as the various heavens:
first, valor and vigor; second, right mindfulness; third, being the place where Buddhas appear in the world; fourth, being the ground for cultivating practice; and fifth—
This is the place where one practices the holy life (*brahmacarya*). Therefore, the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* states: "Due to inferior-inferior causes and conditions, one is born in the Northern Continent;
due to superior-superior causes and conditions, one is born in the Southern Continent. Why is this? If one discusses karmic retribution (*vipāka*), the Southern Continent is the most inferior;
yet if one encounters a Buddha, the Southern Continent is the most superior. For this reason, the various devas descend to hear the Dharma, and they further make this vow: [text continues]
I vow to be born in Jambudvīpa as a human being, to leave the household life, pay homage to the Buddha, and recite the sutras;
may I not receive such karmic rewards of pleasure, lest I fail to encounter the Sage’s transformation. Even if there were a lower [birth], it would still obstruct [the path]. An objection is raised:

the Sage does not appear in the northern continent (Uttarakuru) to propagate his teachings. How is this explained in the *Ratnamegha-sūtra*, which states that Pāṭhadatta was leading six hundred disciples?

A person dwells in Uttarakuru; therefore, it is said generally that although one is not born there, it is not that one does not reside there, and although one dwells there, it is also difficult to propagate the teachings.
The *Fenbie Gongde Lun* (Treatise on the Differentiation of Merits) states: "The Venerable Bakula was foremost in longevity;
he lived for one hundred years plus sixty more. Ānanda asked: 'Venerable One, you have such a long life. Why..."
The Buddhas are not born in the three other directions. The answer is: the Buddhas are not born in the three directions because those people are difficult to transform.
The sentient beings of this land have sharp faculties and quick intelligence; they are diligent and courageous, and it is not difficult for them to attain the Way.
For this reason, all the Buddhas of antiquity were born within this realm. To dwell in the lower realms is the first difficulty in meeting a Buddha; one must be born directly before a Buddha. Or...

It is difficult to encounter a Buddha after he has appeared in the world. Regarding the "one hundred and thirty" [kalpas]: the *Dharmapada* (or *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*) states that in the south, various Brahmās recite in verse:
"The World-Honored One is extremely difficult to behold; having passed one hundred and thirty kalpas, we have now finally obtained a single vision of him, like the udumbara flower.

*Udumbara* is here translated as the "Auspiciously Manifesting Flower" (*lingshui hua*). It appears only once every three thousand years, and its appearance coincides with the emergence of a Golden Wheel-Turning King (*cakravartin*). Thus it is said.
This is a metaphor for how the Buddha appears at the appropriate time and is difficult to encounter. In the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, there is a verse that follows:
"Even if he were to appear in the world, it would be difficult for him to preach this Dharma; and those who are able to hear this Dharma—such people are likewise rare."
If one encounters the lower [rebirth], there are two difficulties regarding the path: namely, being born into a family of wrong views, which is the difficulty of having worldly wisdom and eloquence.
Regarding "Sublime Adornment," the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* states that the two sons, Viśuddhagarbha and Viśuddhanetra, exhorted their mother to listen to the sutra.
Their mother said to her sons, "Your father believes in and accepts non-Buddhist paths; he is deeply attached to the Brahmanical dharma. The two sons replied: "We..."
"These sons of the Dharma King were born into a family of false views; for their sake, I manifested various supernatural transformations before their father.
Upon seeing them, the father rejoiced, left the household life, and practiced the Way. At that time, King Wondrous Adornment addressed the Buddha, saying: "These are my two sons."
"By means of supernatural transformations, they turned away my perverse mind and established me within the Buddha-dharma; these are my spiritual friends (kalyāṇamitra).
The Buddha said: 'It is so. Spiritual friends are a great causal condition, for they transform and guide one so that one may come to see the Buddha.'"
He resolved his mind upon Bodhicitta. As for Ajātaśatru, this is translated as "Unborn Enemy.
Because he was born before [his father] had been born, physiognomists predicted that once this child was born, he would certainly harm his father. The *Amitābha Sūtra* states:
"In the royal city, there was a crown prince named Ajātaśatru. Following the teachings of his evil friend Devadatta, he arrested his father, King Bimbisāra."
Next, he grasped a sharp sword, intending to kill his mother. At that time, the minister Candraprabha and Jīvaka addressed him, saying:
"Since the beginning of the eon, there have been eighteen thousand wicked kings who, out of greed for the royal throne, have murdered their own fathers."
"I have never heard of one who lacks the Way harming his own mother; yet the King has now done so. Your servant cannot bear to hear this. We ought no longer to remain here.
King Ajātaśatru was struck with terror and, repenting, sought deliverance. He immediately cast away his sword and issued a decree to confine himself within the inner palace.
The *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* states: "For all sentient beings to attain Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, there is no [other] proximate cause and condition..."

First is the virtuous friend. Why is this? If King Ajātaśatru had not followed the words of Jīvaka, he would have certainly met his end on the seventh day of the coming month and fallen into the Avīci Hell. Therefore, as for proximate causes, none can compare with a virtuous friend.
The *Puchao jing* (Sutra on Universally Transcending) states that King Ajātaśatru, having repented before Mañjuśrī, attained the patience of compliance (*anulomikī-kṣānti*).
He then realized that among those one associates with, the good bring about blessings while the evil bring about transgression; thus, gain and loss depend upon whom one draws near.
Should not those who seek friends be cautious? Yet, in order to discern them, as Confucius said: "Examine what they do, observe their conduct..."
By examining what brings one peace, it becomes difficult to conceal that there are three types of friends who increase one's virtue and three types of friends who diminish it.
