Although it is difficult to inspire faith even when encountering those of the lower three [vehicles], there are four kinds of faith. As the *Śraddhābala* (The Power of Faith) states:

first, faith in *tathatā* (suchness), which is the root of all dharmas; second, faith in the Buddha, who possesses immeasurable virtues; third, faith in the Dharma, which provides great benefit; and fourth...

Those who have faith in the Sangha and are able to practice correctly for their own benefit and the benefit of others may attain the lower [stages]. The four types of generating the aspiration for enlightenment are difficult to achieve.

Those who do not believe in cause and effect are called the group of the wrongly fixed (*mithyātva-niyata-rāśi*). Those who are determined not to regress are called the group of the rightly fixed (*samyaktva-niyata-rāśi*).
Those who seek the great fruit but whose minds are undecided—neither advancing nor regressing like a hair in the air—are called the group of the undetermined (*aniyata-rāśi*).

This present state is the stage of right concentration (*samyak-samādhi*), characterized by the severance of doubt and deep faith. As for the three minds: first, the straightforward mind (*ṛju-citta*), because it correctly contemplates the dharma of *tathatā* (suchness);

second, the profound mind (*gambhīra-citta*), because it delights in accumulating all virtuous practices; third, the compassionate mind (*karuṇā-citta*), because it desires to uproot the suffering of sentient beings.
As for the four vows: first, the vow to deliver sentient beings; second, the vow to sever afflictions (*kleśa*); third, the vow to study the Dharma.
The gates are four: the vow to attain the Buddha-way. The practices are five: first, the gate of giving; second, the gate of maintaining precepts;

third, the gate of patience; fourth, the gate of diligence; fifth, the gate of cessation and contemplation (*śamatha-vipaśyanā*). The two fruits are: first, transforming afflictions into the fruit of bodhi;
second, transforming birth-and-death into the fruit of nirvāṇa. However, from here below, [the text] next proceeds to demonstrate [otherwise].

Third, it is difficult to encourage [others] to develop [the aspiration]. First, the scriptural evidence is cited: the ocean waters belong to the dragons (*nāga*), who are subsumed within the realm of animals (*tiryagyoni*);
the kalpa-fire belongs to the heavens, specifically the fire-calamity of the first dhyāna. Those born in the long-lived heavens of the second dhyāna and above are not reached by the fire;

they are able to hear [the teaching] here. Within the realms of humans and devas, this already includes those from the Northern Continent (*Uttarakuru*) who possess intelligence, and it does not exclude those with impaired faculties, such as the deaf.
Those who see with their eyes and those who are blind hear with their ears; within the assembly of the Buddha, gods and ghosts are able to listen, and even those in the hells receive his light.
Those capable of receiving it will surely hear it; how could there be any difficulty regarding whether one meets the Buddha before or after [his parinirvāṇa]?

Thus, Qingliang said: "Seeing and hearing serve as the seeds; those who transcend the eight difficulties [of rebirth] surpass the stages of the ten bhūmis. His subsequent verse says: "Those who harbor doubts and do not believe shall never attain..."
Hearing this teaching, one realizes that although five hundred million people in Śrāvastī lived together with the Buddha, they did not see him;

thus, what was not difficult to achieve has become difficult. How much more so for those below this level! Next, to clarify this, among the eight difficulties (*aṣṭāvakṣaṇa*), the three miserable realms constitute three.
That we have each obtained a human body and escaped these three difficulties is itself a triple blessing. Among humans...

Fourth, the perfection of physical marks; being free from physical infirmities; being born in a central land; being free from the northern continent (Uttarakuru); having a counterpart [to practice with]; being free from the periods before or after a Buddha’s appearance;
and having a virtuous friend while being free from families with wrong views—these constitute seven personal celebrations. Being born in the heavens is the sole [circumstance] for that.

Giving rise to faith, aspiration, and so forth, one is freed from the difficulty of long life—this is the eighth personal celebration. Relying on this present sutra, one is freed from ten difficulties—this constitutes the tenth personal celebration. Thus one celebrates.
Since matters are of many kinds, how can one return [to the world] without transcending the sea of birth and death and advance toward the city of Nirvana?

"One should know" and below provide the threefold summary for clarification; this may be understood. △ Third, showing the wondrousness of relying on the teachings, in three parts: first, attaining the Way by following the precepts.
The Buddha said: "O Son of the Buddha, even if you are thousands of li away from me, if you keep my precepts in mind, you will surely attain the fruits of the Way.
Yet, though you may stay by my side and see me constantly, if you do not comply with my precepts, you will ultimately never attain the Way."

[Commentary: Those who study the Buddha-way are called "sons of the Buddha. However, this occurs within the context of initial awakening (*ādikṣaya*). The *Bao'en jing* (Sutra on Requiting Kindness) states:

"There are three grades of precepts: the five precepts are the lower grade; the ten precepts are the middle grade; and the complete precepts (*saṃvara*) are the upper grade. Furthermore, another sutra says:
Precepts are like level ground, from which all myriad virtues arise. Precepts are like a skilled physician, able to cure all ailments. Precepts are like a bright jewel, able to dispel darkness.
Precepts are like a boat or raft, able to ferry one across the sea of suffering. Precepts are like a necklace, adorning the Dharma-body. The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states:
"Those who break the precepts fall into the three evil realms; those who maintain them in an inferior degree are born [in the heavens]."

Among humans, those who maintain the precepts of middling grade are reborn in the heavens of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*). Those who concurrently practice the four dhyānas and eight samādhis are reborn in the heavens of the form realm (*rūpadhātu*) and the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*).
There are three grades of maintaining the precepts: through the purity of lower-grade observance, one attains the fruit of an arhat;
through the purity of middle-grade observance, one attains the state of a pratyekabuddha; and through the purity of upper-grade observance, one attains the fruit of the Buddha-way.
Therefore, if one recollects the precepts even from a thousand *li* away, it is as if one is always in the presence of the Buddha and will swiftly achieve the Way.

Even if one were to let the five faculties run wild among the five desires, if the mind and thoughts discriminate between various evils, unrighteousness, and the lack of merit, no wholesome virtues can arise.
It is like a vicious horse without a bridle, a mad elephant without a hook, or a monkey that has found a tree, leaping and bounding about.

To trample upon another's crops is to lose one's own wholesome deeds. Thus, even if one stands at the Buddha’s side, if the mind of preceptual discipline is not complete, one has no affinity with the Buddha;
this may be called being ten thousand *li* away from his presence before the steps. The case of the two bhikṣus in the kingdom of Polāśī is sufficient evidence for this.
Whether one sees [the Buddha] or not depends solely on the single vessel of the precepts. It is just like this.

"Why not uphold it? [Commentary] "The Buddha-sons... below means that upholding it brings benefit. "In my... below means that violating it causes harm. "Among those with initial awakening" refers to those at the stage of *ādikṣānti*.

The Buddha is awakening (*bodhi*). An ordinary person bound by all fetters is called a "Buddha-son of original awakening" (*mūlabodhi-buddhaputra*). One who has resolved to practice is called a "Buddha-son of initial awakening" (*ādikṣānti-bodhi-buddhaputra*).
Furthermore, there are three stages: first, one who understands the names and meanings of the Dharma-gates is called a "Buddha-son of nominal awakening" (*nāma-mātra-bodhi-buddhaputra*);

next, one who accords with contemplative practice is called a "Buddha-son of semblance awakening" (*pratirūpa-bodhi-buddhaputra*); finally, one who attains partial realization of the Dharmakāya is called a "Buddha-son of conforming [awakening]. (*anupūrva-bodhi-buddhaputra*)
The Bodhisattvas who have attained partial awakening are those who are just reaching the end of wondrous awakening; they are called Bodhisattvas of ultimate awakening.

In this sutra, the names are not used in their conventional order. By recollecting the precepts, one attains the Way, which encompasses both initial awakening and ultimate awakening. Even if one were to let [the practice] lapse below...
The *Śāsanāpadeśa* (The Bequeathed Teaching) says: "You all should abide in the precepts and restrain the five sense faculties, lest they become heedless and enter into the five desires.
It is like a cowherd who holds his staff and watches over them, not allowing them to run wild and trample the crops.
If you let the five faculties run wild, it will not be merely the five desires; they will become boundless and impossible to control. The two lines concerning "all virtues" refer to that sutra.
It is further said: "One should maintain pure precepts without allowing them to be violated or deficient; only then can wholesome dharmas arise.

If one lacks pure precepts, no meritorious virtues will be able to be produced. Regarding the matter of the two bhikṣus, the *Za jing yao ji* (Compendium of Essential Passages from Various Sutras) states:
In the kingdom of Pāṭaliputra, there were two bhikṣus who came to Śrāvastī to inquire after the World-Honored One’s health. On the way, they became exhausted with thirst and came upon a well.
One bhikṣu drew water and drank it immediately; the other bhikṣu examined the water and, seeing insects in it, did not drink.
He asked, "Why do you not drink? He replied, "The World-Honored One has established a precept that we must not drink water containing living beings."
"Water. He further exhorted him, saying, "Drink only water; do not let yourself die of thirst so that you fail to see the Buddha.
He replied, "I would rather lose my life than violate the Buddha’s precepts. Thereupon he died of thirst. The bhikṣu who had drunk the water went to where the Buddha was.
The Buddha, knowing this, asked him, "From where have you come? Did you have companions? He replied, "I came from Pāṭaliputra..."
They came from the kingdom of Sthūla, traveling together as companions. On the road, they were exhausted by thirst; the well water was infested with insects.

Because I drank the water, I was able to see the World-Honored One. He, however, strictly observed the precepts and died of thirst without drinking. The Buddha said: "You think that you have seen me, but in truth you have not seen me.
That deceased bhikṣu had already seen me before. If there is a bhikṣu who is negligent and indolent..."
Laxity. One who does not restrain the sense faculties, though dwelling together with me, is far from me; I do not see them.
If there is a bhikṣu on the other shore of the ocean who is able to be heedful, diligent and untiring, and who restrains his sense faculties, though he is far from me, I always see him;
he is always near to me. "The Single Vessel of Precepts" (Ekasīlaghaṭa), from the *Saṃyukta-avadāna-sūtra*.
It is said: "For one who upholds the precepts, there is nothing that cannot be attained; for one who breaks the precepts, everything is lost.
It is like a poor man who begs in the four directions for twelve years, never ceasing his devotion to Heaven and constantly making offerings while praying for wealth and nobility.
When his sincerity reached Heaven, Heaven took pity on him and asked what he sought. He replied that he sought wealth and nobility."
A deity granted him a vessel called the "Vase of Merit" (*guṇakalaśa*). Whatever he desired would emerge from the vase.
A guest asked him, "How have you suddenly become so wealthy? He replied, "I obtained a divine vase. The guest borrowed the vase to look at it; the man became arrogant and dissolute.
If one's grasp is not firm, the vessel will break from a slip of hand, and all things within will perish simultaneously. This serves as an analogy for those who uphold the precepts:
there is no wish that cannot be fulfilled. However, for one who violates the precepts, the vessel breaks and the contents are lost.

Thus, we know that the precepts are the foremost dwelling place of the merit of peace and security, and the very foundation for correctly following the path to liberation. II. Knowing Life and Realizing the Way.
The Buddha asked a śramaṇa, "In how much time does a person's life reside? He replied, "For several days. The Buddha said, "You do not yet know the Way.
He then asked another śramaṇa, "In how much time does a person's life reside? He replied, "For the duration of a meal. The Buddha said, "You do not yet know the Way.
He then asked another śramaṇa, "In how much time does a person's life reside? He replied, "In the interval between an inhalation and an exhalation. The Buddha said, "Excellent!"
"You understand this, my son. [Commentary]:

The three factors of warmth (*ūṣman*), breath (*āśvāsa-praśvāsa*), and consciousness (*vijñāna*) maintain one another; the uninterrupted continuity of the retribution of a single lifetime is termed "life" (*jīvita*).

This is provisionally established based upon the seeds of the eighth consciousness. Therefore, one knows that human life is impermanent: one cannot guarantee that the next breath will follow the outgoing breath.

If a single breath does not return, one is as good as reduced to dust and earth; yet to say that this occurs within the span of a few days or between meals is to be said to be ignorant of the principle of the impermanence of human life and the doctrine of momentary arising and ceasing. How could such a person be worthy of discussing the Way?

As for King Bimbisāra, he observed that every thought-moment (kṣaṇa) shifts and passes away, and that everything is ever-new and never remains still. This is no different from what the present śramaṇa... [observes].
"Life is as precarious as a breath between the gates"—upon hearing this, one can immediately know that they have understood the way of birth and death.

It goes without saying that one must not let the time slip away, but should instead cultivate with courageous diligence. If this is indeed the case, yet you still claim that it is merely praising their goodness in an exaggerated manner—is that truly so?
[Commentary]: "Warmth" refers to form (*rūpa*); "consciousness" (*vijñāna*) refers to the mind (*citta*). Question: What is the life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*)? Answer:

Based upon the eighth consciousness as projected by karma, the life-faculty is provisionally established as the functional capacity that maintains the continuity of form and mind without interruption. Furthermore, a sutra states:
"Vitality (*āyus*), warmth, and consciousness—these three are called 'life'. The commentary explains: this refers to the form within the objective aspect (*nimittabhāga*) of the *ālayavijñāna*.

The dharma is called "warmth" (*uṣmagata*). The seeds of this consciousness are called "life-force" (*āyus*). The actual manifestation (*pravṛtti*) of this consciousness is called "consciousness" (*vijñāna*).

As the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* states: "However, based on the seeds that directly produce this consciousness, its duration is determined by the specific functional capacity (*śaktiviśeṣa*) induced by karma."
"Provisionally established as the life-faculty (jīvitendriya). The commentary explains: This refers to the seeds of the eighth consciousness that produce [the body] directly.

These seeds are induced by prior wholesome (such as releasing living beings) or unwholesome (such as killing) karma, and possess the functional capacity to determine the duration for which the body is maintained.
They cause the physical and mental aggregates to abide for a period determined by the length of their respective causes. It is based on these seeds that [the life-faculty] is spoken of.

It serves as the life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*). Because this seed functions as the power of karma, there is a specific capacity to maintain the body of a single retribution (*eka-vipāka*), which brings about certainty.
If this seed lacked this capacity, the body would immediately decay and perish. "For how long? means for a certain duration of time.
Regarding "arising and ceasing moment by moment" (*kṣaṇika-utpāda-nirodha*), the *Renwang jing* (Benevolent Kings Sūtra) states: "Within a single thought-moment (*citta-kṣaṇa*) of sentient beings..."
There are ninety *kṣaṇas* [in a single thought-moment], and within one *kṣaṇa*, nine hundred births and cessations occur.
Regarding the King Anala: King Anala of Laṅkā replied, "The subtle shifting of transformations I truly do not perceive;

yet when I contemplate and observe with deep reflection, from moment to moment, from thought to thought, there is no staying still. As stated below in the *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra*: "That which is born at the very first..."
There is cessation. This was not taught for the sake of the ignorant. Now this śramaṇa has realized that all conditioned phenomena are impermanent, like the breath.
In a single word, he suddenly attained accord with the Buddha’s mind. If one does not praise his goodness, whom then would one praise?
△ Third, the verification of the Way through the sūtras.
The Buddha said: "Those who study the Way of the Buddha should believe and comply with all that the Buddha has spoken. It is like eating honey;
it is sweet both in the center and at the edges. My sūtras are likewise; their meaning is entirely refreshing, and the practitioner thereby attains the Way."

[Commentary] Regarding the first section on the Dharma: the first phrase refers to the person; the following two phrases refer to the Dharma. There are four aspects of the Dharma: teaching, practice, principle, and fruit.

"Speech" refers to the teaching, which includes the meditations and precepts of humans and devas; the truths and conditions of the Two Vehicles; the five stages and one hundred dharmas of the categorized teachings of the Mahāyāna;
the eighty-one sections of the Initial Teaching; the one mind and two gates of the Final Teaching; and the Sudden Teaching of the One Vehicle.
The forty-one gates. The ten inexhaustible gates of the Perfect Teaching (Yuanjiao). As for the student, this refers to practice; that is, practicing contemplation based on phenomena:

the contemplation of suffering and emptiness, the contemplation of dharmic characteristics, the contemplation of true emptiness, the contemplation of the storehouse mind, the contemplation of true nature, and the contemplation of the dharma-realm. One must have faith and compliance.
This is the Principle (*li*). Since the Teaching elucidates the Principle, it refers to: the True Suchness of the emptiness of self; the True Suchness of the emptiness of phenomena (*dharma*);

the True Suchness that is not empty in terms of verbal expression; the True Suchness of the absence of nature beyond verbal expression; and the True Suchness of the universal characteristic of the single Dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*).

This is the Buddha-way, which is the Fruit. Because the Buddha has realized the Way, it includes the fruits of the bliss of humans and devas, as well as those of the Arhats, Pratyekabuddhas, and the stages of the Three Sages and Ten Grounds.

The two wondrous awakenings are explained extensively in the *Jiaozhang* (Treatise on the Teachings). Regarding the analogy below: next is the metaphor. Food represents practice; sweetness represents the fruit; flowers represent principle (*li*); honey represents the teaching;
the periphery represents the minor teachings of humans and devas; the center represents the sudden and perfect [teachings]; and being neither peripheral nor central represents the beginning and end.
That "all food is sweet" refers to the vertical sequence of attaining happiness and leaving suffering, transcending the mundane and entering the supramundane.
O Sage, [the teachings] turn the small toward the great; from beginning to end, they accord with the gradual to return to the sudden, and transform the partial to become the perfect.
Thus, the five vehicles of the Dharma are all for the benefit of sentient capacities. Although the small and the great differ, they ultimately must return to the perfect. Why is this?
Because all abide in the nature, because they possess the diamond-seed, because they practice expedient means, and because the perfect is the ultimate. As the Lotus Sūtra says: "Seeking..."

Regarding those who are śrāvakas, those who seek the path of a pratyekabuddha, and those who seek the bodhisattva path—one must not cause them distress or lead them to doubt and regret by saying to them:
"You are very far from the Way; you will never be able to attain all-knowledge (sarvākārajñatā).
Therefore, burning incense, scattering flowers, joining the palms, and bowing the head are all causes for the Buddha-way. Even if...
Speaking from the perspective of perfect interfusion (*yuanrong*), dharmas have no distinction of great or small; rather, "great" and "small" reside in the capacity of the practitioner (*ji*).

Thus, one knows that within every gate there are the five teachings (*wu jiao*), and within every matter there are the three vehicles (*san sheng*); these are likewise clarified within the ritual protocols of the teachings and the benefits accorded to the capacities of practitioners.

Therefore, the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* says: "The nature of the sages is such that nothing is not penetrated; whether following or reversing [the path], all are skillful means (*upāya*). There are many gates to these skillful means, yet the nature of returning to the source is non-dual. The *Lotus Sūtra* says:
All the teachings spoken accord with their intended meaning and do not contradict the true nature of reality (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*).
Even when speaking of worldly scriptures, secular discourse, or the means of livelihood, all are in accordance with the True Dharma. As the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* states:

"Those of inferior wisdom who contemplate the conditions of the truths attain the enlightenment of a śrāvaka; those of middling wisdom who contemplate the conditions of the truths attain [the enlightenment of] a pratyekabuddha..."
*Bodhi*. Those of superior wisdom who contemplate the conditions of the Truths attain the *Buddha-bodhi*. "My Sūtra" refers to the sequence below:
first the *Sūtra* (the teaching), then the *Artha* (the principle), then the *Caryā* (the practice), and finally the *Mārga* (the fruit). How is it attained so swiftly?

It is because of the *Kṣipra-prāpti* (rapid attainment) through the *Śrāvaka-yāna* and *Pratyekabuddha-yāna*, the *Āgama*, the Initial Teaching of the *Saṃdhinirmocana* and *Prajñāpāramitā*, the Final Teaching of the *Suvarṇaprabhāsa* and *Mahāparinirvāṇa*, and the Sudden Teaching.

The *Laṅkāvatāra* and the *Awakening of Faith*—being "perfect" (*yuan*)—are like the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* and the *Avataṃsaka*, all of which flow forth from True Suchness (*tathatā*). The *Liang* commentary on the *Mahāyānasaṃparigraha-śāstra* states:

"True Suchness flows forth as the twelve divisions of the teaching. The *Mahāyānasaṃparigraha-śāstra* itself says: "There is nothing that does not flow from this Dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*). The *Renwang jing* states:
"The Wheel of Dharma (*dharmacakra*) means that the Dharma is fundamentally suchness; the verses are suchness; and so on, up to the treatises being suchness. Since these are one...
All are thus. How could there be anything that does not provide benefit?

[Commentary] "People" refers to students. "Dharmas" refers to what was spoken by the Buddha: the *Śata-dharma-prakāśamukha-śāstra*, the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi-śāstra*, and the *Aṣṭasāhasrikā-prajñāpāramitā-sūtra*.

The two gates: the *Awakening of Faith* has forty; the *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra* has ten gates. The *Avataṃsaka* clarifies the practice of phenomena (*vastu-caryā*), which refers to the contemplation of the six practices.

Because one feels weary of the suffering, coarseness, and hindrances of the lower realms, and rejoices in the purity, subtlety, and transcendence of the higher realms, this belongs to the practices of humans and devas.

The five kinds of true thusness (*tathatā*) appear in the *Awakening of Faith*. The "subtle" [stage] of the three worthies and others subsumes the remaining four teachings; the *Teaching Chapter* points to these five teachings.
[The] Rituals [and] the *Ji yi cheng jiao yi zhang* (Chapter on the Meaning of the One Vehicle Teachings), etc. Regarding those who abide in the nature: all sentient beings possess Buddha-nature;
because those with Buddha-nature will inevitably become Buddhas, as stated in the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* and the *Awakening of Faith*. Regarding those of the adamantine lineage (*vajra-gotra*):
the "Manifestation" chapter of the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* says, "Just as when a person eats a small amount of adamant, it is never digested, but must pass through..."

That body emerges into the external world; having planted even a small root of goodness under the Tathāgata, it must pierce through the entire body of afflictions (*kleśa*) and reach the state of ultimate unconditioned wisdom (*asaṃskṛta-jñāna*). Regarding the skillful means (*upāya*), the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* states:

"All Tathāgatas, by means of immeasurable skillful means, deliver all sentient beings and cause them to enter the Tathāgata’s untainted wisdom (*anāsrava-jñāna*). No [other teaching] is superior to this.
Although various Dharma-gates are enumerated, their reality is but the One Vehicle (*ekayāna*). None of the assembly of śrāvakas have attained final nirvāṇa;
the path you practice is the Bodhisattva path. Through the power of skillful means (*upāya*), the Buddhas distinguish and teach the three vehicles, yet there is only the One Buddha Vehicle.
Because it is a place of rest, two [vehicles] are taught; once they know this to be a place of rest, they are led into the Buddha-wisdom. It is perfected.
Regarding "the ultimate": The *Qingliang shu* states that bodhisattvas of the provisional teachings do not receive the Perfect Dharma;

it is only later, through the influence of cultivation (*vāsanā*), that they come to believe in its perfect fusion. This is because, apart from this universal Dharma, there is nowhere else to which they can turn, and because the fruits of the provisional teachings lack substantial reality.

The *Chao* states: "Regarding the causes and effects of the five teachings, only the Perfect Teaching possesses substantial reality; while the preceding four [teachings] possess it within their causes."
All results are ultimately non-existent because they arise from the cultivation of provisional causes; once one enters the stages (*bhūmi*), one immediately enters the reality (*tattva*).
This is like the myriad rivers that flow for thousands of li in vast expanse, yet have no ultimate place of return, for their ultimate place of return is the ocean itself.
The two lines concerning the burning of incense are explained in detail at the end of the first fascicle of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*.

Regarding the "benefiting sentient beings according to their capacities" (*jìjí yìzhě*), this refers to the fourth section, "The Gate of Gathering and Benefiting According to Capacities," within the *Wǔjiào Yí* (Rituals of the Five Teachings), where it is extensively elucidated.

The *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* and the *Nirvāṇa-sūtra* cite evidence from the teachings for humans and devas (*réntiān xiǎojiào*), yet they also apply to the other four teachings; likewise, the other four teachings also apply to the three [lower] vehicles.

The five natures of the faculties can be understood by analogy with this. The tenth commentary in the *Liang-lun* (Treatise of Liang) states: "By taking True Suchness (*tathatā*) as an object, non-conceptual wisdom (*nirvikalpa-jñāna*) arises;

from this wisdom flows forth subsequently attained wisdom (*prsthalabdha-jñāna*), and the great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*) produced by that subsequently attained wisdom preaches the twelve divisions of the scriptures to rescue and deliver sentient beings.
The *Wu-xing lun* (Treatise on the Five Natures) says: "That which flows from True Suchness [is the twelve...]"
"Divided teachings. The phrase "up to and including" (*yāvat*) refers to an abbreviated enumeration. To state them in full:

the *dharmatā-sūtra*, the *geya-sūtra*, the *vyākaraṇa-sūtra*, the *gāthā-sūtra*, the *udāna-sūtra*, the *śīla-sūtra*, the *avadāna-sūtra*, the *nidāna-sūtra*, the *itivṛttaka-sūtra*, the *vaipulya-sūtra*, the *adbhutadharma-sūtra*, and the *upadeśa-sūtra*. Regarding these, the commentary states: as for the *śīla-sūtra*...

The *Nidāna-sūtra* (Scripture on Causes and Conditions) refers to those scriptures where precepts were established based on specific events; this is because "cause" (*nidāna*) signifies the sense of a causal basis.

The *Dharmadhātu* (Dharma-realm) refers to the *Jātaka-sūtra* (Birth Stories); this is because "realm" (*dhātu*) signifies the sense of a cause. The term "and so forth" (*ādi*) points to other sūtras and treatises. As the *Vajrasamādhi* states:

"What I have spoken is in terms of meaning, not in terms of literary phrasing. And as the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* states: "The teaching that flows from True Suchness (*tathatā*) is the most supreme among all other teachings."

The commentary on that [text] states: Because within the third stage one attains the illumination of the Mahāyāna Dharma through the three types of wisdom, observing this Dharma-teaching and fundamental true suchness (tathatā) is called "the true suchness of the superior outflow" (*viśeṣa-niṣyanda-tathatā*). "Since all [inferior teachings]" refers to all the sacred teachings of the noble ones.
All flow from True Suchness (*tathatā*); thus, there is nothing that is not suchness, nor anything that is not the teaching.

Among sentient beings who hear, contemplate, and cultivate [the Dharma], there are none who do not return to this Dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*) and become encompassed by True Suchness. This is precisely the meaning of what is called "making vessels out of gold": every vessel is gold.
△ Fourth, manifesting the excellence of being in accordance with principle, part two. The first section concludes: severing the root of craving suddenly.
He attained the path of enlightenment.
The Buddha said, "A śramaṇa practicing the Way should gradually uproot the roots of craving and desire. It is like one who plucks hanging beads:
by plucking them one by one, they will eventually be exhausted. When evil is exhausted, one naturally attains the Way."

[Commentary]: This is the first section on the Dharma. The "Path" (mārga) is the principle of True Suchness (tathatā) by virtue of its nature; this transformation of others is called "practicing the Path.
"Craving" (tṛṣṇā) refers to the delusions of affliction (kleśa), and "desire" (kāma) refers to the karma of birth and death; both are false. Among the ten root afflictions, craving comes first;
among the seeds of the ten unwholesome karmas, sexual desire begins them. Therefore, they are called "roots. Realizing the Truth depends upon severing these delusions.
To sever delusions, one must remove their very roots. If the roots of grass are not uprooted, they will sprout again when spring arrives.

As for the term "gradual," the principle is sudden awakening, whereby through awakening everything is simultaneously eliminated; yet phenomena are not suddenly removed, as they are exhausted only through a sequential process.

The analogy that follows is the second metaphor. "Hanging pearls" refers to a species of fruit tree; in Sanskrit it is called *akṣa*, and it is also translated as "stringing pearls. Its fruit is shaped like...
This is like the *akṣa* fruit of the Indian plum tree, which has three seeds on each branch; they must grow from the same stalk and are collectively called an *akṣa*-cluster.

This serves as a metaphor for the three paths of affliction (*kleśa*), karma (*karman*), and suffering (*duḥkha*), which are sequentially connected and simultaneously complete. Now, one must extinguish suffering, cease karma, and sever affliction.
It is like plucking the *kaṇṭaka* fruit: by plucking it away gradually, the fruit is exhausted of itself. "Evil phrases" refers to the subsequent conjunctions.
When the evils of craving and desire are exhausted, the principle of the *dharmatā* is revealed. How could one then fail to attain the fruit of the Way?
[Commentary]: "Hanging beads" refers to three beads sharing a single stem, like colored beads suspended [from a cord].
"Beads strung on a thread" refers to those connected in succession, like beads threaded on a string. The *Śūraṅgama-sūtra* states:

"All sentient beings, from time immemorial, have various inverted karmic seeds that arise spontaneously, like a cluster of *akṣa* fruits. Changshui’s sub-commentary notes: "*Akṣa*" is a Sanskrit term.
This is called "a thread threading beads. Master Ying said: *Akṣa* is the name of a tree; its fruit resembles the *motsu-shi* (myrobalan) seed.
It always grows in groups of three from a single stalk, much like the almonds here. Thus, they are like the three paths. Through beginningless ignorance, karmic seeds are perfumed;
karma inevitably brings forth its fruit, and as one seed produces another, the perfuming continues without interruption. It is like this.

A string passes through pearls; their sequential connection is called an *akṣa-puṭa*. As the Sūtra says: "All phenomena reside in the storehouse-consciousness (*ālayavijñāna*), and the storehouse likewise resides in them.
They mutually serve as the nature of effect, and also constantly serve as the nature of cause. Now, regarding the phrase "extinguishing suffering":

the existence of afflictions is the cause for the arising [of suffering], and extinction follows from the removal of suffering; therefore, it is called "successive extraction. Furthermore, the Śrāvaka knows suffering and abandons its origin.
For those of the Pratyekabuddha vehicle, the "aggregation" (of causes) is the primary gateway; for those of the Bodhisattva vehicle, the "path" is that which awakens them.

Thus, they extinguish the three paths, and there is no fixed priority or sequence among them. This should be contemplated according to the sutras. 2. With a direct mind, one contemplates the path and completely severs all sufferings.
The Buddha said: "One who practices the Way is like an ox carrying a heavy load through deep mud; exhausted, it dares not look left or right.
Only after emerging from the mire can it find rest. A śramaṇa should contemplate that sensual desire is even more treacherous than that mud."
"By maintaining a straightforward mind and recollecting the Way, one may escape suffering.

[Commentary] First, an analogy is presented: the ox represents the practitioner; the heavy load represents the Dharma; the mud represents worldly passions; the exhaustion represents cowardice and weakness;
the left and right represent adverse and favorable conditions; and the resting represents the two types of Nirvana. The ox and cart, burdened by weight, sink into the mud.
Therefore, one proceeds with single-mindedness and dares not be indolent. This is not like the "grinding ox," whose body follows the path while its mind does not follow the path.
"Śramaṇa" (below): Next is the correspondence of the dharma. The śramaṇa corresponds to the ox; practicing contemplation corresponds to walking.

A straightforward mind corresponds to proceeding along the Middle Way without looking left or right. Mindfulness of the Path corresponds to bearing the heavy load; being free from suffering corresponds to [the goal].
This is the place of rest. By dwelling in this transformed city of three hundred *yojanas*, one may escape the suffering of birth and death within the triple world.
Indeed, from the time a person is born until they grow old, from old age until illness, and from illness until death, their suffering is immeasurable.

Suffering gives rise to vexation; a vexed mind is itself a transgression. Thus, as birth and death do not cease, the suffering becomes even more difficult to describe. Such afflictions of suffering are all...
Because of sensual desire, one sinks into the mire of craving; this is indeed more grievous than that. The mind can practice the Path and emerge from the mire of the five desires;
it does not merely rest in the two forms of nirvana, but may also proceed directly to the place of jewels, where one sports in joy, sovereign and unimpeded.
Such a person is said to have completely escaped suffering.

[Commentary] "Practitioners" refers to those of the three vehicles within the provisional teachings. "Path-dharmas" refers to the [Four] Truths, the [Twelve] Links of Dependent Origination, the [Six] Pāramitās, and so forth.
To use "mud" as a metaphor: it represents the defilement of the five desires, which submerges and drowns the mind set on the Path. To use "the timid and weak" as a metaphor:
as the Sūtra says, "If sentient beings hear only of the Single Buddha Vehicle, they would not wish to see the Buddha, nor wish to draw near to him, and would instead think: 'The Buddha...'"

The Path is long and distant; only after enduring diligent toil for a long time can it be accomplished. On the left is a metaphor for the five desires as adverse conditions, because one seeks them but cannot obtain them.

On the right is a metaphor for the five desires as favorable conditions, because of the separation from those one loves. Regarding the two types of *nirvāṇa*, they are *sopadhiśeṣa* (with remainder) and *nirupadhiśeṣa* (without remainder).
The Sūtra says: "The Buddha, knowing that this mind was timid and inferior, employed the power of skillful means within it."

The Way is taught for the purpose of cessation; thus, two types of *nirvāṇa* are spoken of. Furthermore, it is said that the Tathāgata, knowing that their aspirations lie in inferior teachings and that they are deeply attached to the five desires, speaks of *nirvāṇa* for the sake of such people. If these individuals hear it, they immediately believe and accept it.
The "ox that grinds" is a metaphor for the two vehicles who seek quiescence; though they do not sink into the mud, they likewise do not advance. Therefore, it is said: "The mind..."

One does not practice the Way; one should know that a śramaṇa training in the Way must not be like a grinding ox. If the mind-practice of the Way is being carried out, what need is there for the bodily practice?
The "ox-cart" refers to those of the provisional teaching of the Three Vehicles who enter the Buddha-way gradually. Because they possess great compassion, they walk through deep mud;
because they possess great wisdom, they emerge and do not look back. They are not like sentient beings who are completely mired in the five desires.

Within the mud. Those who are submerged in the waters of craving and attachment: thus the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra* says, "Seeing the sentient beings of the six realms deeply attached to the five desires, like a yak cow cherishing its tail, they shroud themselves with craving and attachment;

they do not seek the Buddha of Great Power nor the Dharma that cuts off suffering. Regarding those who seek rest: the Sūtra says that for the sake of providing cessation and rest, he manifested a great city. Only humans...

[The character] "down" (*xià*) explains the character "profound" (*shèn*). It means that while the physical body of a person in this world is submerged for a single lifetime, the Dharma-body is about to be drowned for many kalpas.

Through this, one can infer the depth or shallowness, and the distance or proximity, of their suffering and affliction. When the mind is able to descend [into the depths], it further clarifies the meaning of "exemption.

Because the bodies and practices of the ignorant and the Two Vehicles do not accord with the mind, they merely stop at the "transformed city" (*huàchéng*) and extinguish the suffering of segmented existence (*fēnduàn kǔ*). This is called "partial exemption" (*fēnmiǎn*). Now, by means of skillful means...
He teaches those of the three vehicles so that they may practice the Way with both body and mind; thus, they proceed directly to the treasure-store to extinguish the suffering of change.
This is called "complete exemption. As the *Lotus Sūtra* says: "I originally made this vow: I wish to cause all beings to be no different from myself.
Now I speak the truth for you: what you have attained is not [mere] extinction. It is because it is a place of rest that two [vehicles] were taught. This refers to the stage of learning.
As for the Way of the Buddha, how could one possibly fail it? Third, the conclusion showing that both subject and object are like illusions:
The Buddha said, "I regard the rank of kings and lords as dust passing through a crevice; I regard treasures of gold and jade as tiles and pebbles."
One regards garments of fine silk as worn-out rags; one regards the great trichiliocosm as a single *kośāmbi* fruit; one regards the waters of Lake Anavatapta as oil for anointing the feet;
one regards the gates of skillful means as a heap of conjured jewels; one regards the Unsurpassed Vehicle as gold and silks in a dream;
one regards the Buddha-way as flowers before one's eyes; one regards meditative concentration as a pillar of Mount Sumeru; and one regards *nirvāṇa* as...

Awake day and night, one views the inverted as the upright, like the dance of the six dragons; one views all things with equanimity, like the ground of true reality; one views the flourishing of transformation, like the trees of the four seasons.
[Commentary] First, it is explained that all worldly phenomena are like dreams and illusions. There are five points. The first is "position" (*sthāna*).

"Dust in a crevice" refers to something light and minute; it appears to exist but is not real. Regarding the phrase "the royal position is like dust passing through a crevice," this means it passes away easily and does not endure.
Eighteen thousand years pass, yet the sovereign's power is suddenly withdrawn; seventy-two rulers pass by in the snap of a finger. Thus it is said: "Yang... [text fragment].
Sheng’an said: "Wealth and honor are but a dream upon a phoenix pillow; right and wrong are but the dust beneath a horse’s hooves for a thousand years.

Year after year, mountains remain and waters linger, yet one no longer sees those who sought to establish the great enterprises of kings and hegemonies. Regarding the second [verse], "Viewing Gold as Dung": when people die for the sake of wealth, it is because they regard it as precious.
If one views gold as mere rubble, one would not even look back at it while plowing through a field—even if it were gold. How much less so for other things?
Is it not like a man drifting in the current who receives his execution? As for the view that fine silk (*huán*) is inferior:

clothing made of three layers, brocade, embroidery, *zēng* and *hú* silks, and fresh white *luóqǐ*—these are what people desire. Now, one whose will is set upon the Way does not feel shame in wearing coarse garments;
even if the fine silk robes are added, they are no different from a padded garment of hemp. This is precisely the Kāśyapa of the Buddha’s gate and the Zhōngyóu of the Confucian gate. Observe...
The four worlds of the great chiliocosm, though vast and expansive, are no different from a small myrobalan fruit.

This is because that which is signless and unconditioned is "great," while that which has signs and is conditioned is "small. That which is the eternally abiding fundamental enlightenment is "great," while that which exists through delusion and falsehood is "small.
As the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* says: "If even the lands of a microdust were not without outflows, you should know that empty space itself was born from you."
Within the mind, it is like a single fragment of cloud appearing in the vast expanse of the Great Clarity; how much more so must all worlds exist within empty space?
If even one person among you gives rise to the true mind and returns to the source, this emptiness of the ten directions will entirely vanish and dissolve.
How could the lands not then tremble and split apart? Those who rely on houses, gardens, fields, and property for their livelihood should awaken to this! Behold!

Ānanda. Regarding the five rivers and oceans and Lake Anavatapta: the *Xiyu ji* (Records of the Western Regions) states that the center of Jambudvīpa is Lake Anavatapta, which in the language of Tang means "Free from Heat and Affliction. It is located south of Mount Gandhamādana and north of the Snowy Mountains.
Its banks are adorned with lapis lazuli and crystal. Golden sands spread across it, while silver ripples shine with pure clarity.

From the silver ox-mouth on the eastern side flows the Gaṅgā River; it circles the lake once and enters the southeastern ocean. From the golden elephant-mouth on the southern side flows the Sindhu River;
it circles the lake once and enters the southwestern ocean. On the western side is the lapis lazuli horse-mouth...
From the mouth [of the eastern lion], the Vakṣu River flows out, circles the lake once, and enters the northwestern ocean.
From the northern face of the Vaiḍūrya Lion, the Sītā River flows out, circles the lake once, and enters the northeastern ocean.
As for the statement that it is "like a small amount of oil applied to the feet," although the lake is deep and vast, it is like a mere drop. Why is this? Because all of these are illusory.
Transformation. Because it does not possess substantial reality. [Commentary]:

Regarding the "eighteen thousand," according to the *Jièwáng Jiǎzǐ Jì* (Record of the Sexagenary Cycle of Emperors), it states: "The Heavenly Sovereign (Tiānhuángshì) ruled for eighteen thousand years;
the Earthly Sovereign (Dìhuángshì) ruled for nine thousand years; the Human Sovereign (Rénhuángshì) ruled for four thousand five hundred years. There is...
The original text states: "The Three Sovereigns each ruled for eighteen thousand years. Regarding the 'royal qi' (wángqì):
during the time of the First Emperor of Qin, a diviner reported that there was royal qi in the southeast. Consequently, the Emperor traveled through the southeast to suppress it.
Upon reaching Jianye, he dredged the Qianhuai River and buried gold as a means of ritual suppression; thus, it was called Jinling. This continued until the era of the Six Dynasties."
The last ruler of the Chen dynasty indulged in extreme luxury and extravagance. Emperor Wen of the Sui dynasty ordered his generals to mobilize the army to invade him.

The Ruler of Chen said, "The royal mandate resides here; what can those fellows do? Fu Zai remonstrated, saying, "Your Majesty treats loyalty and integrity as enemies and views the common people as mere weeds.
The gods are incensed and the people resentful; the masses have rebelled and your kin have deserted you. I fear that [the capital] to the east—"

The southern king’s mandate was exhausted in an instant. Regarding the seventy-two rulers, the *Fengshan Shu* (Book on the Feng and Shan Sacrifices) by Sima Xiangru states that there were seventy-two rulers whose succession of ancestral lineages (*zhāomù*), posthumous titles (*shìhào*), and reigns can be roughly recounted.
Thus, the *Guǎnzǐ* says: "In the past, there were seventy-two houses that performed the Feng sacrifice on Mount Tai and the Shan sacrifice at Mount Liangfu. Liangfu is...
Mounta Tai Shan contains a smaller mountain named Yang Sheng-an. Regarding the first four lines [of the poem], it says:
"I recall the Eastern Zhou was annexed by Qin; turning my head, Chu and Han contended for the world. When the time came, torrential rain swept away the marshy waters;
when the momentum failed, a wild wind rolled up a fragment of cloud. There is also a lyric (ci) which says: "Recalling the events of a thousand years past, the traces of the Six Dynasties..."
How bewildering! The Sui and Tang dynasties succeeded one another in ruling the Central Plains; how many times have the conditions of the world shifted like clouds?
Thus we know that fame, achievement, wealth, and rank are but like lightning flashes or sparks from flint, or like awakening from a dream within the Yellow Millet Pot—what is there to smile about?
Alas! Those who contended like dragons and fought like tigers were in error. As for those who turned away from gold while hoeing, Guan Ning and Hua Xin were once together in the garden.
While hoeing vegetables, he saw a piece of gold on the ground. He swung his hoe as if it were no different from a tile or a stone, picked it up, and threw it away.
As for those who suffered execution because of this, the *Ṣaṭpāramitā-samuccaya-sūtra* states: "In the past, the Bodhisattva was a great householder with wealth amounting to billions.
He was compassionate toward all sentient beings. Seeing a turtle being sold in the market, he asked its price. The seller replied, 'One hundred thousand [pieces of gold].'"
"Sāyún, well done," he said. He took the turtle home and released it back into the water. During the latter part of the night, the turtle gnawed at his door and spoke, saying:

"There is no way to repay your kindness, but know that the waters will rise and fall; a great flood shall cause destruction. I pray that you quickly prepare a boat so that we may meet when the time comes.

The Bodhisattva informed the King, advising him to move from the lowlands to high ground. When the water arrived, the turtle came as well; they immediately hurried down from the boat and followed the turtle.
As they traveled, a snake approached the boat. The Bodhisattva said, "Take it. The turtle said, "Very well. A fox came along, and he took it as well;
the turtle approved of this too. Then he saw a man drifting by. The Bodhisattva said, "Take him. The turtle said, "Be careful not to take him! The Bodhisattva replied:
"If even insects are to be rescued, how could humans not be saved? Thereupon, he took them in. Later, the turtle took its leave, saying, "My debt of gratitude is now fulfilled;
I beg to depart. The fox and the snake followed in succession. Because the fox dwelt in a burrow, it discovered a hidden store of one hundred *jin* of gold.
It sought to repay the Bodhisattva for saving its life, saying, "You may share half with me. The Bodhisattva bestowed ten *jin* upon it. The man who had been adrift said, "Dig..."
"Why do you not divide the gold from the tomb equally? The Bodhisattva replied, "I wish to give it equally to other poor and destitute people;
you, however, wish to monopolize it for yourself—is this not partiality? The man adrift then reported this to the authorities, and the Bodhisattva was arrested.
Having no one to whom he could appeal, a snake then carried medicine in its mouth into the prison and presented it to the Bodhisattva, saying, "I shall bite the Prince."

The poison was incurable. The Bodhisattva informed the king of a medicine; upon applying it, [the king] was immediately healed. The snake was exactly as described, and the Crown Prince’s life was in peril.
The king issued a decree: "He who can save him shall be enfeoffed as Prime Minister. The Bodhisattva reported this to the king;

with a single application, [the king] was indeed healed. The king rejoiced and questioned him; he related the beginning and end of the matter. The king reproached himself, saying: "How extremely ignorant I am! He then enfeoffed [him].
He served as the Chancellor. He then executed the man who had drifted away. The one who settled the household was my Buddha;
the King was Maitreya; the turtle was Ānanda; the fox was Śāriputra; the snake was Maudgalyāyana; and the drifting man was Devadatta.

Now, his aspirations are set on the lower [stages]. Taking the Way as his heart, there is nothing he does not regard with equanimity; thus, he views precious garments and coarse cloth as no different.
As for Kāśyapa, because he wears robes of discarded rags (*pāṃśukūla*), he is the foremost among the Buddha’s disciples in the practice of *dhūta*.
Regarding Zhong You, the *Analects* of Lu says: "He wore a tattered inner robe of coarse wool, yet when standing alongside those wearing fox-fur and badger-skin robes, he felt no shame."
As for the reasons for this: it can be understood that since clothing is already provided according to custom, one does not seek excellence in food.
[Commentary] "Looking toward the directions" and below: next, it clarifies that all supramundane dharmas are like dreams and illusions. This also has five parts. First, skillful means:
the Buddha, through various causes, conditions, parables, and skillful means (*upāya-kauśalya*), expounds the various dharmas for the sake of sentient beings.
They cause [beings] to enter the Buddha-way, just as the wandering immortal (yóuxíngxiān) transforms stone into gold, or as Master Gěng fashions snow into silver.
To rescue and relieve the poor and destitute is to move their hearts. Regarding the "no lower" and the "two unsurpassed":

the former refers to the provisional teachings of the Three Vehicles, hence they are called "expedient means" (*upāya*). The present teaching is the true doctrine of the One Vehicle, hence it is called "unsurpassed. Since it is one...
Awaiting the three insights (*trividyā*), even the one does not exist. The real is established in contrast to the provisional; how could the real itself be "true"? Therefore it is said:

"Like gold and silk in a dream—once awakened, where is the gold? When the mind is empty, the teaching is also non-existent. Regarding the passage "viewing the Buddha," there follow the three paths of the Buddhas.
The deranged mind suddenly ceases; this cessation is itself *bodhi*. When *bodhi* is perfected, one returns to the state of non-attainment.

Thus, one knows that the fruit of wisdom is like a flower in the sky—it cannot be grasped. Regarding "viewing dhyāna" below: the four *dhyānas* constitute the practice of meditative concentration taught for those who are distracted.
With the single mind unmoving, what kind of meditative contemplation (*dhyāna-vipaśyanā*) is performed? It is therefore like a pillar supporting Mount Sumeru.
How could there be any reality? Look at the section on the five *nirvāṇas* below. When deluded, one is asleep in birth-and-death (*saṃsāra*); when awakened, one is awake in *nirvāṇa*.
If the sleep of birth-and-death were non-existent, the awakening of *nirvāṇa* would likewise be forgotten. Therefore it is said: "It is like waking from a dream after a long night. As the Sūtra says:
That which has contention is called saṃsāra; that which is without contention is called nirvāṇa. Both saṃsāra and nirvāṇa are ultimately unattainable.
[Commentary] Regarding the supramundane dharmas, there are also five: the first two are the teachings; the third is the fruit; the fourth is the practice; and the fifth is...
This is the principle. Regarding "First, the Expedient Means": because the Buddha manifests the wealth of the Dharma to relieve those in distress and urgency, the *Awakening of Faith* states:
"If there are sentient beings who come seeking the Dharma, one should preach it to them through expedient means according to what they can understand.
If one sees anyone coming to beg, one should give away all one's wealth and possessions according to one's ability. As for the "Wandering Immortal," [it is as stated in] the *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra*.
Yan said: "To be as firm and enduring as metal and stone without ceasing, and to bring the transformative Way to perfection, is called being a 'Wandering Immortal' (yóuxíng xiān).
The commentary states: 'Gathering soil and touching stones, transforming them into treasures and gold, one wanders among the people;

this is called 'wandering. Regarding Master Geng, the *Yìrén lù* says: 'Master Geng possessed the arts of the Way. During the Baotai era, he was summoned into the palace. [The text continues with his shaving...]
Snow becomes silver ingots; when cast into a blazing fire, it does not melt. Regarding those who are moved by the impulse to provide relief, the *Xiyu zhuan* (Records of the Western Regions) states:

"In the past, there was an immortal who could transform tiles and rubble into jewels and change the forms of humans and animals, yet he was unable to ride upon the winds and clouds to enter the celestial palaces.
Later, he obtained a method which required first constructing an altar and commanding a heroic man to hold [the ritual vessel].
The sword stood upright before him; he held his breath and ceased speaking from dusk until dawn.

The seeker of immortality sat upon the central altar, hand pressing a long blade, reciting divine mantras while withdrawing his gaze and reversing his hearing. At daybreak, he ascended to become an immortal.
Thereupon, he sought out a heroic man for many years without success. Later, he encountered him; the man had worked as a hired laborer for five years when, one day, he committed a transgression.
Having been whipped, he was unable to move; he wailed piteously as he wandered along the road. The Immortal ordered him to travel with him to a thatched hut.
By means of his supernatural powers, he transformed various delicacies into food and drink, led him into a pond to bathe, and dressed him in new clothes. He also gave him five hundred gold coins.

He instructed him, saying, "Seek this completely for the future; do not let it go to others. Thereafter, he repeatedly offered heavy bribes and secretly performed acts of hidden virtue, moving the man's heart with gratitude.
The knightly hero earnestly requested to risk his life to repay his benefactor. The immortal said, "I have no other designs;
I only wish that you remain silent for one night. The hero replied, "I would not decline even death; how could I suppress my breath?"
Thereupon, they acted according to the ritual. Yinxian recited divine mantras while the valiant man gripped his sharp blade.
As dawn was about to break, a sudden cry rang out. At that moment, fire descended from the void, and clouds of smoke and flames billowed upward.
Yinxian quickly led this man into the pond to seek refuge. Afterward, he asked him: "I warned you not to make a sound; why did you cry out so alarmingly? The valiant man—
The man said: "After receiving my command, when the night was deep, I fell into a state of profound stupor as if dreaming, and further transformations arose.
I saw my former master come in person to console and apologize to me; yet I remained silent and did not respond. The master became enraged and subsequently killed me.

Nevertheless, I vowed that throughout successive lifetimes I would never speak of it to repay his great kindness. Thus, I took birth into a wealthy and noble family, and upon emerging from the womb, I began my studies."
"At my capping ceremony, my wedding, the mourning for my parents, and the birth of my son, I have always kept in mind my former kindness.
I endured it all and did not speak out. When I reached the age of sixty, my wife said, 'You must speak now; if you do not, I shall kill your son.
Thinking of my own old age and that this was my only young child, I stopped her, saying, 'You must not harm him,' and thus I finally uttered these words. Yinxian said, "This..."
The demon tormented his ears. The knight, grateful for [the Buddha's] kindness, grieved that his mission was unfulfilled; he died in a fit of indignation and rage.

If one can inspire such a spirit of faith by guiding those who have not yet awakened, how could there be anyone who is not saved? (Three strokes. *Bodhi* is the Buddha’s path of awakening; it is the fruit of wisdom.
It is established in contrast to the afflictions (*kleśa*). Since the afflictions are fundamentally empty, how could *bodhi* exist?

The *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* states: "To speak of the false in order to manifest the various truths is for both the false and the true to be equally false. To speak of the existence of Bodhi is likewise like seeing flowers before one's eyes.
It is like someone supporting a pillar of Mount Sumeru: if Mount Sumeru were to collapse, then the pillar would indeed need to be supported;

but since the King of Mountains is firm and secure, what need is there for a pillar to support it? 'Awakening throughout day and night' means that within the cycle of days and nights, whether it be morning or evening, one is either asleep or awake."
If Buddhas, Bodhisattvas, the Form Realm, the Empty Heavens, and so forth, have neither sleep nor awakening, then one knows that awakening is established in dependence upon sleep;
how could awakening be real?

[Commentary] This section on "viewing the overturned" is followed by an explanation that worldly and world-transcending phenomena are like dreams and illusions, which consists of three parts. First is the contemplation of the truth.

Phenomena (*vastu*) are inverted because they arise and perish; principle (*tattva*) is correct because it is non-arising. The conventional (*saṃvṛti*) is inverted because it exists as a mental object (*sattva*);

the ultimate (*paramārtha*) is correct because its nature is non-existent. The conditioned (*saṃskṛta*) is inverted because it arises from conditions; the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) is correct because it lacks intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāva*).

Extremes (*anta*) are inverted because they are parikalpita (imagined); the middle (*madhya*) is correct because it is pariniṣpanna (perfected). Attachment (*yoga*) is inverted because it involves clinging; detachment (*viyoga*) is correct.
Because it is non-abiding; because the partial is biased and restricted to one side, while the round is correct and universally pervasive.

All are established through mutual opposition and possess no substantial reality. It is like the dance of six dragons: whether they soar upward or descend downward, how could there be any fixed determination of right or wrong?
To view them as level or descending is the second, the contemplation of the Two Truths. This is established in contrast to the unequal, just as in the case of "one."

The ground of reality (*tathatā*). Now, the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*) does not admit even a single speck of dust; how could there be such a "ground"? Since high and low do not exist, how can there be equality?

Regarding the phrase "viewing arising as low," this refers to the three conventional truths (*saṃvṛti-satya*): "arising" refers to the production of all phenomena (*dharma*), and "ceasing" refers to their transformation and extinction.
Through the conjunction of causes and conditions, there is illusory birth; through the separation of causes and conditions, there is illusory [extinction].
There is cessation. Birth, abiding, change, and cessation all evolve according to conditions; they possess no real nature. They are like flowering trees:
when spring arrives, they flourish; when winter comes, they wither and fall. All follow the seasonal climate and are not truly permanent. Therefore, the *Prajñāpāramitā* says:
"All conditioned phenomena are like a dream, an illusion, a bubble, and a shadow; they are like dew and like lightning. One should understand them in this way.
Contemplation.

[The *Chao*] states: "The contemplation of the Middle Truth" refers to the non-obstruction between phenomena and principle, and the mutual integration of the ultimate and the conventional; this is called the Truth of the Middle Way.

The simultaneous negation and illumination, and the non-duality of emptiness and existence, is called the Contemplation of the Middle Way. Regarding phenomena as the lower level, there are six divisions according to the teachings (*jiao*), the first being the Hinayana.

Next, regarding the classification [of teachings]: first, the School of Characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*); second, the Initial [School] of Emptiness; third, the Final [School] of Emptiness; fourth, the Sudden [School]; and fifth, the Perfect [School].

None of these possess fixed reality; thus, they are like the dance of the six dragons. How could there be any fixed ground? The *Avataṃsaka-sūtra* says: "The physical marks of Samantabhadra are like empty space."
Abiding in accordance with reality, one does not dwell in a land; therefore, it is said that on the ground of the principle of the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*), there is only the name of "ground.
As for the arising and ceasing of all phenomena: in the correct sense, the mind undergoes arising, abiding, change, and cessation, while the body undergoes birth, aging, sickness, and death.

If one relies on these conditions, the realms undergo formation, abiding, destruction, and emptiness; there are the seasons of spring, summer, autumn, and winter, all of which revolve according to conditions.
As the Sūtra says: "All phenomena arise from conditions, and likewise they cease from conditions. By analogy, their abiding and transformation are known to lack any real nature.
To contemplate arising is like a barren woman conceiving a child; to contemplate abiding is like the surging waves of a mirage.
To contemplate their difference is like observing the myriad transformations of drifting clouds; to contemplate their cessation is like watching mad blossoms wither away into the void.

As the *Mahāyāna-śraddhotpāda-śāstra* says: "The dharmas produced by causes and conditions—I declare them to be emptiness. And as the *Laṅkāvatāra-sūtra* says: "In reality, there is no arising from conditions."
Nor is there extinction through causes and conditions. Contemplate all conditioned phenomena as being like flowers in the sky:

they all follow the seasons—sprouting in spring, growing in summer, withering in autumn, and drying in winter—not by their own volition, but driven by the elemental forces. Thus it is said in the *Prajñāpāramitā*: [the text continues below].

This is to clarify [the meaning] by means of the Dharma. The *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra* also says: "Whether existent (referring to the realm of phenomena) or non-existent (referring to emptiness), the dharma of dependent origination is entirely without arising.
It revolves through the delusion of habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*). From this, the three realms of existence (desire, form, and formlessness; or being, non-being, and neither) manifest.
Thus, it follows that all dharmas, mundane and supramundane, are none other than like dreams and illusions. △ Third, the Section on Circulation.
The great bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha had spoken, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
[Commentary: If there were no one to transmit it, it would not circulate; if the transmission encountered obstacles, it would not pass through.

Now, the words of this text flow without stagnating and pass through without being blocked; therefore, it is called "circulation" (liútōng). The phrase "the bhikṣus" reiterates the mention of the assembly who listened.
Regarding the term "great" (*mahā*): it refers to turning from the Lesser Vehicle toward the Great Vehicle, for they are not of the nature of those who follow the Dharma of the ignorant.

"Upon hearing the Buddha... and so forth clarifies that they all comply with and practice [the teaching]. "Hearing" refers to the wisdom of hearing (*śrutamayī-prajñā*), because one is perfumed by the acceptance and faith [in the teaching].

"Rejoicing" refers to the wisdom of reflection (*cintāmayī-prajñā*), because one gives rise to understanding through celebrating the Dharma. Furthermore, one rejoices when the person who explains it is pure, and one delights when the Dharma being explained is pure.
The fruit realized is also pure; thus, one rejoices and is filled with joy while practicing and cultivating wisdom.

Because one upholds and transmits the teachings according to the instructions, the Dharma spoken by the Buddha accords with both principle and capacity; all who see or hear it will surely obtain benefit.
Not only do those in the ten directions rejoice in its practice in the present, but all sentient beings throughout the three periods of time—past, future, and present—are likewise filled with joy.
"Respectfully received.
[Commentary] "Without inferiority" below explains the title of the section. "The various" below interprets the scriptural text.

As for the repetition, at the beginning it clarifies his listening to the sutra, and at the end it clarifies his receiving of the teaching. Regarding "only the bhikṣu," this mentions one group to include the remaining three.

[The term] "the assembly" [refers to the bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, and upāsikās]. Therefore, from "upon hearing the teaching" onwards, the passage explains by way of the three types of wisdom (*trividya*) in a general sense.

Furthermore, from "and again" onwards, it explains "rejoicing" by way of three distinct meanings: moreover, "hearing the teaching" refers to the instruction (*śāsana*), "rejoicing" refers to the principle (*tattva*), and "practicing" refers to the fruit (*phala*).

Furthermore, the preceding phrase concerns self-benefit, while the subsequent phrase concerns the benefit of others. From "what the Buddha has taught" onwards, this section provides a specific explanation for the preceding part.

General Explanation: Thus, within these forty-two chapters, even a single chapter or a single phrase, according to one's inquiry, can serve as a seed for a proximate reward of rebirth among humans or devas, or the attainment of the Two Vehicles;
and in the distant future, it leads to the fruit of Buddhahood through the Three Vehicles.
How much more so for one who upholds this entire sutra—how can their merit possibly be fathomed?
